## Executive Summary
This budget narrative describes the roles and effort allocations for NASA Ames team members coordinating with Black Swift Technologies on a wildfire monitoring project. The project integrates UAS observations collected by BST with WRF-SFIRE modeling using NASA High Performance Computing resources to improve fire dynamics prediction and spread modeling.

## Technical Approach
- **Coordination & Data Integration**: Dr. Wang will coordinate collaboration between NASA Ames, Black Swift Technologies, and project teams to incorporate NASA Earth System Observation datasets and UAS data into the WRF-SFIRE modeling system
- **Modeling & Analysis**: Jeremy Benik will deploy and run WRF-SFIRE experiments on NASA's Pleiades HPC system using:
  - Reanalyzed meteorology data (GFS or ERA5)
  - Satellite products (land cover maps, surface temperature/moisture)
  - High-resolution UAS fire observations collected by the project
- **Validation & Feedback**: Team will assess the unique contribution of UAS observations in improving modeled fire dynamics and provide feedback to the measurement/collection team

## Products & Capabilities Described
**Black Swift Technologies UAS System**
- Provides high-resolution fire observations during field campaigns
- Data is integrated into WRF-SFIRE modeling for fire spread prediction
- Specific system name/model not mentioned in this document

## Use Cases & Applications
- Wildfire monitoring and fire dynamics prediction
- Integration of UAS observations with fire weather modeling
- Assessment of observational data impact on fire spread simulation

## Budget Details
**Personnel (3-year project):**
- Dr. Weile Wang: 0.6 person-months (0.05 FTE) per year × 3 years
- Jeremy Benik: 1.8 person-months (0.15 FTE) per year × 3 years

**Travel:**
- $2,000/year for wildfire science team meeting (Washington DC)

## Executive Summary
This proposal develops an integrated decision-making system combining UAS-based L-band soil moisture mapping with NASA satellite data (UAVSAR, NISAR) to provide near-real-time, high-resolution live fuel moisture (LFM) and soil moisture maps for wildfire management. The system will enable a single operator to fly up to 8 multirotor UAS simultaneously to cover 3,200 acres daily at 2m resolution, with broader coverage from satellite platforms, optimizing resource deployment for pre-fire situational awareness in California's wildfire-prone regions.

## Technical Approach

The proposal employs a multi-tiered, multi-platform approach:

### Platform Integration:
- **UAS Platform:** Quadrotor-based soil moisture mapping systems (slower flight speed at ~3m/s vs. fixed-wing at 18m/s enables longer integration time and better radiometer measurements through tree canopies; can fly at 15m altitude for 5m or better resolution)
- **Satellite Data:** P-band UAVSAR in Year 1; L-band NISAR satellite (6-day revisit) in Years 2-3
- **Swarm Operations:** Progression from 2 UAS (Year 1) → 4 UAS (Year 2) → 8 UAS (Year 3), all flown by single operator from ground station by Year 3

### Key Technical Objectives:

**Objective 1: Soil Moisture and Live Fuel Moisture Mapping**
- Develop algorithms to convert UAS-derived soil moisture anomaly maps to live fuel moisture (LFM) maps
- Build on prior pilot study (2021-2023) that demonstrated strong correlation between soil moisture and LFM across Chamise and other chaparral species at test site
- Deploy at highly instrumented 3,200-acre nature preserve with 40 active climate/soil stations measuring at 15-minute to hourly intervals to depths of 1m+ or bedrock
- Target: near-real-time, high-resolution maps integrated with current wildfire management systems

**Objective 2: Novel Sensor Platform**
- Miniaturize existing L-band radiometer sensor package for fixed-wing and multirotor UAS
- Develop autonomous flight planning with terrain-aware flight (terrain tracking and avoidance)
- Implement automated pre-flight checks and sensor setup
- Enable 8 UAS operation by single operator through improved autonomy and communications
- System must scale to cover 8 km² in one day at operational cost

**Objective 3: Onboard Soil Moisture Processing**
- Design new FPGA-based digital correlator for L-band radiometer with:
  - Real-time coherence matrix calculation
  - Better immunity to gain fluctuation
  - Self-calibration and real-time calibration capability
- Implement post-processing code onboard for real-time soil moisture calculation
- Enable self-checks on each aircraft (remove non-functioning sensors mid-mission)
- Support re-tasking capability based on live data

**Objective 4: Intelligence Tasking and Data Fusion**
- Use NISAR satellite soil moisture data (global, 6-daily) and UAVSAR (20×60 km coverage) to identify high-risk areas
- Develop algorithms to fuse multi-resolution data (2m UAS, 6m UAVSAR, 200m NISAR)
- Employ L-band forward models ("data cubes") with three axes: dielectric constant, surface roughness, vegetation water content (VWC)
- Implement least-squares soil moisture retrieval algorithm developed for SMAP SAR, extended to P-band (UAVSAR) and L-band (NISAR)
- Direct UAS swarm to priority coverage areas based on satellite data

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Soil Moisture Mapping UAS
- **Fixed-wing version:** Higher altitude operation; 18 m/s flight speed; ~8x more efficient at area coverage
- **Multirotor version (Primary for this project):** 
  - Lower altitude capable (15m AGL for 5m resolution)
  - 3 m/s flight speed
  - Better measurement integration and canopy penetration
  - Instrument package weight: 1.5 kg
  - Power draw: <50W
  - Proven in 100+ operational flights with government agencies, universities, commercial partners

### L-Band Radiometer Sensor
- Originally developed under NASA SBIR program
- Measures L-band brightness temperature
- Integrated with auxiliary sensors for soil type/surface property characterization
- Current version: under improvement with new digital correlator and onboard processing capability
- Demonstrated accuracy: strong agreement with in-situ sensors, even through moderate forest canopy (Figure 9 in document)

### Soil Moisture Data Products
- Resolution: 2m (UAS), 6m (UAVSAR), 200m (NISAR)
- Output formats: HDF, GeoTIFF
- Data volume estimates: 
  - UAS soil moisture maps: 10 GB/year (from 192 flights/year)
  - NISAR soil moisture maps: 6 GB for 6-day interval coverage (from Oct 2025 onward)
  - UAVSAR soil moisture maps: 0.3 GB for 9 flights in Year 1

### Live Fuel Moisture (LFM) Maps
- Derived from soil moisture anomaly maps using species-specific relationships
- Validated against field samples of Chamise and other species
- Prior testing showed high correlation (Figures 4-5)
- Can be generated in near-real-time onboard UAS
- Formats compatible with wildfire management systems

## Use Cases & Applications

### Primary Use Case: Pre-Fire Wildfire Management
- **Situational Awareness:** Rapid characterization of fuel moisture conditions before ignition
- **Controlled Burn Planning:** Provide real-time data to support scheduled controlled burns at test site; inform decisions on fuel loads, timing, and extent
- **Response Readiness:** Enable rapid data collection in response to ignition sources
- **Landscape Management:** Support coordination between state/local agencies and land managers on best practices to decrease fire risk

### Test Site
- 3,200-acre (8 km²) nature preserve in California's fire-prone region
- Existing infrastructure: 40 monitoring stations, extensive vegetation/soil/climate measurements
- Active fuel management: mechanical thinning, prescribed burns
- Ideal for validation: co-located ground truth data

### Geographic Scope
- Focus: California northern coastal mountains and western US fire-prone landscapes
- Extended application potential: broader wildland/fire management community
- Operates within scope of NASA FireSense project goals

### Secondary Applications (Year 3)
- Fire perimeter detection using NISAR disturbance product and L-band data during controlled burns
- Post-fire monitoring capability demonstration

### Final Campaign Results (Figure 9)
- Very good correlation between UAS and in-situ data
- Demonstrated mapping capability even through moderate forest canopy
- Single flight validation showed reliable soil moisture retrieval

## Executive Summary
This is a working outline for a NASA SBIR Phase I final report on terrain-following autonomous flight capabilities. BST conducted extensive sensor integration work (cameras, LiDAR, radar, laser altimeters), developed hardware and algorithms for obstacle detection and avoidance, created Gazebo simulation environments, and implemented terrain-following altitude controllers for both multirotor and S2 fixed-wing platforms.

## Technical Approach

### Imaging Hardware & Machine Vision
- **GPU-accelerated colorization**: Implemented Nvidia TX2 GPU processing to accelerate Bayer format image colorization and correction from 2 FPS to 25 FPS (standard ML camera libraries didn't support performant ARM color processing)
- **Precision timing**: Developed nanosecond-precision camera timestamps with time alignment mechanisms synching camera clocks to TX2 via PPS (pulse-per-second) signals from IMU and GPS
- **Stereo vision**: Designed stereo camera system with calibration, rectification, and deep learning-enhanced block matching algorithms (replacing basic OpenCV approaches)
- **Web video streaming**: Developed 1080p video streaming to web interface for operator feedback and debugging

### LiDAR Integration
- Identified lighter, more accessible options (Ouster OS1, potentially RoboSense)
- Simulated full point cloud matching Ouster 16-channel spinning system in Gazebo
- Demonstrated strong terrain and tree resolution for terrain following

### Radar Assessment
- Reviewed FCC regulations; determined 76/77 GHz automotive radars cannot be used for airborne applications
- 77 GHz preferred over 24 GHz for better range resolution (~5 GHz vs. ~200 MHz bandwidth) and angular resolution
- Identified small patch radar vendor: low power, lightweight, long-range, low-cost, but limited performance (single beam, wide angles, strongest return only, no Doppler)
- Note: Did not obtain actual radar flight data despite efforts; simulated basic radar in Gazebo with path forward for more complex modeling

### Laser Altimetry
- Costa Rica flights showed 1-2 m range degradation in fog
- Heavy snow flights also showed 1-2 m range degradation
- Integrated narrow-beam sonar initially (very noisy/inaccurate), switched to 1D laser for cleaner simulation results

### Sensor Fusion & Obstacle Avoidance
- **SLAM**: Applied SLAM techniques (historically used with LiDAR, stereo, ultrasonic) to build environment maps with heterogeneous sensor fusion
- **Voxel grid overlays**: Short time-history voxel grids filter LiDAR and stereo data to assess obstacle likelihood
- **Obstacle avoidance**: Discretized reactive controllers based on sensor data; identified MIT paper approach as preferred over RRT or vector field methods (latter require good maps not expected in terrain following scenarios)
- **Sensor fusion requirements documented**: Different coverages, rates, noise characteristics, data volumes, and types (intensities for lasers, SNR/Doppler for radar, disparity for stereo)

### Terrain Following Control
- **Altitude controller**: Developed AGL (above-ground-level) controller measuring altitude and correcting for pitch/roll
- **PID control with slope estimation**: PID converts AGL error to z-axis velocity; controller computes terrain slope via regression to smooth control commands
- **Predictive control**: Uses forward-facing laser (on quadcopter) to predict terrain ahead; estimated terrain height from AGL vs. GPS height difference
- **Limitations**: SDK limited to ~20 Hz external control (faster overruns autopilot interface); pure PID fails on large AGL steps (boxes, trees); faster controller needed in firmware
- **Safety logic**: Climbing preferred over descending; descent rate limited

## Products & Capabilities Described

### S2 (Fixed-Wing UAS)
- Created CAD model in Gazebo with sensor integration
- Developed S2-specific SWIL (software-in-the-loop) simulation using bounding boxes for collision detection
- Path forward: incorporate moments of inertia/weight, motor plugin from multirotor, lift/drag plugins for control surfaces, mesh models for ailerons/ruddervators/flaps

### Jetson TX2
- Identified TX2 carrier cards for embedded processing
- Worked extensively on image processing libraries/deployment
- Resolved issues with ML camera Bayer format transmission and colorization (GPU-accelerated solution)
- Integrated with stereo algorithms and deep learning implementations

### SwiftCore Autopilot & SDK
- Published GPS, pressure, magnetometer, and laser altitude data to autopilot
- SDK subscribed to autopilot and provided waypoint/altitude commands
- External control limited to ~20 Hz due to communication interface bottleneck
- Integrated with Gazebo for SWIL testing

## Use Cases & Applications

- **Terrain following autonomous flight**: Low-altitude autonomous navigation maintaining safe clearance above ground/obstacles
- **Forest/canopy environment navigation**: Tested with simulated trees (~6 m tall) and real data from Costa Rica flights
- **All-weather operations**: Laser altimetry degradation in fog/snow noted; radar's all-weather capability emphasized as appealing despite performance tradeoffs
- **Arctic/mountainous terrain**: Implied by emphasis on varied terrain simulation
- **Obstacle avoidance in GPS-denied/complex environments**: SLAM and reactive control for densely vegetated or structurally complex terrain

## Simulation Work (Gazebo)

### Multi-rotor SWIL
- Existing simulation designed to fly like fixed-wing (constant speed, banking for heading)
- Integrated 1D laser, stereo cameras, LiDAR, fixed forward-facing radar
- Designed large square flight paths for testing

### World Development
- Built Cambridge, MA demo world (1 km²) using DAE/STL meshes from QGIS terrain data
- Added obstacles: reactor cooling tower, 8 oak trees (~6 m), 10×10×5 m box
- Identified models available online: light posts, gas stations, pine trees, walls, Jersey barriers
- Path forward: use DAE tools, photogrammetry-based canopy meshes, build procedural terrain

### Sensor Models Integrated
- Stereo cameras with dynamic pixeling
- LiDAR (16-channel spinning)
- Narrow-beam sonar and 1D laser
- Forward-facing radar (basic, with path for advanced ray-tracing)
- Downward camera

## Key Results/Findings

- **Performance improvements**: GPU acceleration increased image processing from 2 FPS to 25 FPS
- **Simulation validation**: SWIL successfully validated terrain following algorithms; demonstrated sensor fusion with heterogeneous data
- **Sensor trade studies**: LiDAR superior for terrain resolution but weight concerns; radar all-weather capability appealing but performance-limited; stereo vision viable with GPU acceleration
- **Terrain prediction**: Historic flight data and height maps can estimate flat terrain vs. canopy (via std. deviation analysis)
- **Control limitations**: Pure PID AGL control fails on step responses; slope-based predictive control improves performance; reactive obstacle avoidance preferred over map-based planning

## Notable Details

- **FCC regulatory constraint**: 77 GHz automotive radars cannot be used airborne (significant finding for sensor selection)
- **Commercialization partnership**: Imaging hardware work done with IPOZ; they requested stereo depth and operator feedback improvements
- **GPU acceleration innovation**: Custom implementation of colorization/correction on Jetson TX2 addresses limitation in commercial ML camera software (Ximea, Point Grey/FLIR)
- **Timing precision**: Developed kernel module for tight nanosecond-precision time alignment critical for multi-sensor fusion
- **Radar data gap**: Despite efforts, did not obtain actual radar flight test data (only simulation)
- **Deadline note**: Phase II Implementation Plan and Final Report marked "in work" at document creation date

## Executive Summary
This is the foundational solicitation document for the Army Applications Lab's Broad Agency Announcement seeking disruptive technology innovations across 16 technology areas. The BAA invites proposals from academia, nonprofit organizations, government, and for-profit companies to develop breakthrough technologies that provide 2-4x improvements over current Army capabilities and support the Army's modernization priorities. Awards will be made as contracts, grants, cooperative agreements, or Other Transactions, with no specific funding reserved and continuous submission windows available.

## Key Program Focus Areas
The AAL seeks innovations in 16 technology domains:

1. **Autonomous Platforms** – Ground and air vehicles operating in cluttered, urban, underground terrains and contested environments; low electronic/physical profiles; rapid operator training; dynamic reprogramming
2. **AI/ML** – Autonomous vehicle behaviors, threat prediction, robust networking, intelligence analysis, multi-source data fusion
3. **Data Visualization & Synthetic Environments** – Sensor data visualization, large datasets, complex multi-source data, training and virtual-live validation
4. **Assured PNT** – GPS-denied operations, commercial tech enhancement, robust security, guidance/control, multi-source fusion
5. **Power Generation & Management** – Power algorithms, low-power electronics, compact sources for small UAVs/robots/munitions, storage/transmission
6. **Sensing** – Detection of people, equipment, weapons; obscured target detection; signature-based detection
7. **Communications & Networks** – Secure/reliable comms, protocols, multi-national interoperability, high-efficiency components
8. **Computation** – Throughput, power efficiency, edge computing for AI/ML algorithms
9. **Space** – Persistent high-resolution sensing, low-cost space access
10. **IoT** – Automated management concepts, ML-accelerated decision-making, secure/resilient networks in mixed cooperative/adversarial environments
11. **Quantum Technologies** – Quantum computing for complex problems, quantum sensing, quantum communications
12. **Signature Reduction** – RF, optical, thermal, acoustic, magnetic signature reduction for Soldiers and platforms
13. **Protection** – CBRN threat sensors, lightweight armor, cyber protection, human performance optimization, counter-UAS/missile/overhead surveillance
14. **Human Performance** – Human-machine interaction, training effectiveness, cognitive/perceptual/physical augmentation
15. **Contested Logistics** – Predictive analytics, autonomous technology for reach/endurance, logistics tail reduction, alternative fuels, point-of-need manufacturing
16. **Kinetic Payload** – COTS aerial system augmentation, additive manufacturing, interchangeable delivery systems, autonomous/semi-autonomous effects delivery

## Application & Award Structure

**Three-Stage Process:**
1. **Whitepaper/Demonstration Submission** – Required initial stage; applicants submit via AAL website tool; AAL provides feedback within 30 days if requested
2. **SAM Registration (Optional)** – Applicants can register early for efficiency
3. **Full Proposal Submission** – Invited applicants submit complete proposals via email (contracts) or Grants.gov (assistance instruments)

**Funding Mechanisms:**

## Document Metadata
- Type: Phase II SBIR Proposal Outline/Planning Document
- Client/Agency: NASA

## Executive Summary
This Phase II proposal outlines Black Swift Technologies' two-year plan to develop autonomous terrain-following and obstacle-avoidance capabilities for fixed-wing UAS, leveraging the S2 platform. The work integrates multiple sensors (stereo vision, LiDAR, radar) with simulation and flight testing to create a modular, fieldable system applicable beyond the S2 aircraft.

## Technical Approach

### Simulation Work
- **Finalize Simulation Environment**: Improve radar model with sensor plugins to control scan volume; develop hardware-in-the-loop (HWIL) interfaces to TX2 and BST Autopilot; explore GPU-accelerated simulation
- **S2 Aircraft Modeling**: Evaluate and integrate existing lift/drag plugins; develop improved models as needed; update plugin and integrate with autopilot
- **Terrain Integration**: Convert photogrammetry to mesh/skin; leverage QGIS data; formalize data collection schemes (timing, images, stereo imagery, laser point clouds, radar point clouds)
- **Scenario-Specific Simulations**: Build canopy, agriculture (with buildings), volcano/mountain, takeoff/landing, homogeneous terrain, and urban simulations

- **Obstacle Avoidance**: Develop climbout and turnout simulations; test with long-range radar, stereo, and LiDAR

  - HWIL systems

- Full EMI testing and mechanical integration

- **Phase 1 (Data Collection)**: No algorithms running, gather sensor data

## Executive Summary
This Phase II workplan outlines BST's approach to developing autonomous terrain-following and obstacle-avoidance capabilities for small UAS. The work spans simulation environment development, algorithm development across multiple sensor modalities (lidar, stereo vision, laser altimeter, radar), hardware integration on the S2 platform, and extensive flight testing validation.

## Technical Approach

### Simulation Environment Development (Section 2)
- Comprehensive sensor modeling (radar, camera, 1D laser, lidar) with realistic noise, fault injection, and point cloud generation
- S2 aircraft CAD model with aerodynamic characterization (coefficients, moments of inertia, motor/prop parameters)
- Integration with BST Autopilot and control surface mapping
- Terrain generation from QGIS data and photogrammetry meshes
- Integration of new data types (images, stereo, laser point clouds, radar point clouds) into BST SDK
- SWIL (Gazebo-based) and HWIL development with TX2 interface
- Scenario-specific simulations: canopy, agriculture, volcano/mountain, takeoff/landing, urban

### Algorithm Development (Section 3)
- **Laser Altimeter (3.1)**: False return mitigation, firmware implementation, flight data verification
- **Lidar (3.2)**: False return mitigation, obstacle injection, TX2 implementation
- **Terrain Following (3.3-3.11)**: PID/slope control on S2, height map control, trajectory generation, discretized climb and turnout controllers
- **Machine Vision - Stereo Depth (3.4, 3.6)**: Stereo depth algorithm evaluation and downselection, homogenous terrain and weather detection, calibration methodology
- **Machine Vision - Downward (3.5, 3.7)**: Z-velocity aided AGL estimation, calibration methodology
- **Obstacle Mapping & Sensor Fusion (3.8-3.10)**: Voxel-based grids, SLAM (LiDAR, stereo, radar, heterogeneous), machine learning obstacle identification
- **Advanced Control**: Wind estimation, trajectory propagation/collision detection, integrated obstacle avoidance simulation
- **Radar (3.17)**: Sensor design, realistic return plugins, signal processing

### Hardware Development (Section 4)
- TX2 firmware development with SDK, autopilot, and sensor interfaces
- Mechanical integration mockup and EMI testing
- S2 component modifications for commercial integration
- Radar sensor procurement from subcontractor

## Document Metadata
- Type: NASA Research Proposal
- Client/Agency: NASA Earth Science Division (Terrestrial Ecology Program)
- Program/Solicitation: NNH16ZDA001N-TE; NASA Proposal Number 16-TE16-0009
- Date: Submitted 08/01/2016
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: SuperSwift airframe, Tempest "Tornado Chaser" platform
- Key Personnel: Maciej Stachura (Black Swift Technologies, Co-I); Zhuosen Wang (UMD, PI); Miguel Román (NASA/GSFC, Co-I)

## Executive Summary
This proposal seeks NASA funding ($496,264 over 3 years, 2017-2020) to deploy MALIBU (Multi-Angle Imaging Bidirectional reflectance distribution function small-Unmanned aerial system) to assess how Arctic shrub encroachment and boreal forest wildfires affect surface energy exchange and climate. The project will use the SuperSwift unmanned aircraft platform (developed by Black Swift Technologies) to collect high-resolution multi-angle reflectance measurements for validating satellite albedo products and characterizing photosynthesis vegetation indices across Arctic and boreal ecosystems.

## Technical Approach

**MALIBU System Overview:**
- Semi-autonomous small UAS (sUAS) with full blanket exemption for US and Canada operations
- Carries two Tetracam Multiple Camera Array (MCA) multispectral imagers in port and starboard configurations (117.2° combined field-of-view)
- Six spectral channels: 442, 488, 531, 560, 650, 861 nm—matching Landsat-8 OLI, Sentinel-2 MSI, MODIS, MISR, VIIRS, and Sentinel-3 OLCI
- Incident Light Sensor (ILS) for downwelling radiation measurement
- Dual GPS units, dual IMU navigation units, Field of View geotagging system achieving <2 cm per-pixel geolocation accuracy
- Each channel: 1280×1024 pixels with ~10 cm spatial resolution at 100m altitude

**Platform Integration:**
- Deployed on Black Swift Technologies' SuperSwift airframe (ruggedized s-UAS)
- 10-foot wingspan, 3-piece easy-assemble design, portable ("carry in small sized bag")
- Rapid "plug-and-play" payload installation (<30 minutes between flights)
- Dynamic nose cone design allows variable instrument roll angle (nadir to horizon)
- Operating cost: <$350/flight hour vs. $3,500-4,000/hour for heritage NASA systems (CAR, AirMSPI)
- Successfully completed NASA Airworthiness and Flight Safety Review Board (AFSRB) certification

**Data Processing Pipeline:**
1. Raw DN values converted to reflectance using simultaneous ILS measurements
2. Geolocation correction using onboard GPS, ground control points (GCPs), and IMU navigation data
3. MODTRAN5 radiative transfer calculations for atmospheric correction
4. Retrieval of surface reflectances, BRDF model parameters, and hemispherically integrated albedo
5. Characterization of measurement uncertainties and geolocation errors in metadata

## Products & Capabilities Described

### SuperSwift Platform
- **What it is:** Ruggedized small UAS based on Black Swift's Tempest design, specifically engineered for harsh high-latitude environments
- **Capabilities:** 
  - Meets FAA and Canada Transport rules with full blanket exemption (FAA No. 13967)
  - Supports rapid pre/post-flight calibration (maintains <5% targeted accuracy)
  - "Dynamic pointing" for variable instrument roll angles
  - Minimal logistical footprint compared to manned aircraft
  - Total development investment to date: $1,114,890 (SBIR-funded)
- **Performance in ABoVE context:**
  - Much higher success rate for clear-sky acquisitions vs. manned platforms (heritage systems achieve <30% usable data; SuperSwift/MALIBU expected to overcome this)
  - Cost-effective rapid deployment for multi-angle sampling
  - Enables repeat flights under varying cloud conditions

### MALIBU/SuperSwift Integrated System
- **Spatial resolution:** Sub-meter (<10 cm) multi-angle spectral reflectance
- **Angular resolution:** 0.5 degree
- **Products generated:**
  - High-resolution BRDF/albedo reference datasets (SI-traceable)
  - Spectral surface albedo maps
  - Reflectance anisotropy (BRDF shape) characterization
  - Photosynthesis vegetation indices (PRI, CCI) with angular variations quantified
  - Fire severity assessments and post-fire albedo dynamics
  - Shrub cover and structural metrics

## Use Cases & Applications

**1. Arctic Shrub Encroachment Assessment**
- Nine field sites across Arctic tundra, shrub, and boreal forest (Table 1):
  - M-01: NEON Toolik tundra site (68.661°N, -149.370°W)
  - M-02, M-03: Shrub sites along Dalton Highway transect (foundational ABoVE flight lines)
  - Control pairs of shrub-free and shrub-covered locations
- Quantify albedo changes from vegetation structure and composition shifts
- Evaluate regional climate feedbacks from shrub cover expansion on North Slope of Alaska

**2. Post-Fire Boreal Forest Dynamics**
- Six boreal forest sites (M-04 through M-09) in Saskatchewan, Canada (supplemental ABoVE lines)
- Temporal comparison: mature, 9-year post-fire, and 17-year post-fire conditions
- Characterize albedo recovery and vegetation succession
- Assess fire severity and black carbon deposition effects
- Improve carbon emission modeling at sub-hectare scales

**3. Satellite Product Validation**
- Generate reference BRDF/albedo datasets for validating:
  - MODIS (Terra/Aqua)
  - Sentinel-2 MSI, Sentinel-3 OLCI
  - Landsat-8 OLI
  - MISR (Terra)
  - VIIRS (Suomi-NPP/JPSS)
- Address heterogeneous landscape validation gaps (tower albedometers insufficient)
- Support GCOS Terrestrial Observing Panel on Climate (TOPC) Action 01 and CEOS-WGCV international commitments

**4. Photosynthesis and Light-Use-Efficiency Modeling**
- Expand PRI (Photochemical Reflectance Index) and CCI (Chlorophyll-Carotenoid Index) characterization beyond previous tower-based forest/cropland studies
- Evaluate angular effects on LUE and gross ecosystem production (GEP) estimates
- Improve carbon cycle modeling in rapidly shifting Arctic/boreal climate zones

## Key Research Objectives

**Objective 1: Characterize BRDF/Albedo Scaling Effects**
- Analyze subpixel reflectance anisotropy biases across satellite retrieval geometries
- Quantify interaction between surface BRDF shape and instrument spatial resolution
- Discriminate end-member components: shrub canopy, forest crown, non-woody background, char, moss
- Compare against NEON tower albedometer data at Toolik site
- Document MALIBU measurement uncertainties (radiometric, geolocation) in metadata

**Objective 2: Assess Albedo Impacts from Shrub Encroachment and Fire**
- Analyze spatial scaling within and across post-fire boreal ecosystems
- Conduct radiative forcing analysis at fine scales (<1 ha)
- Generate fire severity assessments improving carbon emission predictions
- Link shrub structure changes to surface energy exchange and permafrost vulnerability

**Objective 3: Evaluate Angular Photosynthesis Index Effects**
- Assess PRI and CCI angular variations across tundra, shrub, and boreal post-fire ecosystems
- Compare airborne multi-angle indices against tower-based LUE/GEP measurements
- Improve utility of long-term satellite records for carbon modeling

## Notable Details

**Innovation & Competitive Advantages:**
1. **First NASA s-UAS with full blanket exemption:** Unique regulatory status for cross-US/Canada operations
2. **Cost efficiency:** <$350/flight hour vs. $3,500-4,000 for manned platforms; solves high-latitude logistics challenges
3. **Unprecedented spatial-angular resolution:** 10 cm spatial, 0.5° angular at <10 cm resolution
4. **Dynamic instrument pointing:** Overcomes high-latitude solar geometry constraints (SZA ~49° at Barrow mid-summer)
5. **Spectral channel alignment:** Matched to 6+ satellite sensors (MODIS, Landsat, Sentinel, MISR, VIIRS, OLCI) for seamless validation
6. **Multi-scale measurement suite:** Integrates in-situ, tower, terrestrial LiDAR, and airborne observations

**International Collaboration:**

**Regulatory/Safety Achievement:**

- Test flights at Pawnee National Grasslands (June 2016) with Landsat-8 OLI colocation demonstrated instrument consistency and <2 cm pointing accuracy

**Alignment with ABoVE Science Goals:**
- Directly addresses Tier 2 Science questions on disturbance regimes and ecosystem response
- Contributes to ABoVE Science Objective 1: "Determine how interactions among vegetation, soil, hydrology, and disturbances influence surface energy exchange and permafrost vulnerability"
- Supports broader NASA calibration/validation framework and GCOS essential climate variables

**Data Products & Dissemination:**
- SI-traceable reference BRDF/albedo datasets for global satellite validation
- Publication costs: $3,000 over 3 years
- Will contribute to ABoVE Science Cloud and broader open data ecosystems# AF Open Topic 25.5E - S3 UAS for Persistent Operations in Extreme Environments

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposes the S3 UAS, a next-generation VTOL-to-fixed-wing platform designed for autonomous, long-duration, all-weather missions in extreme and contested environments. The system integrates solar-based autonomous recharge, vision-based GPS-denied navigation, and advanced autonomy to enable persistent unattended operations lasting days to months, addressing critical capability gaps for military ISR in CBRN zones, conflict areas, and severe weather conditions.

## Technical Approach

### Platform Architecture
- VTOL transitioning to fixed-wing flight configuration
- Designed for autonomous operation without human oversight
- Capable of operating in adverse weather: precipitation, icing, high winds (up to 50-knot gusts)
- Modular payload bays for flexible mission configurations
- Capable of deployment from unprepared sites without ground infrastructure

### Autonomy & Navigation
- Onboard vision-based navigation using stereo cameras and machine learning
- Optical flow and semantic segmentation for automated landing site detection
- GPS-denied operation capability
- Terrain-following and obstacle avoidance algorithms
- Precision automated landing in austere environments
- Full autonomy for safe operation without human oversight

### Power & Endurance
- Novel solar recharging system integrated into wings
- Smart power management for multi-day deployments
- Unattended operation capability over days to months
- Nomadic deployment paradigm enabling pre-positioned rapid-launch assets

### Environmental Hardening
- Dual pitot-static system for accurate airspeed measurement in heavy precipitation
- Structural redesigns for flight in strong turbulence and icing conditions
- All-weather reliability for continuous data collection

## Products & Capabilities Described

### S3 UAS
- **What it is:** Next-generation small UAS platform based on proven legacy systems, featuring VTOL-to-fixed-wing transition
- **Key capabilities:**
  - Persistent autonomous operation in denied/contested environments
  - All-weather flight (precipitation, icing, high winds up to 50 knots)
  - GPS-denied navigation via vision system
  - Solar-recharged autonomous recharge for sustained unattended operation
  - Multi-day to multi-month deployment capability
  - Modular payload bays
  - Automated landing site detection and precision landing
- **Performance claims:**
  - Can operate without returning to base for extended periods
  - Reduced logistical burden vs. traditional ISR assets
  - Operates safely in conditions where adversaries may not expect UAS surveillance
  - Lower cost than High-Altitude Long Endurance (HALE) platforms

## Use Cases & Applications

### Military/Air Force Applications
- Base perimeter security
- Pre-strike reconnaissance
- Battle damage assessment
- Remote sensing of CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear) threats
- Persistent ISR in contested/denied/degraded environments
- Rapid-response missions in denied areas
- Adaptive ISR with unpredictable redeployment
- Disaster response operations
- Sensor-triggered event response
- Nighttime operations
- Tiered ISR networks (distributed sensing with multiple small assets)

### Commercial/Dual-Use Applications
- Energy infrastructure inspection
- Long-range methane leak detection
- Wildfire monitoring
- Weather research
- Environmental compliance monitoring
- Oil & gas industry monitoring
- Utility infrastructure inspection
- Insurance applications
- Wide-area monitoring across large remote regions
- Critical infrastructure surveillance where manned flights are cost-prohibitive or risky

## Key Benefits

### Military Benefits
- Fills critical capability gap for distributed, long-endurance aerial sensing
- Enables persistent presence at tactical edge without logistical burden
- Provides continuous data collection in challenging conditions
- Supports pre-positioned assets for rapid launch in response to emergent threats

### Commercial Benefits

- Scalable alternative/complement to larger HALE platforms
- Enables long-range sensing missions at significantly lower cost
- Suitable for distributed sensing networks
- Cost-effective for routine monitoring of critical infrastructure

## Notable Details

- **Resilience in contested environments:** Designed specifically for operation in areas where traditional ISR assets (satellites, crewed aircraft, ground sensors) are ineffective or risky
- **Redundancy approach:** Vision system provides critical layer of redundancy for safe operations in austere environments where GPS is unavailable
- **Logistical transformation:** "Nomadic drone-in-a-box" paradigm shifts from base-dependent operations to distributed, autonomous persistence

- **Dual-use market:** Strong commercial potential in energy, utilities, and insurance sectors with growing demand for autonomous, low-cost monitoring

Black Swift Technologies proposes SwiftCore, a full-stack in-house designed avionics ecosystem, to address limitations of legacy airborne ISR systems that rely on inflexible third-party autopilots. The solution enables plug-and-play payload flexibility, real-time reconfiguration, and streamlined sensor fusion to deliver high-fidelity environmental intelligence in diverse and demanding environments.

## Technical Approach
SwiftCore represents a full-stack avionics architecture designed, engineered, and manufactured entirely in-house, comprising:
- Custom autopilot hardware boards
- Integrated flight control firmware
- SwiftTab mission interface/user interface
- Modular architecture supporting multiple aircraft types, payloads, and flight profiles with a single avionics core

Key approach elements:
- Plug-and-play payload flexibility and real-time mission reconfiguration
- Streamlined sensor fusion capabilities
- Support for rapid mission customization and easier payload integration
- Secure communication workflows meeting defense-grade ISR requirements

## Products & Capabilities Described

- Modular design supporting multiple UAS platforms without platform-specific constraints
- Real-time reconfiguration and payload swapping capability
- Operates effectively in extreme and dynamic environments
- Enables data streaming and sensor fusion

**SwiftTab**

- Enables end-to-end system integration and mission adaptability

## Use Cases & Applications

- Environmental intelligence collection in extreme and dynamic environments
- Rapid mission-adaptable operations
- Defense/military applications requiring reliable autonomous flight in diverse conditions

- **Modularity:** Single avionics core supports multiple aircraft types, payloads, and flight profiles without being constrained by platform limitations

- **System Resilience:** Full-stack ecosystem architecture provides unmatched modularity and operational resilience

## Executive Summary

The form documents BST's accounting system compliance with federal contracting requirements, DCAA standards, and cost accounting principles. ## Document Content Summary

## Document Metadata
- Type: Peer-reviewed scientific paper (journal article)
- Journal: Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics Discussions (ACPD)
- Volume/Pages: 3, 6701–6720
- Date: Published December 16, 2003 (received October 25, 2003; accepted December 8, 2003)
- Authors: A. M. Makarieva, V. G. Gorshkov (Theoretical Physics Division, Petersburg Nuclear Physics Institute, Russia); T. Pujol (Department of Physics, University of Girona, Spain)
- Connection to BST: This document appears in BST's NASA 2018 SBIR Venus Phase I proposal reference folder, suggesting it was used as background material for Venus atmosphere research.

## Executive Summary
This paper derives analytical formulas for the height of convective layers in planetary atmospheres containing both condensable (water vapor) and non-condensable (CO₂) greenhouse substances. The authors demonstrate that convective layer height is finite and independent of atmospheric optical thickness at large values, contradicting earlier models that predicted a plateau in outgoing thermal radiation. The work yields accurate predictions for Venus's convective layer (~50 km) and Earth's equatorial convection patterns.

## Technical Approach

### Core Physics Framework
- Uses radiative equilibrium theory with **Eddington's approximation** to relate upward thermal radiation flux to optical depth
- Introduces **brightness temperature** concept (temperature derived from radiation flux in specific spectral intervals)
- Derives relationship between air temperature lapse rate and the onset of convection
- Employs **hydrostatic equilibrium** equations combined with Clausius-Clapeyron relation for water vapor

### Key Equations
1. **Brightness Temperature** (Eq. 2.3):
   - T_b = T_s[(1 + kτ)/(1 + kτ_s)]^(1/4), where k = 3/4
   
2. **Convection Onset Condition** (Eq. 2.8):
   - Convection begins when brightness temperature lapse rate equals critical air temperature lapse rate (Γ)
   - For Earth: Γ = 6.5 K/km; G_max = 8.56 K/km
   
3. **Maximum Convective Height for τ_s ≫ 1** (Eq. 2.11):
   - z_c,max / h_s = 4/α (1 - α^[α/(1-α)]) = 3.03
   - Where α = Γ/G_max and h_s is atmospheric scale height

4. **Water Vapor Compression** (Eq. 3.4):
   - Water vapor distribution compressed by factor β ≈ 3.5 relative to air
   - Scale height of water vapor: h_sL ≈ 2.4 km (Earth)

## Products & Capabilities Described

Not applicable—this is a theoretical physics paper with no BST products or systems. It provides foundational atmospheric science theory relevant to planetary mission planning.

## Use Cases & Applications

### Earth Atmosphere
- **Convective layer maximum height**: 25 km (calculated from Eq. 2.11 with T_s = 288 K, h_s = 8.4 km)
- **Water vapor role**: Convection on Earth driven by water vapor, not CO₂
  - Water vapor optical thickness threshold: τ_sL,min = 0.38 (vs. τ_s,min = 4.5 for CO₂)
  - Observed water vapor optical thickness ≈ 0.53, exceeding threshold by factor of ~2
- **Temperature at convection top**: T_c ≈ 121 K (-152°C)
- **Latitudinal variation**: Convection height peaks in equatorial regions (~15 km) where water vapor content is maximum; reduced in polar regions

### Venus Atmosphere
- **Atmospheric composition**: CO₂ dominant (non-condensable greenhouse substance)
- **Key parameters**:
  - Surface temperature: T_s = 730 K
  - Surface pressure conditions: F⁺_s/F_e = 98 (ratio of surface to space radiation)
  - Optical thickness: τ_s = 131 ≫ 1 (validates asymptotic theory)
  - Scale height: h_s = 15.6 km
  - Temperature lapse rate: Γ ≈ 8 K/km; G_max = 11.4 K/km
  - Critical parameter: α = 0.70
  
- **Predicted convective layer height**: z_c,max = 50.4 km
  - **Validates observational data**: Matches observed Venus cloud layer (~50 km altitude) where temperature lapse rate transitions from steep (convective) to shallow (radiative)
  - **Temperature at top**: T_c = 318 K (44°C)
  - **Physical interpretation**: Cloud tops represent the boundary of the convective layer

## Key Results

### Main Finding
Convective layer height remains **finite** (independent of atmospheric optical thickness τ_s) at large optical depths, contradicting prior "runaway greenhouse" models.

### Mathematical Results
1. **Height asymptote**: For τ_s ≫ 1, convective height approaches z_c,max = 3.03 h_s for any non-condensable greenhouse gas
2. **Temperature at convection top**: For large τ_s, brightness temperature ratio T_bc/T_s = α^[1/(1-α)] = 0.32 (Earth)
3. **Outgoing radiation behavior** (Eq. 3.10):
   - For atmospheres with condensable greenhouse substances, outgoing thermal flux ratio decreases **exponentially** with surface temperature
   - F_e^L / F⁺_sL ∝ (1/τ_sL) ∝ exp(-θ/θ_s), where θ is surface temperature increment
   - This contradicts earlier models predicting a radiation plateau

### Physical Implications
- **Convection height is fixed in altitude space**, not in optical depth space
- As atmospheric opacity increases, optical depth grows exponentially at fixed altitudes
- Convective energy contribution therefore decreases inversely with optical thickness
- **Radiative equilibrium dominates** at high optical thicknesses, even in troposphere
- Water vapor saturation only occurs within convective layer; upper radiative layer is unsaturated at high optical depths

### Observational Validation
- **Earth**: Calculated maximum convective height (25 km) and minimum temperature (188 K) match observed tropopause structure
- **Venus**: Calculated height of 50.4 km matches observed cloud layer altitude; predicted top temperature (318 K / 44°C) consistent with Venus observations
- **Scale heights**: Calculated water vapor scale height (2.4 km) agrees with observational estimates

## Notable Details

### Theoretical Significance
- Resolves decades-long debate in climate modeling over whether greenhouse effect reaches a saturation limit
- Shows earlier models (Komabayasi 1967, Ingersoll 1969, Kasting 1988, Goody & Yung 1989) made incorrect assumption that entire atmosphere remains saturated with water vapor
- Demonstrates that upper radiative layer transitions to unsaturated state at high optical thicknesses

### Methodological Contributions
- Derives **exact analytical solutions** for convective layer height (not numerical models)
- Develops dimensionless framework using G_max scale for universal applicability
- Provides unified treatment of condensable and non-condensable greenhouse substances via substitution rules (α → α_L, h_s → h_sL)

### Key Physical Insights
1. **Compression factor β ≈ 3.5**: Water vapor distribution is much steeper than air because saturation vapor pressure decreases exponentially with altitude, creating strong compression in humid troposphere
2. **Role of hydrostatic equilibrium violation**: Steep water vapor gradients violate hydrostatic equilibrium, driving evaporation-precipitation cycles
3. **Solar radiation constraint**: Convective power is fundamentally limited by incoming solar flux (~240 W/m² for Earth), preventing arbitrarily tall convection

### Implications for Planetary Science
- Framework applies to any planet with condensible volatiles and greenhouse atmosphere
- Predicts convergence to radiative equilibrium at high surface temperatures/opacities
- Relevant for early Earth climate, Venus evolution, and exoplanet atmospheres

### References Context
Paper cites seminal climate modeling works (Kasting on Venus/Earth evolution, Ramanathan on radiative-convective equilibrium, Goody & Yung on atmospheric radiation) establishing connection to NASA mission planning concerns.# Actuator Board V18 Schematic

## Executive Summary
This proposal describes the TTwistor UAS, an advanced small unmanned aircraft system derived from the successful Tempest UAS heritage. The system combines an improved twin-motor airframe design (manufactured by UASUSA) with Black Swift Technologies' SwiftPilot Pro autopilot to enable superior payload integration, flight performance, and mission flexibility for civil and commercial applications. NOAA UAS Program Office committed as first customer and investor.

## Technical Approach

**Airframe Design:**
- Twin-propeller configuration with motor-propeller mounted on each wing (vs. single fuselage-mounted motor in Tempest)
- Enables instruments/probes to be mounted near airframe centerline with extensions into undisturbed airflow
- Incorporates swappable modular "nosecones" custom-designed for specific instruments or payloads
- Propeller airflow increases local circulation to improve lift during takeoff
- Manufactured by UASUSA Inc.

**Autopilot:**
- BST SwiftPilot Pro autopilot integrated for autonomous flight control
- Derived from proven Tempest UAS deployments in severe weather research

**Communications:**
- Prototype 900-MHz phased-array antenna system under development (not included in this proposal)
- Electronic beam-steering technology superior to mechanically-steered alternatives
- Second prototype in development with First RF Corp.
- Designed for improved communication between aircraft and ground station autopilot

## Products & Capabilities Described

**SwiftPilot Pro Autopilot:**
- Advanced autopilot system developed by Black Swift Technologies
- Provides autonomous flight control for TTwistor UAS
- Evolved from lessons learned in Tempest UAS operations
- Supports modular payload configurations

**TTwistor UAS (overall system):**
- Small electrically-powered unmanned aircraft system
- Designed for public/civil applications requiring cost-effective solutions
- Improved over Tempest with expanded capabilities
- Carries meteorological sensors, cameras, communications hardware, and other payloads
- Targets performance advantages in small electric UAS class

## Use Cases & Applications

- Severe weather research (tornado genesis studies, supercell sampling)
- Atmospheric sensing and meteorological research
- Emergency/first response operations
- Precision agriculture
- Surveying and mapping
- Education and science research
- Mobile communications experiments

**NOAA-Specific Applications:**
- Monitoring dangerous/remote areas (poles, oceans, wildlands, volcanic islands, wildfires)

## Document Metadata
- Type: Solicitation/Call for Proposals
- Client/Agency: Department of Defense (DoD) via ESTCP (Environmental Security Technology Certification Program)
- Program/Solicitation: ESTCP FY 2026, Natural Hazards Adaptation Program Area
- Date: Released January 7, 2025
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: None explicitly mentioned
- Key Personnel: J. Kevin Hiers (ESTCP Program Manager for Natural Hazards Adaptation)

## Executive Summary
This is a DoD ESTCP solicitation seeking demonstrations of tools that forecast wildfire activities and prescribed fire opportunities at military installation scales for 1-10 year time horizons. The goal is to improve wildfire risk management and optimize prescribed burn planning by incorporating weather-to-climate forecasting data with high-resolution fuel and vegetation inputs.

## Technical Approach
Proposed solutions should:
- Incorporate fire environmental conditions from weather-to-climate forecasting models to assess wildfire exposure and identify prescribed burn windows
- Demonstrate forecasting capability for extreme fire weather conditions (drought, excessive heat, extreme energy release components) at 1-10 year horizons
- Validate modeling accuracy against historical fire activities
- Accurately model prescribed burning windows using 1-10 year weather-to-climate forecasting tools
- Incorporate high-resolution fuel and vegetation condition data at least annually to update future hazard forecasts
- Operate at DoD installation-relevant spatial scales
- Show dynamic skill in projecting fire activities over the "weather-to-climate continuum"

## Use Cases & Applications
- Wildfire risk reduction and management at DoD installations
- Prescribed fire opportunity forecasting and optimization
- Budget and resource planning for fire management (1-10 year planning horizons)
- Military mission planning considering fire risk exposure
- Habitat management for threatened and endangered species (fire-dependent species)
- Ordnance-caused wildfire reduction planning

## Key Context
- DoD applies approximately 800,000 acres of prescribed fire annually across all military Services
- Prescribed fire is the primary treatment for wildfire risk reduction on DoD lands
- Current wildfire risk assessment tools lack validation at installation scales and show limited skill at 1-10 year forecasting horizons
- Many existing tools are static or infrequently updated for fuel/vegetation data
- Emerging weather-to-climate forecasting and AI approaches offer new potential solutions

## Notable Details
- Emphasis on interannual forecasting capability—a gap in current operational tools
- Integration of multiple data streams (weather, climate, fuel conditions, vegetation dynamics)
- Focus on actionable, operationally relevant assessments for resource managers
- Recognition that emerging AI and advanced forecasting methods warrant evaluation for this application
- Program manages significant acreage (800,000 acres/year prescribed fire) requiring improved planning tools

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposes to conduct an experimentation campaign using its S0-VTOL UAS to collect high-resolution atmospheric data in the arctic region to improve combat weather forecasts. The experiment will demonstrate the S0's reliability in harsh arctic conditions and validate improved operational weather forecasting capabilities, with deployment planned for March 2026.

## Technical Approach
- Deploy S0-VTOL UAS for targeted atmospheric data collection in arctic environment
- Conduct multiple flights (~60 minutes total) at various altitudes: transit below 400' AGL, data collection blocks up to 1 km × 1 km at 4,000' AGL
- Transmit/collect data on standard 2.4 GHz and 900 MHz bands
- Transfer collected atmospheric data via CD/DVD to host unit's weather forecasting models
- Self-funded by BST using internal R&D funds; no direct government funding for this experimentation

## Products & Capabilities Described

**S0-VTOL UAS**
- Vertical takeoff and landing UAS
- Specifically designed to operate in harsh conditions including arctic environment
- Capable of atmospheric/weather data collection
- System components fit in hard case (50" × 30" × 18"): aircraft, ground station, batteries, battery charger
- Uses standard 2.4 GHz and 900 MHz communication bands
- Does not currently have an airworthiness certificate
- Can be assembled/launched/landed in any outdoor location clear of obstructions within 30'

## Use Cases & Applications
- **Arctic weather data collection**: Address scarcity of fixed weather data collection stations in arctic region
- **Combat weather forecasting**: Enable improved operational weather forecasts for military operations in data-sparse arctic environment
- Supports expeditionary and forward-deployed combat weather squadron operations

## Notable Details

- **Host Unit Requirements**: Any USAF Combat Weather Squadron or Expeditionary Combat Weather Squadron with operational weather forecasting capability; must be able to receive and process data on CD/DVD; requires standard 110V/10A outlet access
- **Deployment**: 2 BST civilian personnel deploy alongside USAF weather personnel; BST staff remain outside classified spaces; commercial air and rental vehicles used for transportation
- **Operational Requirements**: Requires coordination with aviation planning/control organizations for flight deconfliction; exercises must accommodate ~60 minutes of flight operations
- **Availability Target**: March 2026

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** White Paper / SBIR Phase I Proposal
- **Client/Agency:** Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR)
- **Program/Solicitation:** AFOSR SBIR (topic area not specified)
- **Date:** Submitted December 15, 2012 (modified January 9, 2013)
- **BST Products/Systems Referenced:** Communication-aware avionics system (prototype under development); Tempest UAS system (Vortex2)
- **Key Personnel:** Jack Elston (President, Black Swift Technologies); Eric Frew (Director, Research and Engineering Center for Unmanned Vehicles, University of Colorado Boulder)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposes to develop a commercially viable, tightly integrated avionics system that unifies autopilot, flight computer, and mesh-based network functionality for small unmanned aircraft. By enabling direct communication between the communications subsystem and control algorithms, the system will support advanced autonomous capabilities including delay-tolerant networking, data ferrying, and communication-aware mission planning—addressing a critical gap in current small UAS avionics offerings.

## Technical Approach

**Core Innovation:** Tight integration of three traditionally separate systems:
- Autopilot
- Flight computer
- Mesh-based network solution (using COTS radios)

**Key Integration Features:**
- Low-level interfaces between communication, flight computer, and autopilot subsystems
- Communications subsystem has access to aircraft telemetry to intelligently route data and adjust radio parameters based on aircraft state
- Control algorithms have direct access to autopilot and communication interfaces
- Support for multiple link interfaces and radio types per platform
- Modular and programmable router architecture with hierarchical management
- Gateway functionality to bridge legacy and disparate networks

**Software Architecture:**
- Implementation of NetUAS architecture (developed at University of Colorado)
- Service discovery mechanisms
- Firmware providing communication statistics and control
- Communication-centric libraries for networking and control primitives
- Real-time user interface updated dynamically based on environmental changes

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Communication-Aware Avionics System
- **What it is:** An integrated avionics package combining autopilot, flight computer, and mesh networking into a single, tightly coupled system
- **Proposed use:** Enable small UAS to conduct communication-aware missions where routing, network topology, and mission planning are jointly optimized
- **Key capabilities:**
  - Support for multiple COTS radios with different protocols and frequencies
  - Mobile ad-hoc quasi-stable mesh network management
  - Interdependent switching/routing, topology management, and QoS
  - RF localization, delay-tolerant networking, controlled mobility in airborne mesh networks, RF-based SLAM

### Prototype (Existing System)
- BST has already developed a prototype at University of Colorado Boulder
- Interfaces to three different COTS radios operating on different protocols and frequencies
- Airborne and ground-based node capability
- Onboard NetUAS implementation enabling service discovery and heterogeneous network gateways

## Use Cases & Applications

- **Data ferrying:** Using aircraft mobility to transport data between disconnected network segments
- **Delay-tolerant networking:** Operating in environments with intermittent connectivity
- **Network-centric missions:** Maintaining constant communication with ground stations or specific nodes
- **Cooperative multi-platform operations:** Chaining aerial and mobile ground nodes to extend and maintain data links
- **Real-time collaborative sensing:** Gathering data from distributed ground nodes using aircraft as mobile relays
- **RTK GPS applications:** Leveraging network timing precision for accurate positioning
- **Road surveillance:** AFRL-referenced application using communication-aware chaining

**Historical Examples Referenced:**
- Vortex2 Tempest UAS system (tornado observation, demonstrated chaining of aerial and mobile ground nodes)
- AFRL road surveillance UAS (cooperative tracking with communication-aware coordination)

## Technical Objectives

1. **Hardware modification:** Implement full communication-aware solution as commercially viable product with low-level interfaces between communication, flight computer, and autopilot

2. **Firmware development:** Provide communication statistics and control, aircraft control and telemetry through standard interfaces for autonomous guidance algorithms

3. **Software libraries:** Create communication-centric libraries providing networking and control primitives for communication-aware tasks (data gathering from ground nodes, maintaining contact with specific nodes)

4. **User interface:** Tailor interface to provide mission planners with real-time information on communication capabilities and control state of all network nodes; update dynamically based on environmental changes (noise, interference)

## Program Timeline & Budget

**PHASE I:** Concept and design (6 months assumed)
- Deliverables: Conceptual models, functional requirements, component architectures, communications radio identification and interfaces, avionics system design, autopilot interfaces, user interface design, test plan with airspace access strategy

**PHASE II:** Prototype development and flight validation
- Deliverables: Functional prototype demonstration, final documentation and software, Concept of Operations for sampling missions, Phase II final report
- Key objective: Gain airspace access and validate system through experimentation

**PHASE III:** Commercialization and regulatory pathway
- Deliverables: Production-ready software, hardware, documentation
- Focus: Path to commercialization, NAS (National Airspace System) compliance, targeting public entities initially (predating commercial UAS authorization)

## Notable Details

**Competitive Position:**
- Identified gap: No commercially available integrated avionics system currently supports communication-aware mission architectures
- Existing work has been "very specific to the particular application" and lacks generalizability
- BST's approach provides the first general, commercializable solution

**Existing Research Foundation:**
- Based on peer-reviewed publications and proven field operations (Tempest/Vortex2, AFRL projects)
- Builds on University of Colorado's NetUAS architecture research
- Jack Elston and Eric Frew are recognized experts in UAS communications and control

**Regulatory Awareness:**
- Document acknowledges current regulations require mission termination upon communication failure
- Phase III explicitly addresses how to overcome NAS (National Airspace System) regulations
- Strategy includes targeting public entities initially, before commercial airspace is opened

**Technology Maturity:**
- Prototype already operational at University of Colorado
- Proof-of-concept demonstrated in field research
- Proposal moves from research prototype to commercial product# AFRL - Other Capabilities

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies presented its UAS capabilities to AFRL, emphasizing the S2 fixed-wing platform and E2 multi-rotor variant for soil moisture mapping and other ISR/monitoring applications. The document highlights BST's modular payload architecture, field-tested sensor integration across multiple domains (atmospheric, volcanic, wildfire, coastal monitoring), and advanced autonomy/avionics solutions.

## Technical Approach

### S2 Fixed-Wing Platform
- Rugged, modular fixed-wing UAS originally designed for atmospheric and volcano research
- Field-swappable payload nose cone with common power, data, and mechanical interfaces (no specialized tools required)
- Controlled by SwiftCore FMS (mature, scalable Flight Management System)
- Payload capacity: multiple sensor configurations (single, dual, or triple)
- Operates in extreme conditions: -20°C temperatures, altitudes up to 14,000 ft

### S2 VTOL Configuration
- Solar panels on wings for extended endurance (4-6 hours per flight)
- Machine vision-based automated landing (no pre-planning required)
- Terrain-aware flight planning using onboard elevation models
- Wind-aware flight planning for energy harvesting
- Rugged ingress protection rated for -40°F to 120°F operations

### E2 Multi-Rotor Platform
- Originally designed for autonomous infrastructure inspection; adapted for ISR missions
- Proprietary carbon fiber and polyamide 12 airframe
- Max takeoff weight: 25 lbs
- 35-minute nominal flight duration
- 6.5 lb max payload capacity
- Forward-mounted payload for full field-of-view
- 900 MHz telemetry frequency
- Flight ceiling: 14,000 ft
- Max winds endured: 30 mph
- Built for rugged field conditions and inclement weather

- **Capabilities:**
  - Patented radiometer technology penetrates vegetation
  - Measures soil moisture up to 10 cm below ground surface
  - Accuracy within 3% of true volumetric soil moisture
  - Moisture maps at up to 5m resolution
  - Mapping rate: 1 km² per hour (up to 600-1,200 acres per day)
  - Additional data products: orthomosaic maps, NDVI maps, thermal maps
- **Recent deployment:** May 2022 USGS soil site for wildfire mitigation; mapped 8 km² in 1.5 days

### SwiftCore Flight Management System
- Mature, scalable FMS for S2 control
- Integration with advanced avionics

### Advanced Avionics Solutions
- **Improved Autonomy:**
  - AI and machine vision-based systems
  - GPS-denied navigation
  - ADS-B integration
  - Real-time semantic segmentation (demonstrated in NASA-funded project)
  - Automated emergency landing plan generation
- **Improved Reliability:**
  - ML predictive maintenance
  - Web-based user portal for flight analysis and maintenance recommendations
- **Advanced Sensors:**
  - SwiftFlow 3D wind probe
  - Heated pitot
  - Rain mitigation for air data

## Use Cases & Applications

### Soil Moisture Monitoring
- Wildfire mitigation planning
- Runway assessment (unimproved runways)
- Quick-scan capability with complementary E2 for higher resolution

### Atmospheric Research

### Unique Capabilities

### Advanced Autonomy Demonstrations
- NASA-funded project demonstrated real-time semantic segmentation and emergency landing planning
- Web-based maintenance portal and ML predictive maintenance represent modern fleet management approach# AFVentures 2020 Annual Report

## Document Metadata
- Type: Annual Impact Report
- Client/Agency: Department of the Air Force (DAF), AFWERX
- Program/Solicitation: AFVentures (Division of AFWERX); SBIR/STTR Open Topic Program
- Date: FY18–FY20 (Report published 2021, cleared for public release by AFRL/PA)
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: None
- Key Personnel: Maj. Jason Rathje, PhD (Director, AFVentures); Ryan Helbach (Chief Intrapreneur, AFRL); Scott Schneider (CEO, HTX Labs); Caleb Carr (President & CEO, Vita Technologies)

## Executive Summary
AFVentures, a division of AFWERX established in 2018, leverages commercial innovation to deliver improved capabilities to the warfighter faster by matching operator needs with private sector solutions through the SBIR/STTR Open Topic program. From FY18–FY20, AFVentures awarded 2,299 contracts totaling $710 million to 1,433 companies, achieving a 5.8:1 return on investment and generating $2.21 billion in post-award private sector investment. The program successfully transitioned 538 capabilities to testing or prototyping with over 300 Air Force/DoD units, while accelerating average contracting timelines to 72 days.

## Technical Approach
AFVentures operates through a three-phase SBIR/STTR structure designed to accelerate technology transition:

- **Phase I**: $50,000 short-term contracts for concept development, feasibility testing, and customer identification
- **Phase II**: Up to $750,000 for prototyping, research, development, test and evaluation based on Air Force operator needs
- **Phase II Supplemental Funding Pilot Program (SFPP)**: Up to $15M in matched funding (requiring 3rd-party private or government co-investment) for scaling
- **Phase III**: Commercialization phase funded through non-SBIR/STTR sources (FAR-based contracts)

The program inverts the traditional acquisition model by enabling any qualifying commercial innovator to propose openly, rather than pursuing pre-determined, government-specified requirements. This decentralized, user-need-driven approach prioritizes early linkage between technology developers and DAF end-users to ensure subsequent funding addresses real Air Force problems.

Key process innovation: AFVentures achieved 100+ contract awards in 40 hours (November 5-9, 2019), reducing typical 6-month evaluation timelines to under 1 week evaluation + 1 week to contract award.

## Products & Capabilities Described
This document is not about Black Swift Technologies products. AFVentures is a Department of the Air Force funding and investment program, not a product or technology developer. The report catalogs portfolio companies and their various technologies but does not describe BST-specific systems.

However, the document identifies technology areas AFVentures prioritized:
- Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (18.06% of funding)
- Information Technology (22.84%)
- Hardware (20.01%)
- Aerospace (8.98%)
- Advanced Materials (8.41%)
- Cyber Security (5.40%)
- Autonomy/Robotics (5.29%)
- Telecommunications (5.26%)
- Augmented/Virtual Reality (3.44%)
- Quantum Computing (3.18%)
- Space-related technologies ($90.7M allocated to 292 awards across 215 companies)

## Use Cases & Applications
AFVentures portfolio companies address diverse Air Force mission sets across multiple domains:

**By Major Command:**
- Air Force Materiel Command (AFMC): 134 Phase II projects
- Air Combat Command (ACC): 83 Phase II projects
- Air Force Special Operations Command (AFSOC): 74 Phase II projects
- Air Force Education and Training Command (AETC): 58 Phase II projects
- United States Space Force (USSF): 42 Phase II projects

- Air Force Global Strike Command (AFGSC): 20 Phase II projects

**Geographic Distribution**: 538 testing/prototyping projects supported across 300+ offices/units spanning Pacific Air Forces (PACAF), U.S. Air Forces in Europe (USAFE-AFAFRICA), Air Force Reserve Command (AFRC), Air National Guard (ANG), and Air Forces Central Command (USAFCENT).

**Example Case Study—Vita Technologies**: Load Stability System (LSS) for helicopter payload/personnel stabilization. First Phase I contract (October 2018) for chaotic motion control system feasibility. Success led to $1M+ angel investment within 20 days and multiple follow-on Phase II contracts.

**Example Case Study—BrainGU, LLC**: Received first SBIR/STTR award (August 2019), followed by $12.3M sole-source follow-on contract from Cryptologic and Cyber Systems Division (Lackland AFB, November 2019) with 4-month commercialization timeline.

## Executive Summary
This is a template memorandum issued by AFRL/RGK designating a Technical Point of Contact (TPOC) for AFWERX Phase II SBIR proposals post-award. It outlines the TPOC's responsibilities, authorities, limitations, required training, and compliance obligations for monitoring contractor performance and managing contract deliverables.

## Document Purpose & Context
This is a **template/form document** establishing the formal designation and responsibilities for the Air Force's TPOC role in AFWERX Phase II SBIR contracts. It is not a proposal or technical document but rather an administrative/contractual framework document.

## Key TPOC Responsibilities Outlined
1. Monitor cost, technical, and schedule performance; identify and report marginal/unsatisfactory performance
2. Ensure contractor personnel receive required briefings on security, emergency management, and accountability
3. Receive and accept contract deliverables to enable timely contractor payment
4. Maintain liaison with Phase 2 PM (p2@afwerx.af.mil) and Contracting Officer
5. Work with contractor and government organizations to obtain required approvals/waivers for:
   - Security requirements (CACs, DD254 coordination)
   - Program protection compliance
   - Cybersecurity compliance
   - Flight testing and UAS regulations
   - Safety measures
6. Maintain comprehensive project documentation and case files
7. Identify replacement TPOC if unable to continue

## TPOC Authorities & Limitations
**Authorized to:**
- Monitor performance
- Accept deliverables
- Coordinate approvals and resolve execution issues

**NOT Authorized to:**
- Discuss performance or proposal details prior to contract award
- Make commitments or changes affecting price, quality, quantity, delivery schedule, scope, or contract terms
- Instruct contractor on performance methods (only communicate requirements)
- Participate in contractor hiring/termination
- Obligate Government funds or execute contract changes

## Required & Optional Training
**Required:**
- AFWERX-specific TPOC training (online)
- Additional training based on contract-specific activities and regulatory requirements

**Optional:**
- ACQ 1010: Fundamentals of Systems Acquisition Management (8 hrs)
- CLC 106: Contracting Officer's Representative with Mission Focus (3 hrs)
- CLC 011: Contracting for the Rest of Us (2 hrs)

Training deadline: 30 days after award selection

## Compliance & Standards
- Compliance with DOD 5500.7-R (Joint Ethics Regulation)
- Compliance with FAR 3.2 (Contractor Gratuities)
- Conflict of interest avoidance
- Strict adherence to contractor proprietary data and business-sensitive information restrictions
- Personal liability warning for unauthorized acts

## Notable Details
- TPOC role designation is mandatory and must be signed with CAC-enabled digital signature
- Signed letter must be renamed per format: "Proposal#_TPOC Name" and emailed to p2@afwerx.af.mil
- Phase 2 Program Manager contact: p2@afwerx.af.mil (all PM-related correspondence)
- Document applies to open-topic AFWERX Phase II proposals
- Explicit restriction on discussing acquisition plans/strategies that could advantage one contractor over another

## Executive Summary
This is an internal reference document providing regulatory definitions and compliance guidance for SBIR/STTR proposal development. It clarifies what constitutes eligible Research, Development, Testing, and Evaluation (RDT&E) activities versus ineligible commercial purchases, and explains how COTS/NDI items are treated under SBIR/STTR funding rules.

## Document Purpose
This attachment provides BST proposal teams with authoritative definitions governing SBIR/STTR eligibility to ensure Phase I and Phase II proposals comply with federal regulations (15 USC 638, SBA Policy Directive, DoD FMR). It is explicitly marked as "Info only; do not include in Memo."

## Key Regulatory Definitions

### Phase I and Phase II Conditions
- **Phase I**: Conduct feasibility-related experimental/theoretical research to determine scientific and technical merit and feasibility
- **Phase II**: Continue R&D from Phase I; includes special testing and evaluation authority
- **Direct-to-Phase II**: Requires agency determination that offeror's idea has sufficient scientific and technical feasibility despite skipping Phase I

### Research or Research and Development (R/R&D) - Eligible
Includes systematic studies directed toward:
1. Greater knowledge/understanding of subject
2. Applying knowledge/innovation to meet unmet needs
3. Production of useful materials, devices, systems, or methods (including design, development, improvement of prototypes and new processes)

Covers R&D in all fields: physical sciences, engineering, etc.

### COTS and NDI Treatment - Not Eligible
- Ready-to-use products purchased directly from commercial sources without alteration are NOT suitable for SBIR/STTR funding
- Examples: ready-to-use products, training services, software licenses, SaaS
- First article purchases and minor adjustments not funded
- Commercial items acquired for testing without RDT&E engineering/design/integration effort not funded

**Exception**: COTS/NDI required for RDT&E test purposes may be funded.

### Modified COTS/Modified NDI - Eligible (with conditions)
- Commercially available items modified to satisfy user requirements ARE eligible
- Eligible costs: first article, modification of first article, first article testing
- Follow-on purchases not eligible
- Quantity limited to what's needed for RDT&E acceptance tests
- Modification must significantly change performance envelope (differs from incremental technology refreshment)

**Distinction**: Continuous technology refreshment (incremental improvement during maintenance) is NOT funded; developmental modification is.

### Developing COTS or Commercial Product
- Offeror must explain intended modifications to COTS or commercial product
- Proposal must identify scientific/technical baseline from literature
- Must describe RDT&E efforts advancing this baseline

## Proposal Requirements

### For Direct-to-Phase II Awards
- Provide sufficient information for agency to determine scientific and technical feasibility and merit per 15 USC 638(cc)
- Team discussion must address:
  - Qualifications for conducting RDT&E
  - Commercialization pathway

### Tie to Defense Acquisition Program
- Offeror must identify any Defense Acquisition Program tied to proposal (if known)
- Used for tracking in Federal Procurement Data System (FPDS)
- If unknown, state so in proposal

## Notable Details
- Document is regulatory guidance based on: 15 USC 638, SBA SBIR/STTR Policy Directive (Oct 2020), and DoD FMR Vol. 2A, Chapter 1, Section 0102 (June 2004, as amended)
- Applies to both Phase I and Phase II conditions
- Creates clear boundaries between eligible RDT&E funding and ineligible commercial procurement
- File location indicates this was used in BST's 2022 AFWERX SBIR Phase II soil moisture mapping proposal effort# AFVentures Customer Memorandum Form (CAS 29MAR23)
