## Executive Summary
DARPA's ERIS is an open, continuous call for disruptive technology solutions from U.S. and international companies, universities, and individuals. The initiative operates as a digital marketplace where pre-vetted "awardable" solutions are made available to DoD activities for rapid acquisition through Other Transaction Authority. Companies submit 7-minute video pitches that are assessed monthly against four required elements and can receive awards for research, development, prototyping, and testing.

## Key Program Elements

### Eligibility & Participation
- **Who can submit:** U.S.-based (large/small business, university, non-profit, individual), plus foreign universities/research institutions (subject to export control compliance)
- **Topic areas:** Four focus areas defined by DARPA:
  - Detecting and tracking elusive objects of interest (air, land, space)
  - Overcoming sensing system limitations (SWaP-C, performance)
  - Advanced antenna technologies
  - Technologies for resilience/efficiency of strategic systems (critical infrastructure, command-and-control networks)

### Submission Timeline & Process
- **Open period:** December 9, 2024 – May 30, 2025
- **Collection cycles:** Monthly (deadline 12:00 Noon ET last day of month)
- **Assessment window:** Results within 30 days of collection period close
- **Continuous resubmission:** Non-awardable solutions can be resubmitted in subsequent months with feedback sessions available

### Technical Submission Requirements

**Video Format:**
- Maximum 7 minutes (exceeding this is primary rejection reason)
- HD 1280x720 resolution, .mp4 format under 1 GB
- Rec709 or sRGB color space
- No restrictive markings except copyright notice

**Required Video Content Elements (4):**
1. Define the problem and current state of the art
2. How the solution advances the state of the art
3. Team capability (key personnel vision, expertise, experience)
4. Defense and/or commercial market use case/impact

**Required Submission Form Elements:**
- Company/individual name (must match SAM.gov if applicable)
- Website, UEI (Unique Entity ID), business size classification
- Nontraditional vs. traditional contractor status
- Socioeconomic designations
- Principal place of business address
- Topic area selection
- Technology Readiness Level (TRL)
- At least 5 relevant keywords
- Video submission point of contact with email/phone
- Submission title (< 128 characters)
- Abstract description (1,500 characters max)
- Four supplemental slides in prescribed format (Appendix B)

**Supplemental Slides (4 mandatory):**
1. ERIS Submission Information (general submission data)
2. Company Introduction (succinct overview of company and motivation)
3. ERIS Submission Criteria Quad Chart (summary of four video content requirements)
4. Solution Overview & DARPA White Space Chart (what is being done and how; metrics demonstrating impact)

### Assessment & Evaluation

**Compliance Review (within 1 business day):**
- Video length, viewability, graphic legibility
- Prohibited markings check
- Format/resolution/file type compliance
- Submission form completeness
- SAM.gov accuracy verification
- Topic area fit and TRL consistency
- Supplemental slides format compliance

**Peer Assessment:**
- 3+ member panel (government, industry, academic subject matter experts)
- Non-government SMEs operate under NDAs
- Assessment against published scoring rubric (Appendix C)
- Final awardable/non-awardable decision by Government Selecting Official (GSO)
- Scoring and assessor comments provided to all submitters

**Organizational Conflicts of Interest (OCI) Mitigation:**
- SMEs prohibited from assessing their own solutions or competitors where they hold financial interest
- All assessors complete government ethics training
- Minimum 3-member peer panel format with government official final decision authority
- Government monitors assessor scoring consistency to identify bias

### Post-Award & Marketplace Terms

**"Awardable" Status Benefits:**
- Solutions deemed "post-competitive" under 10 USC 4021, 4022, 4023
- Eligible for research, development, prototyping, test/evaluation, and procurement contracts
- Fully negotiable award terms (payment, IP rights, data rights, schedule, milestones, pricing)
- Potential for multiple awards with single/multiple customers
- No price ceilings or duration limits on awards

**Marketplace Management:**
- "Awardable" solutions remain in ERIS marketplace for 12 months, then expire/removed
- DARPA may remove awardable submissions before 12-month expiration at its sole discretion
- Company names and solutions published on DARPAConnect.us (can opt out with written notice to ERIS@darpa.mil)
- Submitting entity retains ownership of video and submission data; may request removal anytime

### Data Rights & Licensing
By submitting, companies grant DARPA government-wide, nonexclusive, fully paid-up, non-assignable, non-royalty bearing licenses:
1. To view, review, research, comment, share video/data within government and covered contractors (assessments, market research, requirements development, procurement consideration, award)
2. To view, review, research, share for process improvement (assessment/selection/criteria/interface refinement) in perpetuity
3. To transcribe video for search, accessibility, marketing, reporting, market research, requirements development (perpetual license in transcription data)
4. To use video/data for government training (ERIS planning, implementation, processes, assessment, feedback, administration)

### Important Notes for Submitters
- All submission preparation costs borne by submitter; no government reimbursement
- "Awardable" rating does not guarantee any award
- Can submit one or multiple video solutions during open period
- Feedback sessions available via office hours to review scoring and plan resubmissions
- Questions directed to ERIS@darpa.mil
- More information: www.darpaconnect.us/ERIS

## Notable Details
- **Streamlined pathway:** ERIS designed as low-barrier entry point vs. traditional DARPA solicitations
- **Rapid timeline:** 30-day assessment turnaround; continuous monthly collection cycles
- **Multiple award potential:** Single submission can lead to awards from multiple DoD customers
- **Weekly office hours:** ERIS Manager (Applied Research Institute/ARI) provides feedback sessions to improve resubmissions
- **Non-proprietary submissions:** All videos/supplemental materials must be unclassified, non-proprietary, non-export controlled, non-CUI
- **SME pool:** Assessors from industry, academia, non-profit research institutions with programs aligned to DARPA mission
- **Dispute resolution:** Any scoring disputes addressed to GSO

## Document Metadata
- Type: Invited extension proposal
- Client/Agency: NASA (Science Activation Collective/SciAct)
- Program/Solicitation: AREN (AEROKATS and ROVER Education Network) - Program Years 6-10
- Date: April 16, 2020 (submission date); covers PY6-PY10 (2021-2025)
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: Aeropod, kite systems, sensor platforms
- Key Personnel: Paul (Andy) Henry (PI, Wayne RESA); Kay Rufty and Jack Elston (BST); Geoff Bland (NASA GSFC co-inventor of Aeropod/ROVER)

## Executive Summary
AREN is a NASA-funded experiential STEM education program that trains the next generation of scientists and engineers to observe Earth using novel low-cost kite-borne remote sensing technologies (Aeropods) and remotely operated vehicles (ROVERs). This invited extension proposal seeks to expand and deepen AREN's reach from 17 states to all 50 states while increasing participation from underserved populations, developing GLOBE-integrated learning activities, establishing sustainable hardware distribution, and advancing technology development through Years 6-10 (2021-2025).

## Technical Approach

### Overall Strategy
AREN employs experiential, hands-on learning centered on authentic NASA Earth science concepts and operational practices. The approach includes:
- Kite-borne sensor platforms (Aeropods) for remote sensing education
- ROVER platforms for spatially variable in-situ measurements
- Engagement across K-12, undergraduate, informal, and community science settings
- Integration with GLOBE Program protocols and data systems
- Engineering design activities (wind tunnels, sensor package development, kite design)
- Data analysis and visualization tools development
- Dissemination through online training, lending libraries, and distributed 3D printing

### Key Technical Areas for PY6-10:
1. **Activity & Curriculum Development**: Nine-week middle school course in progress; simplified introductory materials (MiniKites, "Middle Kite" in development); Wind Direction activity at 10-50m altitude; GIS data visualization; ROVER pilot activities
2. **ROVER Platform Evolution**: ROVER X7 and X10 (kit-based) versions with glue-free construction; integration of Arduino-based sensor systems; Vernier-compatible sensor packages
3. **Aeropod Development**: Multiple new designs tested and deployed; 3D printing enabled local production at multiple sites; "Thermopod" (thermal imager) kit development; enhanced online content
4. **Wind Tunnel Development**: UMES wind tunnel design/fabrication/testing for aerodynamic understanding; team-based learning component
5. **Data Infrastructure**: Working with GLOBE to develop array-based (multidimensional) data capabilities for transect/profile data; moving beyond single-point observations typical of GLOBE protocols; image/raster data support

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Aeropod
- **What it is**: Miniaturized, low-cost NASA remote sensing instrument for kite-borne deployment
- **Status**: Multiple stable designs developed; 3D printing enables distributed production; licensed to GLOBE and American Kitefliers Association
- **Proposed use in AREN**: Core platform for introducing remote sensing and in-situ observation concepts; used in formal and informal educational settings
- **Key milestones**: GLOBE license acquisition (2020/21); commercial production (2022/23); integration with GLOBE protocols
- **Related products**: Thermopod (thermal infrared imager variant) for Urban Heat Island studies and engineering design

### ROVER (Remotely Operated Vehicles)
- **What it is**: Remotely operated platform for spatially distributed in-situ measurements, particularly water quality
- **Versions**: ROVER X7 (current stable); ROVER X10 (new kit-based version)
- **Design features**: Glue-free construction for classroom assembly; multiple dissemination options (plan-built with suggestions, kits-in-a-box, fully assembled)
- **Sensor packages**: Vernier-based standard package; custom Arduino-based alternatives in development
- **Proposed use**: Highlight spatially variable measurements; water quality monitoring; integration with GLOBE water quality protocols
- **Key milestones**: ROVER X10 kits available (2021/22); ROVER GLOBE Learning Activity (2022/23); GLOBE license acquisition (2023/24)

### Kite Systems
- **Great Winds "Frustrationless Fliers"**: Introductory training kites
- **"Middle Kite"**: New student-built design in development with Great Winds Kites (2022); designed for meaningful lift capacity for small instruments
- **MiniKites**: Simplified dissemination approach in development
- **Wind Direction instrument** ("Windirator"): For measuring wind direction at altitudes ≤50m
- **Supplier partnership**: Into The Wind (kite vendor); Great Winds Kites (manufacturer)

### Data Tools & Platforms
- **MapKnitter** (Public Lab): Enhanced tool for stitching aerial images; ongoing investment by commercial partner
- **Fish-Eye GL Barrel Distortion Removal tool**: Image processing from AREN 1.0
- **Image Sequencer**: Image processing tool developed under AREN 1.0
- **AEROKATS.org website**: New platform for hosting training modules (2021 onward)
- **GLOBE Database enhancement**: Working to support multidimensional array data; raster/image data capabilities

## Use Cases & Applications

### Educational Settings
1. **K-12 Formal Education**: Cohort-based training for educators; implementation in classrooms and units; standards-aligned learning experiences
2. **Middle School**: Nine-week course in Remote Sensing using AREN technologies (in development)
3. **University Level**: Semester courses in aviation and engineering design; freshman engineering labs with Aeropod/ROVER design activities; junior-level aerial operations in remote sensing
4. **Informal Science Education**: Family Science Nights, public events, environmental centers, community science groups
5. **Teacher Professional Development**: Multi-day summer institutes and successive online webinars

### Research & Real-World Applications
- **Assateague Island Mapping**: Implemented and supported by National Park Service (highlighted as "real-world research" example)
- **Water Quality Monitoring**: ROVER platform for creek/water body assessment
- **Urban Heat Island Studies**: Thermopod deployment
- **Atmospheric Profile Measurement**: Kite-borne profiling with multiple sensors
- **Arctic Communities**: Alaskan villages using AREN remote sensing to identify physical pathways to food sources

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** Annual Progress Report
- **Client/Agency:** NASA Science Mission Directorate Science Activation Program

  - PocketLab Weather Profiler AeroPod

## Executive Summary

AREN is a NASA Science Activation initiative focused on training the next generation of scientists, engineers, and professionals through experiential learning with kite-borne instrumentation (AEROKATS) and instrumented mobile platforms (ROVERs). In Year 9 (2023-2024), the program reached participants across diverse settings including K-12 schools, universities, indigenous communities in Arctic Alaska, and public citizen science events. The project operates through 10 partner institutions and achieved significant milestones in technology development, educator training, and community engagement while advancing toward commercialization of key platforms.

## Technical Approach

### Education & Training Model
- **Two primary flagship events:** TerraROVER workshop (May) and Summer Institute (July-August)
- **Virtual training delivery** for geographically dispersed educators (35-46 participants in main events)
- **Tiered engagement:** Individual consultations, small group training, large public events, formal/informal education
- **Train-the-trainer model** emphasizing sustainable implementation in partner institutions

### Technology Development Approach
- **Iterative hardware maturation:** Progression from in-house manufacturing to commercial production readiness
- **Lightweight platform philosophy:** MiniCam <40g enables use on smaller, more manageable kites
- **Modular instrumentation:** UHIP (Universal Hardware Instrumentation Package) provides flexible sensor integration
- **Production optimization:** Transitioning from 3D printing to injection-molded components and domestic commercial manufacturing partners
- **Version control & documentation:** Comprehensive operational manuals, tutorial videos, and lesson plans

### Integration with Broader NASA Mission
- Alignment with 4 NASA SMD Science Activation Mid-Level Objectives (MLOs)
- Focus on diversity, STEM career development, and community science
- Cross-collaboration with other SciAct initiatives (GLOBE, NEBP, PLACES)

## Products & Capabilities Described

### MiniCam Aeropod
- **What it is:** Lightweight (<40g) kite aerial imaging platform with fixed camera system
- **Evolution:** Progressed from V1 to V4 with improvements in durability, functionality, image quality
- **Latest upgrades:** Color correction filter for high-quality imagery from low-cost camera
- **Production:** ~80 units provided for Summer Institute and partner use in 2024
- **Uses:** Remote sensing education, community science, citizen science applications
- **Advantages:** Simple, affordable, easily flies on smaller kites, accessible for inexperienced participants
- **Commercial status:** Licensed for external production; prototypes from Great Winds Kite Co. (GWK) also deployed

### MiniTwinCam
- **What it is:** Lightweight iteration of dual-camera concept with different optical filters
- **Purpose:** Basic spectral comparisons from aerial platform
- **Status:** In development; prototype tested with favorable results at ISARRA conference

### TerraROVER (Terrestrial Remote Observation Vehicle)
- **What it is:** Wheeled ground platform for close-range remote sensing and thermal imaging
- **Status:** Approaching mature configuration; 40 units produced in 2024
- **Design updates:** Simplified for reduced production time/costs; purchased wheels and outsourced polymer decks (moved from in-house 3D printing)
- **Instrumentation:** Integrates with UHIP V2 (Universal Hardware Instrumentation Package) with FLIR thermal camera
- **Primary mission:** Urban Heat Island effect mapping and surface temperature measurement
- **Production evolution:** Boston University engineering capstone project investigating scaling and kit-based solutions
- **Commercialization:** Production transitioning to domestic commercial partner

### UHIP (Universal Hardware Instrumentation Package)
- **What it is:** Modular sensor integration platform for TerraROVER
- **Current versions:** UHIP V1 and UHIP V2 (newer)
- **Core capability:** Surface temperature mapping and data visualization
- **Developer:** James Moon-Dupree (RESA) with support from BST team
- **Future development:** TRIP (Totally Remote Instrumentation Package) using Raspberry Pi 5 with web-based user interface and autonomous operation capability

### Aeropod Systems (Various Payloads)
- **Standard imaging:** MiniCam for basic aerial photography
- **Atmospheric profiling:** Kestrel Profiler AeroPod (flagship high-capability option)
- **Air quality monitoring:** AtmoTube particle sensors, AtmoTubePro
- **Weather measurement:** PocketLab Weather Profiler AeroPod (entry-level atmospheric profiler in development)
- **Spectral imaging:** MiniTwinCam (dual-camera with different filters)
- **Concept stage:** AeroAcq Zero (minimal sensor package with Aeropod, small/lightweight)

### AquaROVER
- **What it is:** Water-based platform for aquatic science observations
- **Recent milestone:** Sailing AquaROVER successfully fabricated and tested (2024, Boston University collaboration)
- **Uses:** Water quality monitoring, habitat assessment
- **Educational focus:** Integration into formal and informal education settings (e.g., Living Classrooms Foundation)

### Kite Systems
- **Frustrationless Flier:** Beginner-friendly kites for training
- **Delta kites:** Stable platform for aerial work
- **Tower Kite:** Purpose-built for AREN, developed by Ken and Suzanne Sadow; field tested with larger audiences in 2024
- **Aerovee:** Standard research kite with documented aerodynamic characteristics
- **Edo kite:** Reference platform for aerodynamic validation

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** Proof-of-Concept Proposal (TTO Colorado Advanced Industries Accelerator Program)
- **Client/Agency:** Colorado Advanced Industries Accelerator Program; NOAA Unmanned Aircraft Systems Program Office (first customer/investor)
- **Program/Solicitation:** Colorado Advanced Industries Accelerator Program
- **Date:** March 3, 2014
- **BST Products/Systems Referenced:** SwiftPilot Pro autopilot; command/control/communications/data networking software
- **Key Personnel:** Brian Argrow (PI, University of Colorado RECUV); Jack Elston (BST founder, former RECUV PhD researcher); James Mack (RECUV Professional Research Assistant, chief technician)

## Executive Summary
This proposal describes the TTwistor, an advanced small unmanned aircraft system (UAS) derived from the successful Tempest UAS that was developed by RECUV researchers and deployed in the VORTEX2 tornado research campaign. The TTwistor improves upon the Tempest design through a twin-propeller configuration and integration of BST's SwiftPilot Pro autopilot, enabling better instrument payload placement and modular nosecone designs. The proposal positions TTwistor to address NOAA's vision of revolutionizing observing strategies while capitalizing on anticipated growth in the small electric UAS commercial market.

## Technical Approach

**Airframe Design:**
- Twin-propeller design (motor-propeller mounted on each wing) replacing the single fuselage-mounted motor of Tempest
- Enables instruments and probes to be mounted near the airframe centerline with forward-facing capability into undisturbed airflow
- Propeller airflow increases local circulation to improve takeoff lift
- Swappable modular "nosecones" custom-designed for specific instruments or payloads
- Manufactured by UASUSA, Inc.

**Autopilot & Control:**
- Integration of BST SwiftPilot Pro autopilot
- Custom command, control, communications, and data networking software developed by BST (proof-of-concept deployment software)

**Communications (Planned):**
- 900-MHz phased-array communications system with electronic beam steering (superior to mechanically-steered antennas used in Tempest)
- Prototype tested; second prototype in development
- Partnership with Boulder, CO antenna manufacturer First RF Corp. for development and commercialization
- Not included in current proof-of-concept but noted as future capability

## Products & Capabilities Described

### SwiftPilot Pro Autopilot
- **What it is:** Advanced autopilot system for small UAS
- **How proposed to be used:** Integrated into TTwistor airframes to replace/improve upon earlier Tempest autopilot systems
- **Performance context:** Enables reliable, robust operation with unmatched performance in small electric UAS class

### BST Command/Control/Communications/Data Networking Software
- **What it is:** Software architecture for UAS mission operations
- **How proposed to be used:** Custom development of proof-of-concept demonstration software for TTwistor deployment
- **Heritage:** Derived from Dr. Jack Elston's NetUAS communications architecture successfully deployed with Tempest in VORTEX2

### TTwistor Aircraft (Airframe + Autopilot Integration)
- **What it is:** Complete small electric UAS combining UASUSA airframe with BST SwiftPilot Pro
- **Specifications:** Small, electrically-powered, twin-propeller configuration with payload capacity and modular nosecone design
- **Performance claims:** Superior to Tempest design; expanded capabilities for scientific and commercial applications

## Use Cases & Applications

**Historical Context (Tempest):**
- Severe weather research (VORTEX2 tornado research campaign, spring 2009-2010)
- Atmospheric sensing and mobile communications experiments
- Demonstrated successful operation in supercell storms and tornado environments

**Proposed TTwistor Applications:**
- NOAA environmental monitoring and observing (addressing NOAA UASPO vision)
- Precision agriculture
- Emergency/first responder operations
- Surveying and mapping
- Education and science research
- Monitoring dangerous or remote areas (poles, oceans, wildlands, volcanic islands, wildfires)

**Market Targets:**
- Public entities (government agencies, state universities)
- Civil/commercial operators (once FAA regulatory framework established)
- Former Tempest UAS customers (University of Nebraska, MIT, US Navy Research Lab, Raytheon, Lockheed Martin, Airware)

## Market & Commercial Context

**Existing Market Validation:**
- More than 50 Tempest UAS units sold by UASUSA
- Proven customer base across government, defense, and academic sectors

**Growth Projections (from 2013 AUVSI Report):**
- Small electric UAS market identified as emerging high-growth sector
- Precision agriculture and public safety cited as most promising commercial and civil markets
- Projected $13.6 billion economic impact in first three years of NAS integration (2015-2017)
- Projected $82.1 billion cumulative impact 2015-2025
- Estimated 103,776 new jobs by 2025

**Regulatory Context:**

- NOAA Unmanned Aircraft Systems Program Office identified as first customer and investor
- TTwistor directly addresses NOAA UASPO goals: increase observing capacity, develop high science-return missions, transition cost-effective operationally feasible UAS into routine operations

## Document Metadata
- Type: Proposal/White Paper
- Client/Agency: Army Research Laboratory (ARL)
- Program/Solicitation: ARL Broad Agency Announcement (BAA) W911NF-12-R-0011-04
- Date: November 9, 2016
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: Soil Moisture Mapping (SMM) sUAS
- Key Personnel: Maciej Stachura (Black Swift Technologies, CTO and NASA SMM sUAS PI); Andrew S. Jones (CSU, PI); Steven J. Fletcher (CSU, Co-PI); Jeffery D. Niemann (CSU, Co-PI); Al Gasiewski (CU, Co-PI)

## Executive Summary
This three-year Army-funded research project (Feb. 2017 – Jan. 2020, $3.33M total) proposes to improve Army operational capabilities in soil moisture characterization, numerical weather prediction error quantification, and land surface data assimilation at high spatial resolutions (1-30 m). The work integrates small UAS remote sensing systems (operated by Black Swift Technologies and CU) with satellite microwave data to support Army applications including ISR, artillery meteorology, boundary layer analysis, and vehicle/robotics mobility assessment. The project leverages existing CSU soil moisture downscaling capabilities and the recently developed Soil Moisture Mapping sUAS.

## Technical Approach

The project comprises three integrated theme areas:

**Theme A: Met Office UM NWP Error Characterization ($674,916 total)**
- Compare Met Office Unified Model output from USAF sources against in situ measurements
- Create statistical analyses to identify performance bottlenecks and mismatches in NWP model inputs for Artillery Met systems
- Team training with Met Office data assimilation team in May-June each year
- Collaborate with ARL/BED NWP and Artillery Met scientists

**Theme B: Soil Moisture Remote Sensing Data Assimilation ($967,070 total)**
- Perform innovation vector/perturbation sensitivity analysis of soil moisture and land surface properties using downscaled data
- Design Army-relevant scale data assimilation system with design experiments and tests
- Years 1-2: Testing at USDA Reynolds Creek, ID site using observational datasets
- Year 3: Extend to White Sands Missile Range (WSMR) site with ARL/BED collaboration
- Leverage existing CSU Equilibrium Moisture from Topography, Vegetation, and Soil (EMT+VS) soil moisture downscaling system—a high-resolution Army GIS-compatible framework created through prior Army Phase 2 SBIR

**Theme C: Collaborative Remote Sensing Cal/val Field Studies ($1,686,183 total)**
- Year 1: Prepare for Reynolds Creek field experiment (summer 2018); develop sUAS and satellite microwave sensor forward operator simulation capabilities
- Year 2: Conduct Reynolds Creek field experiment; intercompare, calibrate, and validate results; characterize sensor and model initialization errors
- Year 3: Replicate experiment at WSMR, New Mexico to test portability and characterize microwave sUAS sensor data for Army-scale data assimilation

## Products & Capabilities Described

**Soil Moisture Mapping (SMM) sUAS**
- What it is: A small unmanned aircraft system developed over three years through NASA funding (partnership between Black Swift Technologies and University of Colorado) for high-resolution soil moisture measurement
- Capabilities: Equipped with L-band radiometer and MiCo antenna for accurate soil moisture measurements; includes soil moisture extraction algorithm
- Proposed use: Primary sensing platform for field calibration/validation studies at Reynolds Creek (2018) and WSMR (2019-2020); high-resolution observational data collection to validate satellite microwave sensors and test data assimilation systems
- Deployment history: Successfully deployed at NASA Cal/Val site in Canton, OK and precision agriculture site in Eastern Colorado; both included in situ validation

**L-Band Radiometer & MiCo Antenna**
- Designed and tested by CU team (Prof. Gasiewski's lab)
- Key enabling technologies for accurate soil moisture measurements from small UAS

**CSU EMT+VS Soil Moisture Downscaling System**
- What it is: High-resolution soil moisture downscaling capability operating at 1-30 m spatial resolution
- Status: Created through prior Army Phase 2 SBIR (CSU with Technology Services Corporation); currently in Subsequent Phase 2 activity
- Features: Army GIS-compatible framework
- Proposed use: Foundation for developing high-fidelity soil moisture data assimilation framework in Theme B

## Use Cases & Applications

**Army Operational Applications:**
- Intelligence/Surveillance/Reconnaissance (ISR)
- Atmospheric boundary layer analysis systems
- Artillery meteorological systems
- Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) error characterization and impact assessment
- Vehicle and robotics mobility assessment on battlefield
- Vector-borne disease and phytobiome system interaction analysis within battlefield environment
- Land surface characterization of battlefield environments

**Specific Test Sites:**
- USDA Reynolds Creek, ID (Year 2 field study)
- White Sands Missile Range (WSMR), New Mexico (Year 3 field study/transition)

This is a proposal document; no results are presented. The document establishes the project framework and anticipated deliverables rather than reporting completed work.

- BST expertise includes:
  - Integration and operation of advanced payloads on sUAS
  - Development of systems for NOAA and NSF for severe storm and boundary layer sampling
  - Ongoing NASA effort sampling active volcanic plumes
  - Flight certification and safety reviews for sUAS operations
  - 150+ FAA Certificates of Authorization written and utilized
  - Successfully completed four NASA Flight Safety Review boards for sUAS
  - Experience operating at DoD facilities
  - Over 500 flight experiments conducted
  - 10+ years of sUAS experience

**Project Budget:**
- Total 3-year budget: $3,328,168
- BST Subaward: $498,858 total (Year 1: $179,395; Year 2: $176,116; Year 3: $143,347)
- BST provides significant equipment support in Year 1 ($63,198 for SMM sUAS deployment equipment)

**Institutional Integration:**
- Partnership with Colorado State University (prime contractor), University of Colorado, and Black Swift Technologies
- Integration with NATO Applied Vehicle Team (AVT-248) for Next Generation NATO Reference Mobility Model
- Ongoing SBIR collaborations with Army (ARL, TARDEC), ERDC/CRREL, ERDC/CHL
- Proposed CRADA (#16-15) between CSU and ARL for future collaborative research

**Critical Needs Addressed:**
- Current satellite soil moisture products inadequate for Army operations (250-1000 m resolution provided by USAF insufficient)
- Need for high-resolution (1-30 m) data assimilation systems at Army-relevant scales
- Requirement to understand Met Office UM NWP error impacts on Artillery Met systems
- Transitionable solutions through existing GIS industry partner linkages for battlefield deployment

- Type: White paper (proposal)
- Client/Agency: Army Research Laboratory (ARL)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposed a three-year collaborative effort (2017–2019) to develop Army-relevant capabilities in data assimilation and UAS-based remote sensing for soil moisture characterization and boundary layer meteorology. The work integrates soil moisture data assimilation, UAS remote sensing validation, and numerical weather prediction (NWP) error characterization to support target recognition, trafficability assessment, and artillery meteorology applications.

## Technical Approach

### Theme A: Boundary Layer Data Assimilation at Army-relevant Scales
- Develop soil moisture data assimilation and surface energy balance modeling for boundary layer improvement
- Conduct innovation vector analysis on soil moisture estimates using existing downscaled datasets
- Design and implement Army-scale data assimilation components and synthetic experiments
- Apply innovation vector analysis to Reynolds Creek, ID and White Sands, NM field datasets in collaboration with ARL/BED
- Focus on data distribution-dependent design for data assimilation systems

### Theme B: UAS Remote Sensing of Soil Moisture and Land Surface Characteristics
- Deploy UAS-based remote sensing platforms for fine-scale soil moisture measurement
- Year 1 (2017): Prepare for Reynolds Creek field experiments; coordinate with team on microwave sensor forward operator simulation capabilities
- Year 2 (2018): Conduct Reynolds Creek, ID field experiment; perform calibration/validation intercomparisons; characterize sensor and model initialization errors
- Year 3 (2019): Conduct White Sands, NM field experiment; integrate characterized microwave UAS sensor data into Army-scale data assimilation systems

### Theme C: UKMET Unified Model NWP Error Characterization
- Perform error characterization of the UKMET Unified Model for Artillery Met and Boundary Layer applications
- Analyze model biases and error distribution patterns
- Explore atmospheric profiling capabilities; leverage balloon sounding data from ARL collaborators

## Products & Capabilities Described

**UAS Remote Sensing System**
- Purpose: Fine-scale soil moisture measurement and land surface characterization
- Equipped with microwave sensors for soil moisture estimation
- Used for calibration/validation of data assimilation algorithms
- Supports error characterization of sensor and model initialization

**Data Assimilation Framework**
- Army-scale soil moisture data assimilation system
- Integration of innovation vector analysis methodology
- Support for data distribution-dependent design
- Synthetic experiment capabilities for validation

**Microwave Sensor Forward Operator**
- Simulation tools for microwave sensor behavior
- Support for cal/val activities and error characterization

## Use Cases & Applications

- **Artillery Meteorology (Artillery Met)**: Improved meteorological support for artillery targeting and fire control
- **Boundary Layer Characterization**: Enhanced understanding of boundary layer phenomena for military operations
- **Target Recognition**: Soil moisture and surface characteristics as inputs for target detection and classification
- **Trafficability Assessment**: Soil moisture data to support military vehicle mobility predictions
- **Army-scale Operations**: Capabilities scaled appropriately for Army operational planning and tactical support

## Field Sites and Collaborations

- **Reynolds Creek Experimental Watershed, Idaho**: Primary field validation site for soil moisture and boundary layer measurements (experiments planned for summer 2018)
- **White Sands Missile Range, New Mexico**: Secondary field site for extended validation; collaboration with ARL/Battlefield Environment Division (ARL/BED)
- **Academic Partners**: Colorado State University (Andrew S. Jones, Steven J. Fletcher, Jeffrey D. Niemann) and University of Colorado–Boulder (Al Gasiewski)

## Requested Resources

- Use of White Sands facilities for Year 3 field experiments
- Boundary layer modeling coordination with ARL/BED
- Access to Army High-Performance Computing (HPC) facilities for NWP data analysis

## Executive Summary
This three-year research initiative proposes to develop high-resolution soil moisture and land surface characterization capabilities for Army boundary layer and Artillery Meteorology applications. The work integrates existing EMT+VS soil moisture downscaling systems with new data assimilation frameworks, UAS/satellite remote sensing, and field validation studies at Army-relevant scales (1-3 meter resolutions), with operational transition pathways into Army GIS frameworks.

## Technical Approach

**Overall Strategy:** Three integrated theme areas addressing Army NWP/Artillery Met needs:

**Theme A: Met Office Unified Model (UM) NWP Error Characterization and Error Modeling**
- Characterize biases and error distributions of the Met Office Unified Model as it relates to Artillery Meteorology and boundary layer applications
- Error modeling for Army-specific systems
- Exploration of error dependencies and distributions
- Balloon sounding collaborations with ARL

**Theme B: Boundary Layer Remote Sensing Data Assimilation at Army-Relevant Scales**
- Soil moisture data assimilation and surface energy balance studies to improve boundary layer representation
- Innovation vector analysis of soil moisture estimates using existing downscaled datasets
- Design and implement Army-scale data assimilation synthetic experiments with data distribution-dependent design
- Applications to trafficability and target recognition
- Extensions to Reynolds Creek, ID and White Sands, NM sites

**Theme C: Collaborative Calibration/Validation Field Studies Using UAS/Satellite Remote Sensing**
- UAS remote sensing of fine-scaled soil moisture for calibration/validation
- Integration of UAS/satellite observations within data assimilation frameworks
- Field experiments at Reynolds Creek, ID (summer 2018) and White Sands Missile Range, NM
- Characterization of microwave sensor errors and model initialization errors
- Joint preparations with ARL/BED Atmospheric Science Center staff

## Products & Capabilities Described

**EMT+VS Soil Moisture Downscaling System**
- CSU-developed system built on existing Army Phase 2 SBIR results
- Demonstrated capability at 10-30 meter resolutions
- Current work transitioning to 3 meter resolutions with anticipated achievement of 1 meter spatial resolution
- Enables very high-fidelity soil moisture data assimilation matching unprecedented downscaling capabilities
- Integrates into Army GIS spatial frameworks for operational transition

**Black Swift Technologies UAS Platform**
- Small UAS (sUAS) with soil moisture mapping capabilities
- Role: High-resolution remote sensing for field validation studies
- Three years of NASA soil moisture mapping sUAS development
- Over 500 flight experiments conducted by BST team
- Will conduct direct observations at Reynolds Creek and White Sands for cal/val integration

**Data Assimilation Frameworks**
- Army-scale innovation vector analysis capabilities
- Data assimilation systems designed for high-resolution (1-meter) soil moisture fields
- Advanced error handling addressing non-Gaussian error biases
- Quality control and sensor error modeling at fine spatial scales

## Use Cases & Applications

1. **Artillery Meteorology**: Improved accuracy for fire control and ballistics calculations
2. **Boundary Layer Applications**: Surface energy balance studies and atmospheric boundary layer characterization
3. **Trafficability and Mobility**: Soil moisture characterization for vehicle movement prediction (NATO NG-NRMM collaboration, terramechanics community)
4. **Target Recognition**: Enhanced through improved land surface characterization
5. **Arctic and Field Operations**: Addressing current inadequacy of satellite products (250-1000 meter resolution from USAF) for Army battlefield applications
6. **DoD Weather Satellite Follow-on (WSF) Program**: Direct relevance to future satellite system requirements

N/A – This is a proposal document; no results yet. Work scheduled Feb. 1, 2017 – Jan. 31, 2020.

- Program/Solicitation: NextGen (Next Generation Air Transportation System); JPDO (Joint Planning and Development Office)

## Executive Summary
This document outlines NASA's role in supporting the Next Generation Air Transportation System (NextGen), a comprehensive modernization initiative to transform the U.S. National Airspace System (NAS). Written in the context of NextGen's development timeline (Epochs 1-3, spanning 2006-2025), the paper describes how NASA's Aeronautics Research Mission Directorate (ARMD) contributes to NextGen's key characteristics and capabilities through three core research programs: Airspace Systems, Aviation Safety, and Fundamental Aeronautics.

## Technical Approach
NASA's approach is structured around three core principles:
1. Mastering core competencies in aeronautics for the Nation across all flight regimes
2. Focusing research in areas appropriate to NASA's unique capabilities
3. Directly addressing fundamental NextGen research needs while collaborating with JPDO partner agencies

The research portfolio is organized to address air traffic management, environmental compliance, efficiency, and safety challenges. NASA contributes approximately $18 million annually in labor and procurement to JPDO planning and development activities, including staffing of the JPDO Deputy Director and division leadership roles.

## Products & Capabilities Described

### NASA-Developed Systems/Tools Referenced (Past Contributions):
- **Airspace Concept Evaluation System (ACES)** - Used to analyze initial NextGen concepts; result of NASA airspace-related research
- **Traffic Management Advisor** - Air traffic management tool
- **Multi-Center Traffic Management Advisor**
- **Surface Management System**
- **Synthetic Vision technology**
- **System-Level Design, Analysis and Simulation Tools**
- **Vehicle Health Systems**
- **Resilient Aircraft Controls** - For recovery from upset conditions

### NASA Programs and Their Focus Areas:

**1. Airspace Systems Program (Two Projects)**
- **NGATS ATM-Airspace Project:**
  - Develops fundamental concepts for optimal allocation of ground/air automation
  - Focus: Where, when, how, and extent of automation application
  - Key research areas:
    - Trajectory-based operations with 4D trajectory accuracy
    - Trajectory prediction, synthesis, and uncertainty management
    - Separation assurance and automated sequential processing/merging
    - Traffic Flow Management (TFM) with 2-3x current capacity handling
    - Dynamic airspace configuration
    - Performance-based services
    - Super-density operations near congested airports
    - System analysis and design tools

- **NGATS ATM-Airportal Project:**
  - Develops trajectory-based automation for surface operations
  - Key research areas:
    - Safe and efficient all-weather surface operations
    - Runway incursion minimization
    - Arrival/departure separation reduction
    - Metroplex (regional inter-airport) operations optimization
    - Coordinated arrival/departure operations
    - Airportal transition and integration management

**2. Fundamental Aeronautics Program (Three of four projects contribute to NextGen)**
- **Subsonic Fixed Wing Project:**
  - Noise reduction technologies (conventional and unconventional configs)
  - Emissions reduction (NOx, CO2, particulates)
  - Alternative fuels development
  - Noise and emissions prediction capabilities
  
- **Subsonic Rotary Wing Project:**
  - Similar environmental focus for helicopter/rotorcraft applications
  
- **Supersonics Project:**
  - Low-boom, low-drag supersonic configurations
  - Advanced aircraft concepts for enhanced capacity

**3. Aviation Safety Program (Four Projects)**
- **Integrated Vehicle Health Management (IVHM):**
  - Advanced health management technologies
  - Self-diagnostic and self-correcting onboard systems
  - Data mining tools for distributed aviation-safety data sources
  - Prognostic safety analysis capabilities

- **Integrated Intelligent Flight Deck (IIFD):**
  - Crew workload optimization
  - Situational awareness adaptation for NextGen environment

- **Integrated Resilient Aircraft Control (IRAC):**
  - Aircraft flight control automation/autonomy
  - Loss-of-control prevention
  - Fault, damage, and upset tolerance

- **Aircraft Aging and Durability (AAD):**
  - Advanced diagnostic and prognostic capabilities
  - Aging-related hazard detection and mitigation

## Use Cases & Applications

### NextGen Operational Scenarios:
- **Capacity Growth:** Handling 2-3x current traffic demand by 2025
- **Trajectory-Based Operations:** Gate-to-gate 4D commitments including gate identification, pushback time, takeoff time, complete airspace trajectory, touchdown time, gate arrival time
- **Mixed Fleet Operations:** Accommodating airline operations, air taxi operations, general aviation, and unmanned air vehicles
- **Dynamic Airspace:** Real-time airspace reconfiguration to balance workload, capacity, and demand
- **Weather Integration:** Integrated digital, probabilistic weather information in automation and decision-support tools
- **Super-Density Airport Operations:** Increased throughput at congested hub airports through reduced separation minima
- **Surface Operations:** All-weather runway complex optimization with efficient gate, taxiway, runway, and final approach management
- **Environmental Compliance:** Noise and emissions management for en route and airport operations
- **Safety-Critical Operations:** Enhanced aircraft health monitoring and prognostic safety analysis for higher-volume operations

- Chevron and noise reduction technologies in deployment

## Notable Details

### NextGen Vision & Timeline:
- **Three Epochs:** Epoch 1 (FY06-11 develop, FY10-15 implement), Epoch 2 (FY12-17 develop, FY14-19 implement), Epoch 3 (FY18-21 develop, FY20-25 implement)
- **NextGen Key Characteristics:** User focus, distributed decision-making, human/automation balance, scalability, robustness/resiliency, integrated safety management, environmental framework
- **NextGen Key Capabilities:** Network-enabled information access, performance-based operations, weather assimilation, layered adaptive security, PNT services, trajectory-based operations, equivalent visual operations, super-density operations

### Critical Research Challenges Requiring Resolution:
- Whether separation assurance should be performed by ground-based navigation service provider or aircraft
- Human vs. automation management and control responsibilities
- Uncertainty impacts on traffic flow management (particularly weather)
- Stability of aircraft gate-to-gate 4D trajectories
- Development of prognostic analysis to identify inadvertent safety impacts of NextGen concepts
- Aircraft efficiency and performance within environmental compliance constraints

### Current System Problems Addressed:
- **Capacity Limitations:** Current system already strained; forecast demand increase of 2-3x by 2025 unsustainable with existing infrastructure
- **Cost Impact:** Projected shortfall estimated at $9.2-23 billion annually in lost productivity, increased operational costs, higher fares, and eliminated flights
- **Rigidity:** Current airspace structure is rigid, restricts flexibility, increases queuing delays during weather
- **Mixed Fleet Challenges:** Cannot currently accommodate diverse aircraft types and equipage levels
- **Environmental Issues:** Noise and emissions constraining airport growth; en route emissions becoming problematic
- **Safety Approach:** Currently reactive rather than proactive; based on prescriptive rule compliance

### Organizational Structure:
- **JPDO Member Agencies:** DOT, DOD, DOC, DHS, FAA, NASA
- **NASA's ARMD Structure:** Three primary programs (Airspace Systems, Aviation Safety, Fundamental Aeronautics) plus supporting research
- **NASA Personnel in JPDO:** Deputy Director, Systems Engineering and Analysis Division Director, Enterprise Architecture and Engineering Division Director, representatives on executive council and multiple Independent Product Teams

### Technology Transition Approach:
Document emphasizes close collaboration between NASA researchers and FAA/user community throughout development to ensure effective transition from R&D to operational implementation. Notes tension between pressure to show quick near-term results (Epochs 1-2) versus necessity of long-term research investment (Epoch 3) for transformational NextGen capabilities.

## Document Metadata
- Type: Field campaign final report
- Client/Agency: US Department of Energy (DOE) Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Program
- Program/Solicitation: SBIR Phase II, Atmospheric Sounding topic
- Date: October 2021
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: S0 UAS
- Key Personnel: Jack Elston (Black Swift Technologies), Maciej Stachura (Black Swift Technologies), Gijs de Boer (Boreas Consulting, lead), Adam Houston, Ashraful Islam, Daniel Rico, Matthew Wilson (University of Nebraska-Lincoln)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies and University of Nebraska conducted a week-long field campaign at the DOE ARM Southern Great Plains facility in Oklahoma to evaluate and intercompare small uncrewed aircraft systems (sUAS) for atmospheric research. The campaign involved 95 sUAS flights totaling 18.6 flight hours, comparing data from the BST S0 fixed-wing UAS against radiosondes, tower instruments, and other UAS platforms (University of Nebraska M600 and Meteodrone). Results showed generally good agreement with radiosondes and tower measurements, though identified a ~1-1.5°C warm bias in the S0's temperature sensor.

## Technical Approach
- Conducted coordinated multi-platform flights at ARM SGP facility and Marshall (OK) mesonet site
- S0 operated both north and south of SGP 60 m tower; M600 and Meteodrone operated east of tower
- Flights designed to follow extra radiosondes launched as campaign component and conduct extended statistical sampling at tower instrument heights
- Data collection focused on system evaluation and intercomparison across multiple platforms
- Compared UAS-measured atmospheric quantities (temperature, relative humidity, wind speed/direction) against radiosondes, tower instruments, and sister platforms
- Ground testing conducted comparing UAS sensors against ARM ECOR (Energy Balance Bowen Ratio) system (results not finalized in report)

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Black Swift Technologies S0 UAS
- **What it is:** Fixed-wing small uncrewed aircraft system for atmospheric research
- **Configuration:** Equipped with temperature, relative humidity, and wind measurement sensors
- **Performance in campaign:**
  - Successfully conducted 95 total flights across the campaign
  - Showed capability to conduct extended hover/station-keeping at tower heights for statistical sampling
  - Wind measurements agreed well with radiosondes (mean errors near zero, ±5 m/s spread attributed to spatial variability)
  - Temperature sensor exhibited ~1-1.5°C warm bias relative to radiosondes and other platforms
  - Temperature bias showed slight dependence on solar incidence angle (~0.2°C smaller bias when heading directly into sun)

## Use Cases & Applications
- **Atmospheric boundary layer characterization:** Measuring lower atmosphere conditions critical to weather/climate understanding and numerical prediction models
- **Observing system intercomparison:** Validating UAS platforms against established observing systems (radiosondes, tower instruments, research aircraft)
- **Atmospheric research infrastructure:** Contributing to improved representation of boundary layer in atmospheric models
- **Multi-platform coordination:** Operating alongside established research teams (University of Colorado, University of Oklahoma, Oklahoma State University) in TRACER-UAS initiative

## Key Results

### Quantitative Findings:
- **Campaign scope:** 95 sUAS flights, 18.6 total flight hours
- **Temperature bias (S0):** ~1-1.5°C warm bias relative to radiosondes; slight variation with solar angle
- **Wind measurements:** Both S0 and Meteodrone generally captured wind speeds and directions measured by radiosondes; mean wind errors close to zero
- **Relative humidity variability (M600):** Significant variability noted; unclear if due to measurement bias or pressure-based altitude sensing issues
- **Tower-based wind comparison:** Mean errors near zero, ±5 m/s spread likely due to spatial variability in boundary layer winds
- **Temperature sensitivity to solar orientation:** S0 showed ~0.2°C smaller bias when aircraft heading directly into sun (0° sun angle)

### Qualitative Findings:
- Generally good agreement between UAS measurements and radiosondes/tower instruments
- Wind measurements from UAS platforms validated as reliable (previously considered uncertain)
- S0 temperature sensor housing identified as area for design improvement to address warm bias
- Rich dataset generated for continued UAS platform evaluation

## Notable Details

### Data Archiving & Access:
- All campaign data deposited in ARM Data Portal with digital object identifiers (DOIs)
- S0 data: de Boer et al. (2021), DOI: 10.5439/1824862
- Platform data publicly available through ARM for research community

### Publication Plan:
- Peer-reviewed manuscript in preparation for *Journal of Atmospheric and Oceanic Technology* (J. Tech)
- Will include comparisons with University of Colorado and University of Oklahoma platforms as part of TRACER-UAS initiative
- Conference presentations delivered at AGU Fall Meeting (December 2021) and ARM/ASR PI meeting (June 2021)

- Part of broader TRACER-UAS (TRACER Science Team Meeting, April 2021) effort

- S0 temperature sensor housing to be revisited to address documented warm bias

- Suggestion for tower enhancement: adding pressure sensors to enable altitude verification and calculation of derived variables (potential temperature)

- Weather conditions during campaign: generally good with moderate winds, favorable for operations
- High partnership satisfaction; strong collaboration with SGP facility team# ARM_Pre_Proposal: OPTIMUS Campaign

## Executive Summary
OPTIMUS proposes a two-week summer 2015 field campaign using the BlackSwift Tempest unmanned aircraft system to map high-resolution terrestrial surface properties at Oliktok Point in the Arctic tundra. The campaign would measure soil moisture, soil temperature, NDVI, surface elevation, and visible imagery to bridge the gap between point-scale ARM measurements and satellite-scale observations, improving understanding of atmosphere-surface interactions.

## Technical Approach

**Primary Platform:** BlackSwift Tempest UAS (3-meter wingspan, small unmanned aircraft system)

**Measurement Strategy:**
- Multiple mapping passes over two-week deployment period
- Coarse-resolution mapping of entire land-covered airspace
- High-resolution passes at lower altitudes near AMF3 instrumentation for cross-validation
- Data collection timing: Mid-July (post-snowmelt period), repeated over three years

**Sensor Suite & Specifications:**
1. **Soil Moisture:** Passive L-band microwave radiometer
   - Depth: ~5-20 cm
   - Resolution: 15 m at 15 m flight altitude
   
2. **Soil Temperature:** Infrared camera
   
3. **NDVI:** Near-infrared/red camera system
   
4. **Surface Elevation:** Onboard laser altimeter, EO camera, post-processing
   
5. **Visible Imagery:** Onboard EO (electro-optical) camera

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** Technical Manual / Standard Operating Procedure
- **Client/Agency:** U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center (ERDC); Joint Program Office - Joint Light Tactical Vehicles (JPO-JLTV)
- **Program/Solicitation:** JLTV Vehicle Acquisition Support
- **Date:** August 2013
- **Report Number:** ERDC/GSL SR-13-2
- **BST Products/Systems Referenced:** None (this is a reference document for BST's AFWERX SBIR Phase I project on Soil Moisture Mapping)
- **Key Personnel:** Maria T. Stevens, Brent W. Towne, George L. Mason, Jody D. Priddy, Javier E. Osorio, Clint A. Barela (ERDC authors)

## Executive Summary

This ERDC technical report establishes standardized procedures for measuring Vehicle Cone Index (VCI1)—the minimum soil strength required for a vehicle to consistently complete one pass over soft terrain without immobilization. The procedures define site selection criteria, test lane layouts, soil data collection methods using cone penetrometers and remolding equipment, and analysis methodology. VCI1 is used as a vehicle performance metric for ground vehicle acquisition to quantify mobility on soft soils.

## Technical Approach

### VCI1 Measurement Methodology

**Vehicle Testing Procedures:**
- Vehicles operate in optimal off-road configuration (lowest gear, all-wheel-drive, locked differentials where available)
- Slow, steady speed (2-3 mph) through test lanes
- For zero-pass tests: vehicle driven until immobilized; reverse attempted to confirm no-go condition
- For multi-pass tests: vehicle makes forward and reverse passes in same tracks until immobilization occurs
- Typically 5-10 zero-pass tests and equal number of multi-pass tests required to establish VCI1

**Soil Strength Characterization:**
- Measured via **Rating Cone Index (RCI) = Cone Index (CI) × Remold Index (RI)**
- **Cone Index (CI):** Soil shear strength obtained using standardized trafficability cone penetrometer
  - 30° cone with 0.5 sq-in. base area
  - Standard 300 psi dial (0-300 psi range; 300 psi = 150 lb vertical force)
  - Optional 750 psi dial available for firmer soils
  - Penetration rate: ~0.1 ft/s
  - Minimum 20 measurements per lane (10 per side, with 6 minimum adjacent to immobilized vehicle)
  
- **Remold Index (RI):** Soil sensitivity to strength loss under traffic
  - Measured on soil samples from three depths: surface-6", 6-12", 12-18"
  - Hvorslev sampler collects undisturbed samples
  - Cone measurements taken at 0-4" depth in sample, then sample remolded with 100 drops of 2.5-lb hammer
  - RI = remolded strength / initial strength (minimum RI = 1.0 if remolded strength exceeds initial)

### Site Selection Criteria

Test lanes must meet strict requirements:
1. **Location:** Naturally occurring off-road areas; floodplains, swampy areas, seasonal lakebeds
2. **Soil Type:** High Plasticity Clay (CH) per USCS—worst-case fine-grained soil for vehicle mobility
   - Minimal sand content (< ~2% sand acceptable)
   - No visible sand grit feel during cone penetration
3. **Physical Characteristics:**
   - Flat, level terrain
   - Minimum 2 vehicle lengths long
   - Straight with uniform consistency
   - Free of rocks, logs, tree roots, debris
   - No prior ruts or disturbance; natural sedimentary shaping only
4. **Moisture:** Appropriate moisture for necessary strength range; no excess free surface water
5. **Soil Properties Documentation:**
   - USCS classification per ASTM standards
   - Natural moisture content and density for each 6" layer
   - Liquid limit (LL), plastic limit (PL), plasticity index (PI)
   - Sand and fines percentages

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Cone Penetrometer
- **What it is:** Standardized trafficability measurement device consisting of 30° cone, 18"-long rod (can be extended to 36"), proving ring, dial gage (0-300 psi or 0-750 psi), and handle
- **Use:** Direct measurement of soil shear strength (Cone Index) by forcing cone into ground at constant rate; stress indicated on dial indicates soil resistance
- **Specifications:** 0.5 sq-in. base area cone; 300 psi dial calibrated to 150 lb vertical force; penetration rate ~0.1 ft/s

### Remolding Equipment Kit
**Components:**
- Hvorslev sampler (piston sampler for undisturbed soil samples)
- 2.5-lb drop hammer with 12-inch drop
- Cylindrical remold tube and base plate
- Cone penetrometer (same as above)
- Wire saw for sample preparation
- Sample containers

**Use:** Measure soil sensitivity to traffic-induced strength loss by comparing undisturbed vs. remolded cone index values

## Use Cases & Applications

**Primary Use Case:** Ground vehicle acquisition support—determining if vehicles meet soft-soil mobility performance requirements

**Application Context:** 
- Specifically for fine-grained soils (CH clay being worst-case scenario)
- Off-road vehicle testing in soft-soil environments
- Vehicle comparison regardless of traction type (wheeled vs. tracked)
- Force projection and modeling/simulation development

**Referenced in BST's Context:** This document was retained as a reference for Black Swift Technologies' AFWERX SBIR Phase I proposal on Soil Moisture Mapping (Project X22.4), suggesting BST's soil moisture mapping capability may support or complement VCI testing operations.

## Key Findings & Standards

### Critical Layer Determination
- **Definition:** Soil layer exerting greatest influence on VCI1 performance (not necessarily where vehicle rests when immobilized)
- **Related to:** Critical depth of sinkage mobilizing stress within soil beneath center of running gear ground contact
- **Selection Method:** 
  - Analyze overlapping 6-inch layers at depths 0-6", 3-9", 6-12", 9-15", 12-18"
  - Select layer with best go/no-go separation and clearest upper-bound trend
  - Reference normal critical layers based on vehicle type (Table 3):
    - **Wheeled:** 3-9" (< 2000 lb wheel load); 6-12" (2000-15000 lb); 0-12" (> 15000 lb)
    - **Tracked:** 3-9" (< 4 psi contact pressure); 6-12" (< 100,000 lb); 0-12" (> 100,000 lb)

### Drop Layer Rule
- For test points where layer below critical layer is weaker, use the weaker soil strength
- Example: If 12-18" RCI < 6-12" RCI, use 12-18" value for analysis
- Significant impact on final VCI1 determination (example shows difference between VCI1 = 33 without rule vs. VCI1 = 29 with rule)

### Data Quality Standards
- **Cone Index:** 
  - Normal profiles uniform or uniformly increasing with depth preferred
  - Anomalies (hardpans, inconsistent layers) cause exclusion
  - Left/right wheel path comparison essential—significant differences (vehicle lean) may warrant exclusion
  - Individual measurement data typically noisy but valuable for trend analysis
  
- **Remold Index:**
  - CH soils unlikely to have RI < 0.5 per Collins (1971) analysis
  - RI values < 0.5 should be scrutinized against nearby measurements
  - Consistency checks across layers and neighboring lanes recommended

### VCI1 Analysis Rules
1. Remove suspect lanes (field observations and office analysis)
2. Use conservative RCI values (round up to next integer)
3. Use FM 5-430-00-1 (1994) critical layer unless superior correlation exists
4. Apply Drop Layer Rule
5. Scrutinize zero-pass lanes with RCI > 10-pass lane values
6. Define VCI1 as minimum of highest legitimate zero-pass RCI + 1

## Notable Details

### Historical Context
- VCI methodology originated with U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) in 1945 to address WWII mobility issues
- Procedures standardized within Corps for decades but not previously documented in centralized accessible format
- USACE has developed extensive VCI1 database over 5+ decades, predominantly focused on CH soil
- Five to ten test lanes typically required for reliable VCI1 determination despite sparse dataset considerations

### Soil Profile Considerations
- Vehicle sinkage proceeds through critical layer in normal soil profiles
- Standardized test conditions (straight lanes, level terrain, non-slippery conditions) ensure repeatability
- Testing on worst-case CH soil ensures vehicles can operate on any fine-grained soil type
- Sand content significantly skews results downward—even small percentages problematic

### Equipment Standardization
- All equipment calibrated to WES (Waterways Experiment Station) standards
- Cone penetrometer is primary trafficability measurement tool
- Remolding procedures standardized for consistent RI measurement
- Data collection forms standardized for consistent documentation

### Test Duration & Resource Requirements
- Typically 5-10 lanes of zero-pass and 5-10 lanes of multi-pass testing
- Field data collection requires trained operators for cone penetration and soil sampling
- Analysis phase benefits from rapid completion post-testing (for quality decisions on suspect data)
- Ideally hundreds of data points would define go/no-go boundaries, but sparse datasets (5-10 lanes per condition) have historically yielded consistent, predictable results over decades of USACE use

## Document Metadata
- Type: Engineering services proposal
- Client/Agency: Black Swift Technologies (BST)

## Executive Summary
ATA Engineering proposes a comprehensive aeroelastic analysis and parameter study for Black Swift Technologies' NASA SBIR Phase II effort to develop an unpowered UAS capable of operating in Venus's upper atmosphere via dynamic soaring. The work includes finite element modeling, flutter analysis, and hinge stiffness optimization studies for both a Venus-bound aircraft and an Earth demonstration vehicle, with emphasis on characterizing aeroelastic behavior under Venusian atmospheric conditions and establishing wing-fold hinge design requirements.

## Technical Approach

**Overall Strategy:**
- Develop structural finite element models (FEMs) and panel method aerodynamic models for both Venus and Earth UAS
- Perform baseline aeroelastic analyses (flutter, divergence, loads) assuming perfect hinges
- Execute parametric stiffness studies on wing-fold hinges to establish acceptable design space
- Deliver insights into aeroelastic drivers specific to Venusian flight conditions

**Tools & Methods:**
- Structural modeling: 1-D beam or 2-D shell FEM in Nastran format
- Aerodynamic modeling: Panel method using Nastran doublet lattice or ZAERO ZONA6
- Flutter analysis: Computationally efficient subsonic panel methods; CFD-based time-domain techniques when needed
- Nonlinear analysis capability: CFD-FEM co-simulation using Loci/CHEM, FUN3D, STAR-CCM+, and Abaqus

**Key Technical Insight:**
Document highlights unique aeroelastic challenges of Venusian flight: dramatically lower stall speeds (~6.5 knots vs. 50 knots for Cessna at Venus surface) create unusually high reduced frequencies for structural modes and potential for counterintuitive aeroelastic phenomena. Combined with folding wing hinges, this necessitates detailed parametric analysis.

## Products & Capabilities Described

**Venus UAS:**
- Unpowered unmanned aerial system designed for extended flight in Venus upper atmosphere
- Operates via dynamic soaring (extracting energy from wind shear layers)
- Features folding wing with hinged joints to accommodate launch/deployment constraints
- Intended for scientific measurements

**Earth Demonstration UAS:**
- Technology demonstration platform for Venus design
- Similar aeroelastic analysis requirements
- Serves as validation/testing vehicle for Venus concepts

**ATA's Capabilities Applied:**
- 40+ years of aerospace analysis and testing experience
- Expertise in flutter analysis, ground vibration testing (GVT), finite element modeling, and aircraft dynamics
- Specific precedent: Led all aeroelastic work for Airbus Perlan 2 glider (which reached 76,000 ft in 2018), including ground vibration testing
- Subsonic through hypersonic aeroelastic analysis experience
- CFD-based computational aeroelasticity for nonlinear flow regimes

## Use Cases & Applications

**Primary Mission:**
- Scientific measurements in Venus upper atmosphere via long-endurance dynamic soaring flight

**Design Challenges Addressed:**
1. Aeroelastic stability assessment under Venusian atmospheric conditions (pressure, density, speed of sound, turbulence profiles)
2. Wing-fold hinge design optimization for both flight regimes
3. Flutter and divergence onset speed characterization
4. Dynamic load assessment (root bending moment, shear, hinge loads)
5. Comparison of baseline continuous-wing performance vs. hinged configurations

## Scope of Work (8 Tasks)

1. **Earth UAS Model Development** – Structural FEM and panel aerodynamic model
2. **Earth UAS Baseline Aeroelastic Analyses** – Flutter, trim, gust loads for limited flight conditions
3. **Earth UAS Hinge Parameter Study** – Parametric variation of hinge stiffness (5 values assumed) to bound design space
4. **Venus UAS FEM Development** – Structural and aerodynamic models from CAD geometry
5. **Venus UAS Baseline Aeroelastic Analyses** – Flutter, loads analysis tailored to Venusian atmosphere; identifies design drivers
6. **Venus UAS Hinge Parameter Study** – Hinge stiffness parametric exploration for Venus vehicle
7. **Program Management & Meeting Support** – Weekly teleconferences, status presentations, project management
8. **Final Report** – Documentation of methods, results, recommendations for detailed design phase

**Key Tracked Parameters:**
- Flutter onset speed and frequency
- Flutter mode shapes
- Divergence onset speed and mode shapes
- Peak root bending moment and shear
- Hinge loads
- Relative changes from baseline aircraft

## Notable Details

**Relevant Precedent:**
- ATA's Perlan 2 engagement is explicitly positioned as the most relevant experience: high-altitude glider with similar design constraints (long wingspan, flutter risk, dynamic soaring), requiring ground vibration testing and aeroelastic characterization—direct analog to BST's Venus vehicle concept.

**Contractual & Commercial Terms:**
- Fixed-price proposal: **$119,830**
- Delivery: 14 weeks for analysis tasks (Tasks 1–6) plus 2 weeks for final report from receipt of purchase order and all data
- Invoice: Monthly based on progress, net 30 days
- Validity: Until June 30, 2020
- ATA retains right to use similar techniques for other clients (non-proprietary know-how)

**Key Assumptions:**
- Hinge parameter studies assume stiffness as primary variable; span-wise position and rotation axis fixed per initial scope
- Five hinge stiffness values per parametric study
- BST provides timely delivery of CAD geometry, airfoil data, mass properties, and flight envelope definitions
- Scope is fixed; out-of-scope requests require change order

**Dependencies:**
- Requires fully defined CAD models of both Venus and Earth UAS from BST
- Requires flight envelope, atmospheric data (Venus standard atmosphere), and hinge location/axis definitions
- Success dependent on timely delivery of receivables from BST

## Competitive Positioning

ATA emphasizes its unique qualification through:
1. **Deep aeroelastic expertise** – 40+ years, subsonic through hypersonic regimes
2. **Perlan 2 precedent** – Direct experience with high-altitude, long-span, flutter-sensitive glider design and testing
3. **Integrated modeling capability** – FEM-to-flight test pipeline including GVT correlation
4. **Venusian physics insight** – Explicit recognition of unique atmospheric/dynamic conditions and their aeroelastic implications

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** SBIR Phase II Proposal
- **Client/Agency:** U.S. Air Force
- **Program/Solicitation:** AF192-005 (SBIR Topic); Proposal Number F2-12711
- **Date:** Submitted 2019 (created October 7, 2019)
- **BST Products/Systems Referenced:** S0 UAS (modified atmospheric sounding variant), S0-AD (air-deployed version), Multi-hole Probe (MHP)
- **Key Personnel:** Dr. Jack Elston (PI, CEO), Josh Fromm (Lead Engineer), Dr. Maciej Stachura (Aerospace Engineer)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposes to develop a hand-launched, purpose-built unmanned aircraft system (S0) for rapid atmospheric profiling to support Air Force weather operations, Army, and Special Operations Forces. The system would provide vertical wind profiles up to 15,000 feet in under 20 minutes with autonomous operation, precision landing within 10 feet, and high-wind tolerance (30+ mph), while maintaining a target cost of approximately $5,000 per unit and compatibility with existing Air Force data systems.

## Technical Approach

### Problem Statement
Current atmospheric data collection relies on balloon-borne soundings and dropsondes, which provide limited spatial-temporal density and are not recoverable. Satellite systems (ASTER, MODIS, AIRS, OMI) suffer from low spatial resolution and infrequent measurement cycles. A need exists for targeted, repeatable, recoverable in situ measurements that can be quickly deployed by small teams in remote locations.

### Proposed Solution
BST proposes to adapt the S0-AD (originally designed for hurricane sampling) into a ground-deployed atmospheric sounding platform with the following key modifications:

1. **Airframe Design:** Modified wings and tail optimized for hand-launch, fast climb rate (~4 m/s or 787 ft/min), and precision deep-stall landing (vertical descent, landing within 10 feet). Design analysis conducted using XFRL5 vortex lattice method during Phase I.

2. **Flight Characteristics:** 
   - Cruise speed: 35-40 mph
   - Cruise angle-of-attack: 1.5° (zero elevator deflection)
   - Efficient CL/CD across broader speed range
   - Endurance: 60 minutes flight time
   - Target climb performance: reach 15,000 ft AGL in under 20 minutes

3. **Onboard Algorithms:** Novel control algorithms for accurate profiling at fast climb rates, maintaining consistent angle-of-attack and zero sideslip to maximize 3D wind estimation accuracy. Aircraft will maintain set angle-of-attack during climb phase.

4. **Autonomy & Communications:** Dual-mode operation—fully autonomous with no wireless communications (for stealth/denied-area operations), or real-time wind data downlink to ground operator. Two-mode capability adds Air Force exclusivity to commercial version.

5. **Data Integration:** Automated data formatting and transmission compatible with Air Force standard desktop systems and Air Force Data Centers. Support for text file, BUFR, GRIB, and netCDF formats for weather model ingestion.

## Products & Capabilities Described

### S0 UAS (Modified Atmospheric Sounding Variant)
- **What it is:** Hand-launched, fixed-wing UAS purpose-built for atmospheric profiling; adaptation of BST's commercial S0-AD platform
- **Proposed uses:** Tactical upper air measurement to support Air Force Weather, Army, and Special Operations Forces operations; rapid wind field characterization for precision operations (e.g., airborne drops)
- **Key specifications:**
  - Weight: 2 lbs
  - Wingspan: 31 inches
  - Cruise time: 60 minutes
  - Launch type: Hand-launch (modified from S0-AD's air deployment)
  - Communications range: 100 miles (one-way)
  - Setup/deployment time: <5 minutes by single operator
  - Landing precision: 10-foot radius
  - Target cost: ~$5,000 per unit

### Multi-hole Probe (MHP)
- **What it is:** BST-designed and manufactured sensor instrument for measuring 3D wind velocity, pressure, temperature, and humidity. Uses 3D printing to reduce cost by 10x compared to traditional instruments; originally developed under NASA SBIR.
- **Integration:** Core sensing component of S0; provides real-time wind data at 100 Hz sampling rate
- **MHP Specifications:**
  - Weight: 1.8 oz (50 g)
  - Cost: $2,000
  - Wind velocity resolution: 0.03 m/s
  - Wind velocity accuracy: 0.29 m/s
  - Temperature range: -40° to 85°C
  - Temperature accuracy: ±0.3°C
  - Pressure resolution: 0.012 mbar
  - Pressure accuracy: 1.5 mbar
  - Relative humidity range: 0-100% RH

- **Type**: SBIR Phase II Proposal
- **Client/Agency**: U.S. Air Force

- **Proposal Number**: F2-12711
- **Date**: Submitted December 2019

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposes to develop the S0 UAS (Unmanned Aircraft System) as a purpose-built atmospheric sounding platform for the U.S. Air Force and commercial users. Based on the successful S0-AD (air-deployed variant used by NOAA for hurricane sampling), this Phase II effort will create a hand-launched system capable of providing vertical wind profiles up to 15,000 feet in under 20 minutes with autonomous operation and precise landing accuracy (within 10 feet). The system will integrate BST's proven Multi-hole Probe (MHP) sensor for 3D wind measurement and provide data in formats compatible with Air Force weather systems.

## Technical Approach

### Core Design Modifications
The S0 will be modified from the S0-AD platform (originally designed for air deployment from manned aircraft into hurricanes) to enable:

1. **Airframe Optimization**: 
   - Different wing/tail design for hand-launch capability
   - Optimized for fast climb rate (15,000 ft in under 20 minutes = ~4 m/s or 787 ft/min vertical rate)
   - Deep-stall landing capability enabling near-vertical descent with landing precision within 10 feet
   - Compact form factor suitable for field transport

2. **Flight Control & Wind Estimation**:
   - Novel onboard algorithms for rapid profiling while maintaining 3D wind accuracy at fast climb rates
   - Aircraft maintains constant angle of attack (~1.5°) and zero sideslip during climb to maximize wind estimation accuracy
   - Unique tail design enabling precise autoland capability

3. **Sensor Integration**:
   - Uses BST's Multi-hole Probe (MHP) as primary sensor (50 grams, $2000, 100 Hz sampling rate)
   - Measures 3D wind velocity, pressure, temperature, humidity with specifications:
     - Wind velocity resolution: 0.03 m/s
     - Wind velocity accuracy: ±0.29 m/s
     - Temperature range: -40° to 85°C (±0.3°C accuracy)
     - Pressure accuracy: ±1.5 mbar
     - Humidity accuracy: ±1.3% RH
   - Temperature range: -40° to 85°C
   - Sensor rate: 100 Hz sampling

4. **Communications & Data**:
   - Dual-mode operation: fully autonomous (no wireless) OR secure real-time wind data downlink to operator
   - Data formatted for integration with Air Force standard systems and upload to Air Force Data Centers
   - Supports multiple radio configurations: AVAPS, iMet base station, ISM 900MHz frequency-hopping, cellular network, or radio-silent mode
   - One-way legacy communication system capability (inherited from S0-AD hurricane work)
   - Ground system interface via web browser (no specialized software installation required)

5. **Operational Parameters**:
   - Hand-launch capable (deployable by single AF Weather operator)
   - Cruise speed: 35-40 mph (optimized for efficiency)
   - Endurance: 60+ minutes flight duration
   - Recovery radius: 10 feet maximum error
   - Setup/deployment time: under 5 minutes for trained operator
   - Total system cost target: ~$5,000 per aircraft (matching S0-AD pricing)

### Aerodynamic Design (Phase I Results)
- XFRL5 computational analysis completed showing:
  - Pitching moment coefficient zero at 1.5° angle of attack (natural cruise angle)
  - CL/CD ratio at maximum efficiency with flat curve allowing wider speed range (35-40 mph) without significant endurance loss
  - Stable design with tail providing negative lift at cruise conditions (tail incidence: 2° down)

## Products & Capabilities Described

### S0 UAS (Modified Atmospheric Sounding Variant)
**What it is**: Hand-launched, fixed-wing unmanned aircraft system purpose-built for atmospheric vertical profiling with integrated meteorological sensors

**Specifications**:
- Weight: 2 lbs
- Price: $5,000
- Wingspan: 31 in
- Cruise time: 60 minutes
- Propulsion: Electric
- Launch type: Hand-deployed
- Comm range: 100 miles (one-way)
- Sensing: Winds (3D), pressure, temperature, humidity
- Performance target: 15,000 ft altitude in <20 minutes, landing accuracy within 10 ft

**Use in this context**: Primary platform for Air Force rapid atmospheric sounding capability providing tactical upper air measurements to support weather forecasting and modeling for Army and Special Operations Forces operations

**Unique capabilities**: 
- Only currently available U.S.-made system specifically designed for vertical wind profiling
- Reusable vs. balloon-borne disposable systems
- Sensor-reactive control algorithms enabling adaptive sampling patterns
- Capability to operate autonomously with no wireless communications (important for undetected operations)

### S0-AD (Air Deployed Variant)

- Humidity accuracy: ±1.3% RH
