## Executive Summary
This is BAE Systems' standard terms and conditions template for subcontracts and purchase orders issued to suppliers performing work on U.S. Government prime contracts. It establishes comprehensive contractual requirements covering administrative procedures, legal compliance, quality control, payment, intellectual property, security, and termination rights applicable to all BAE Systems subcontractors and vendors.

## Document Purpose & Scope
This document serves as BAE Systems' master contractual framework for managing supplier relationships on government-funded work. It is not specific to any particular product, program, or technical capability but rather establishes baseline legal and administrative requirements that flow down to all suppliers working under BAE Systems government contracts.

## Key Sections & Requirements

### Section A: General/Administrative Clauses
**Contract Administration:**
- Supplier must register in BAE Systems' HICX portal (https://baesystems.hicx.net)
- Only BAE Systems Procurement Representative has authority to issue Change Orders
- BAE Systems appoints Technical Representative; Supplier appoints Lead Supervisor
- Claims process: Suppliers have NO recourse directly with U.S. Government; must work through BAE Systems

**Payment Terms:**
- Net 45 days from latest of: accurate invoice receipt OR service acceptance
- Small business concerns may invoice/be paid every 2 weeks
- All prices include federal, state, local taxes (listed separately on invoice)
- Travel reimbursement: coach class airfare, no alcohol, per diem per Federal Travel Regulations
- BAE Systems right of setoff against any payments owed

**Cost-Type Contracts (Special Provisions):**
- Reimbursement for recorded costs actually paid
- Progress payments to subcontractors under similar cost standards
- Final indirect cost rates per FAR Subpart 31.2
- Billing rates pending final overhead rate establishment
- Quick closeout procedures available per FAR Subpart 42.7
- Audit rights for BAE Systems and U.S. Government at any time
- Interim billings with indirect rate adjustments required

### Section B: Laws and Regulations
**Compliance Requirements:**
- Full compliance with all applicable laws, orders, rules, regulations
- Priority rating compliance
- Gratuities/Kickbacks prohibition and ethical conduct requirements
- Export Control compliance
- Occupational Safety and Health compliance
- Foreign Corrupt Practices Act compliance

### Section C: BAE Systems Information Protection
**Critical Security & Confidentiality Requirements:**
- 5-year confidentiality period post-contract termination
- No transfer of BAE Systems Information to Cloud or external systems without written approval
- No storage outside U.S. without advance written approval
- No remote access to BAE Systems networks without authorization and business security screening
- 48-hour incident notification requirement for unauthorized disclosure, cyber-attacks, or breaches
- Supplier must implement reasonable written security program with administrative, technical, organizational, and physical safeguards
- Compliance with all U.S. Government laws regarding safeguarding government covered information
- Cyber Security Verification Form (CSV) completion required upon request
- Records of incidents must be maintained and made available to BAE Systems and Customers
- Supplier bears costs of remedial steps for incidents

### Section D: Personnel & Premises Access
**Background Screening & Access Control:**
- Non-U.S. citizens/non-permanent residents require written BAE Systems approval
- Unescorted facility access requires pre-employment background screening including:
  - I-9/E-Verify verification
  - Criminal conviction check (7-year minimum)
  - Education verification (degreed positions)
  - 3-year employment history verification
- Zero tolerance for harassing behavior
- BAE Systems/Customer can remove personnel from premises at sole discretion
- All personnel, property, vehicles subject to monitoring/search upon entry/exit

**On-Premises Conduct Requirements:**
- No weapons
- No controlled substances or alcohol
- No hazardous materials (except personal computing devices with lithium batteries)
- Remain in authorized areas only
- No solicitation of BAE Systems employees
- No unauthorized sales/marketing
- Cannot remove BAE Systems assets without written authorization
- Cannot share user credentials or access information
- BAE Systems may monitor all communications and data on its networks

### Section E: Records & Audit
**Record Retention:**
- Minimum 5 years from final payment (or longer if specified)
- Records include: financial, proposal, procurement, specifications, inspection, test, certifications, time records, expense reports, travel receipts, employee clearances
- BAE Systems and Customer have audit access during normal business hours with reasonable notice
- BAE Systems has audit rights on all performance reports except proprietary indirect cost data
- Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA) or Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) may conduct indirect cost audits

### Section F: Intellectual Property & Software
**IP Ownership & Rights:**
- BAE Systems Information remains BAE Systems property
- Supplier must comply with proprietary markings and restrictive legends
- Cannot remove proprietary markings
- Non-exclusive, non-transferable, royalty-free license to use BAE Systems Information only for contract performance
- Restrictions on Open Source and Restricted Software usage
- Supplier responsible for declaring and managing software compliance

### Section G: Termination Rights
**Termination for Convenience:**
- BAE Systems may terminate at any time after 30 days from effective date with written notice
- Immediate effect possible
- Procedures per FAR 52.249-4 (or 52.249-6 for cost-reimbursable work)

**Termination for Default:**
- Failure to perform within specified time
- Failure to perform material provisions with 8-day cure period after written notice
- Default on other BAE Systems contracts
- Bankruptcy or insolvency
- BAE Systems may acquire replacement services; Supplier liable for excess costs
- BAE Systems may require transfer of materials, parts, tools, plans, drawings, subcontract assignments

### Section H: Dispute Resolution
**Litigation & Jury Waiver:**
- Disputes must be filed in court of competent jurisdiction within the state from which contract was issued
- Both parties consent to personal jurisdiction and venue in that state
- **Both parties WAIVE RIGHTS TO JURY TRIAL** (to extent permitted by law)
- Patent actions may be initiated at U.S. Patent and Trademark Office or International Trade Commission
- Until dispute resolution, Supplier must diligently proceed with contract performance

### Section I: Additional Requirements
**Non-Solicitation:**
- During contract and 1 year after expiration/termination: Cannot recruit/solicit BAE Systems technical or professional employees supporting the contract
- Exception: Non-targeted recruiting efforts permitted
- BAE Systems entitled to injunctive relief for violations

**Subcontractors:**
- Supplier must bind subcontractors to substantially similar terms
- Supplier assumes liability for subcontractor acts/omissions
- Upon BAE Systems request, must provide: subcontractor names, supply locations, sourcing, supply categories, financial health, performance issues
- Cannot use cost-plus-percentage-of-cost subcontracts
- Subcontractor fee limitations per FAR 15.404-4(c)(4)(i)

**Business Continuity Planning:**
- Supplier must establish disaster recovery and business continuity plan (BCP)
- BCP must include vital records protection
- Must activate BCP upon necessity
- If unable to perform >10 consecutive days, BAE Systems may terminate for default without penalty

**Stop Work Orders:**
- Supplier must stop work upon written notice
- Must minimize cost incurrence during stoppage
- BAE Systems will then notify continuation or termination

**Assignment:**
- Any assignment of contract rights/delegation of duties void without BAE Systems written consent
- Change of control constitutes impermissible assignment
- Exception: May assign payment rights to financing institutions after furnishing signed assignment
- BAE Systems may freely assign contract

- State law of state from which contract issued (excluding choice of law rules)
- Exception: FAR/DFARS-incorporated provisions governed by U.S. federal common law of government contracts

- Supplier personnel are employees of Supplier, not BAE Systems
- Supplier responsible for all insurance, benefits, workers' compensation
- BAE Systems has no liability for Supplier personnel
- Former BAE Systems employees require approval for assignment

**Indemnification & Liability:**

- Failure to perform liability
- Insurance requirements

**References to External Documents:**

- Includes USGOVA (DoD) and USGOVB (Other Agencies) FAR/DFARS flow-down provisions

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** Compliance/Regulatory Guidance Form
- **Client/Agency:** DARPA (via BAE Systems RFP)
- **Program/Solicitation:** DARPA Albatross (Subcontract RFP from BAE)

## Executive Summary
This is a DFARS-compliant regulatory guidance document instructing proposers on how to properly disclose and assert restrictions on technical data, computer software, and intellectual property when responding to a DARPA BAA solicitation. It outlines requirements for identifying noncommercial items, commercial items, patents, and other IP that will be used or generated under a proposed contract or Other Transaction award.

## Technical Approach
Not applicable—this is a compliance/procedural document, not a technical proposal.

## Key Requirements & Assertions Categories

### Noncommercial Items (Technical Data and Computer Software)
- Proposers must identify all noncommercial technical data and software planned for generation, development, or delivery
- Must assert specific restrictions on deliverables where Government will acquire less than unlimited rights
- Must follow DFARS 252.227-7017 format
- **Default assumption:** If no list submitted, Government assumes "unlimited rights"
- **Government Purpose Rights (GPR):** Mixed-funded data/software subject to GPR with automatic 5-year limitation (DFARS 252.227-7013, 252.227-7014)
- Failure to provide full information may result in proposal non-compliance and rejection

### Commercial Items (Technical Data and Computer Software)
- Must identify all commercial technical data and software that may be embedded in noncommercial deliverables
- Must list any applicable restrictions on Government use
- **Default assumption:** If no list submitted, Government assumes no restrictions
- Government may evaluate impact during source selection

### Patents
- Must document ownership or appropriate licensing rights to all patented inventions used in the proposal
- For pending patent applications containing proprietary information: may provide only patent number, inventor/assignee names, filing dates, patent title summary, plus representation of ownership or proof of licensing rights

### Other IP
- Proposers must provide good faith representation of ownership or appropriate licensing rights to all other IP
- Must provide short summary for each item asserted with less than unlimited rights, describing:
  - Nature of the restriction
  - Intended use in proposed research

## Notable Details
- Document emphasizes compliance risk: "Failure to provide full information may result in a determination that the proposal is not compliant with the BAA – resulting in nonselectability of the proposal" (stated multiple times)
- DFARS clauses cited: 252.227-7013, 252.227-7014, 252.227-7017
- Government may request additional information during source selection to evaluate assertions
- For Other Transaction awards, similar format recommended but not required; applicable regulations for that instrument type govern
- Document references "See attached for summaries of each asserted item listed" (attachments not provided in this extract)

## Assessment
This is a procedural compliance document with no substantive information about Black Swift Technologies' products, capabilities, or technical approach. It serves as guidance for proposal preparation rather than a proposal document itself. No BST-specific IP, patents, or technical data assertions are disclosed in this extract.# Disclosure of Technical Data Assertions - DARPA Albatross

## Document Metadata
- Type: Technical proposal / RFI response
- Client/Agency: U.S. Army
- Program/Solicitation: ARMY25-COE02
- Date: April 30 – May 3, 2016
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: Soil Moisture Mapping (SMM) Small Unmanned Aircraft System (sUAS); SuperSwift aircraft
- Key Personnel: Dr. Maciej Stachura (PI), Dr. Cory Dixon (BST, SuperSwift integration lead); Partners: Prof. Albin J. Gasiewski (University of Colorado CET, sensor technical lead), Prof. Venkat Lakshmi (University of South Carolina, soil integrity algorithms)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposes to adapt its existing NASA-developed Soil Moisture Mapping sUAS platform into an end-to-end soil integrity measurement system for the U.S. Army. The system combines an airborne L-band radiometer with soil integrity processing software to provide low-latency soil moisture and trafficability assessments at 15-meter spatial resolution to ~10 cm depth, enabling Army personnel to evaluate terrain suitability for heavy vehicle trafficking and aircraft landing operations.

## Technical Approach

**Core System Architecture:**
- Leverages the existing SMM sUAS (developed under NASA Phase II SBIR) as primary data source
- Integrates soil moisture measurements with soil type data and soil integrity algorithms to produce permissible vehicle tire pressure assessments
- Incorporates state-of-the-art RF interference (RFI) mitigation via digital detecting and processing receiver technology
- Uses SuperSwift airframe (radio-quiet aircraft design) necessary for robust radiometer performance

**Key Technical Tasks:**

1. **Aircraft/sUAS Modifications:**
   - Ruggedization of airframe and support equipment for Army field operations
   - Adoption of wireless communication system for control and data downlink on approved DoD frequencies with encryption
   - Development of third-generation sensor electronics using mil-spec components
   - Enhanced RFI/EMI mitigation for reliable operations in difficult environments
   - Local flight testing throughout project to validate modifications

2. **Software Development:**
   - Soil integrity processing algorithms to convert soil moisture + soil type into maximum permissible surface soil pressure data products
   - Integration of antecedent rainfall and drying data
   - Formatting of outputs for existing Army data systems
   - Ground control station ruggedization and redesign
   - Algorithm refinement using local flight test data

**Validation Approach:**
- Local flight experiments at Irrigation Research Fund (IRF) test site, Yuma, Colorado (existing BST FAA authorization)
- Final demonstration and evaluation at Army Corps of Engineers ERDC Environmental Laboratory, Vicksburg, Mississippi
- Army personnel feedback incorporated into final modifications

## Products & Capabilities Described

**Soil Moisture Mapping (SMM) sUAS:**
- Existing platform developed in collaboration with University of Colorado CET under NASA Phase II SBIR
- High-resolution L-band radiometer (currently used in precision agriculture applications)
- Measurement capability: 15-meter spatial resolution, ~10 cm soil depth penetration
- Current TRL: 7; expected TRL 8 by fall 2016
- Already validated against in situ sensors and NASA calibration sites
- Demonstrated soil moisture mapping at 30-meter resolution (example: Canton, OK)

**SuperSwift Aircraft:**
- Radio-quiet airframe design essential for radiometer performance
- Will be modified for Army operational requirements
- Integration point for ruggedized third-generation sensor electronics

**Soil Integrity Data Product:**
- Measures permissible vehicle tire pressure thresholds
- Relates soil moisture to soil strength based on soil type
- Incorporates temporal rainfall/drying factors
- Provides low-latency operational decision support

## Use Cases & Applications

**Primary Army Applications:**
- Heavy vehicle trafficking assessment over varied terrain
- Aircraft landing zone suitability evaluation
- Operations in unstable/high-risk terrain: river valleys, wetlands, coastal regions
- Post-precipitation terrain assessment (thunderstorm/heavy rainfall scenarios)
- Pavement integrity assessment (soil foundation stability under vehicular loads)

**Technical Rationale:**
The system addresses critical gaps in existing soil moisture assessment methods:
- *In situ probes:* Impractical for Army field operations
- *Satellite sensors (e.g., SMAP):* Insufficient spatial resolution (km-scale vs. sub-100m Army requirement) and temporal frequency (2x/day vs. rapidly changing soil conditions)

The spatial heterogeneity of soil moisture directly determines soil strength and vehicle load-bearing capacity—only achievable at the high spatial resolution provided by the SMM sUAS.

## Key Results
No results reported; this is a proposal document. The document references prior validation:
- SMM sUAS successfully flight-tested at NASA calibration site
- Extensive in situ sensor comparison completed
- Phase II-E ongoing validation over different vegetation densities at Yuma, Colorado test site
- Soil moisture maps generated at 30-meter resolution in Canton, Oklahoma

## Notable Details

**Technology Readiness:**
- SMM sUAS: TRL 7 (TRL 8 expected by fall 2016)
- Soil integrity system overall: TRL 5
- Proposed project goal: Advance complete system to TRL 7 and position for Army TRL 8-9 qualification

**Institutional Partnerships:**
- University of Colorado Center for Environmental Technology (Prof. Gasiewski): sensor development, 64 competitively awarded environmental remote sensing projects
- University of South Carolina (Prof. Lakshmi): soil integrity algorithm development
- Leptron Unmanned Systems: identified as potential partner for DoD certification and approval pathway
- Army Corps of Engineers ERDC: proposed test/demonstration site

**Facilities:**

- CET facility access at University of Colorado for radiometric/radar sensing equipment
- Existing FAA authorization for UAS operations at IRF Yuma test site

**Budget & Schedule:**

  - BST: ~$1,963,800
  - University of Colorado CET (Gasiewski, PhD student, equipment): $250K
  - University of South Carolina (Lakshmi, PhD student, equipment): $250K

**Competitive Advantages:**

- Existing collaboration structure and validated partnerships
- Prior DoD experience (Dr. Dixon's two Phase II SBIR programs)
- Ready-to-transition technology reducing Army acquisition risk# MS4515 Pressure Transducer Datasheet

## Document Metadata

- Client/Agency: Internal BST reference (TE Connectivity MS4515 component)

## Executive Summary
This is a technical datasheet for the MS4515, a small PCB-mounted ceramic pressure transducer manufactured by TE Connectivity (formerly Measurement Specialties). The document provides complete specifications, performance parameters, dimensional drawings, and ordering information for this component, which was apparently being evaluated or integrated by BST for the NASA volcano monitoring SBIR Phase II project.

## Technical Approach
The MS4515 is a CMOS-based pressure transducer with the following technical characteristics:
- Ceramic-based sensing element with integrated signal conditioning circuitry
- Fully calibrated and temperature-compensated
- Single supply operation (3.3V or 5.0VDC)
- Requires single external 100nF capacitor for operation
- Ratiometric analog output

## Products & Capabilities Described

**MS4515 Pressure Transducer:**
- **What it is:** Small, PCB-mountable differential or gage pressure transducer from TE Connectivity
- **Specifications:**
  - Pressure ranges: 2 to 30 inches H₂O
  - Total Error Band (TEB): <1.0% over compensated range (2.0% for ≤4 inH₂O ranges)
  - Accuracy: ±0.25% of span
  - Operating temperature: -10°C to +85°C
  - Compensated temperature range: 0°C to +60°C
  - Response time: 1 ms
  - Start time to data ready: 6 ms
  - Supply current: 3 mA
  - Output voltage: 0.5–4.5V (5.0V supply) or 0.165–2.97V (3.3V supply)
  - Weight: 3 grams
  - MTTF: >10 years at 70°C with 1.188 million pressure cycles at 120% FS

- **Physical configurations:** Dual side port (DS), single side port (SS), top port (TP), or manifold mount (MM)
- **Pressure port specifications:** 1/8" barbed ports mate with 3/32" ID tubing
- **Pressure type options:** Differential (bidirectional) or gage
- **Output options:** Type A (10%–90%) or Type B (5%–95%)
- **Pin options:** Through-hole (P), J-lead (S), in-line (L), or castellated (C)

**Environmental Ratings:**
- Storage temperature: -40°C to +125°C
- Operating humidity: up to 95% RH (non-condensing)
- Overpressure rating: 300 psi maximum
- Burst pressure: 10–20 psi depending on range and style
- Mechanical shock: MIL-SPEC 202F Method 213B (3 drops)
- Mechanical vibration: MIL-SPEC 202F Method 214A (1 hour per axis)
- Thermal shock: 100 cycles over storage temperature range
- Life rating: 1 million full-scale cycles
- ESD rating: ±4 kV (HBM per EN 61000-4-2)

**Media compatibility:** Non-corrosive dry gases compatible with ceramic, silicon, borosilicate glass, RTV, gold, aluminum, and epoxy
- Optional gel-coat (-F option) available for high-humidity or slightly corrosive environments

## Use Cases & Applications
The datasheet lists the following typical applications:
- Altitude and airspeed measurements
- Medical instruments
- Fire suppression systems
- Panel meters
- Air movement/environmental controls
- Pneumatic controls
- Blocked filter detection

## Notable Details
- The MS4515 is a commercially available component from TE Connectivity (Measurement Specialties division)
- Multiple port and pinout configurations available for different integration scenarios
- Custom configurations possible (lower power consumption, higher accuracy) upon request to factory
- Complete dimensional drawings provided for all package styles
- Temperature compensation active over 0–60°C; extended temperature multiplier chart provided for operation outside compensated range
- Output is ratiometric to supply voltage (valid for <10% variations)
- Standard pressure ranges from 2 inH₂O (very low differential) up to 30 inH₂O
- Ordering information system allows configuration of all options

**Note:** This document is purely a component specification sheet and does not contain information about BST's specific application, integration approach, or how this transducer was used in the volcano monitoring project. ## Executive Summary
Datasheet for three variants of silicon photodiodes with integrated low-noise JFET amplifiers (JI 546, JI 547, JI 548) designed for radiation/light measurement applications. Three models offer different feedback resistances and corresponding responsivity levels, operating across visible and near-infrared spectral ranges.

## Products Described

### JI 546 Photodiode
- Feedback resistor: 1 MΩ
- Max spectral responsivity: 0.6 mV/nW
- Rise time: 3 μs
- Bandwidth: 120 kHz
- Dark offset voltage: ±0.5 mV

### JI 547 Photodiode
- Feedback resistor: 10 MΩ
- Max spectral responsivity: 6 mV/nW
- Rise time: 15 μs
- Bandwidth: 25 kHz
- Dark offset voltage: ±0.5 mV

### JI 548 Photodiode
- Feedback resistor: 100 MΩ
- Max spectral responsivity: 60 mV/nW
- Rise time: 35 μs
- Bandwidth: 10 kHz
- Dark offset voltage: ±2 mV

## Technical Specifications (Common to All Variants)

**Optical Performance:**
- Active area: 4.8 mm²
- Spectral range: 400–1100 nm (VIS and NIR)
- Peak spectral response: 850 nm
- Opening angle: ±50°
- Very low offset and drift parameters
- High dynamic range

**Electrical Performance:**
- Operating voltage: ±5 to ±15 V
- Operating temperature: -25°C to +85°C
- Storage temperature: -40°C to +100°C
- Current consumption: 2.2 mA (typical), 2.6 mA (max)
- Short circuit current: ±45 mA
- Saturation voltage (RL = 2 kΩ): -14.8 V typical, -14.5 V max

**Mechanical:**
- Package: Hermetically sealed TO-5
- Assembly isolated to ground
- RoHS and WEEE compliant
- Replacement for JI 4, JI 8 (not pin-compatible)

## Applications Listed
- General light/radiation measurement
- Detection of low radiation intensities with high signal-to-noise ratio
- Spectroscopy
- Medical diagnostics

## Notable Details
- "Decadic staggered responsivity" design allows selection of appropriate gain for different measurement scenarios (three models with 10× responsivity differences)
- Integrated feedback resistor and capacitor reduce component count
- Dual power supply configuration (±V)
- Three variants cover range from fastest/lowest-gain (JI 546) to slowest/highest-gain (JI 548) operation

## Document Metadata
- Type: Broad Other Transaction Authority Announcement (BOTAA) / Solicitation
- Client/Agency: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) Engineer Research and Development Center (ERDC)
- Program/Solicitation: ERDC BOTAA 25-01
- Date: October 2024
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: None mentioned in this document
- Key Personnel: N/A (this is a government solicitation, not a BST proposal)

## Executive Summary
This is an open, continuously available solicitation from the ERDC seeking prototype projects from nontraditional defense contractors (NDCs), traditional defense contractors, and nonprofit research institutions. The announcement covers two broad focus areas (Military Engineering and Engineered Resilient Systems) with multiple sub-focus areas, using Other Transaction authority under 10 U.S.C. 4022 for flexible prototype development.

## Process Overview
The BOTAA operates in stages:
1. **White Paper Submission** (max 3 pages): Continuous submission through ERDCWERX platform
2. **Government Evaluation** (60-90 days): Assessment against technical merit and eligibility criteria
3. **Selection**: If advantageous, government may request solution pitch, technical demonstration, or issue Request for Prototype Proposal (RFPP)
4. **Proposal Development**: Collaborative scope-of-work development with government
5. **Award & Performance**: Firm fixed-price basis with milestone payment schedules

## Eligibility Requirements
To qualify for award, at least ONE of these must be present:
- At least one NDC or nonprofit research institution participating significantly, OR
- All significant participants (other than Federal Government) are small businesses or NDCs, OR
- At least one-third of total project cost paid by non-Federal sources

## Focus Areas

### Military Engineering (ME)
1. **Protective Structures and Systems**: Force protection infrastructure, planning tools, TTPs for perimeter/port/border security
2. **Protection and Survivability**: Detection, defeat of threats; infrastructure hardening, camouflage, vulnerability assessment
3. **Geophysical Sensors and Data Fusion**: Multi-sensor integration, automated fusion for Common Operating Picture, sub/super-surface monitoring
4. **Vulnerability Assessment, Detection, and Analytics**: Strategic/operational/tactical analysis frameworks for force protection posture, population vulnerability, infrastructure disruption
5. **Geoscience, Environmental, Geospatial, and Material Modeling and Simulation**: Materials-by-design, computational modeling of sensors, structural response prediction, environmental impact modeling
6. **Enhance and Assess Mobility of Manned and Unmanned Systems**: Autonomous systems, obstacle clearing/breaching, terrain interaction, dynamic mobility hazard detection, M&S for mobility prediction
7. **Engineering and Engineering Enabling Technologies**: Combat engineering, materials, manufacturing, modeling/simulation, autonomous systems, engineer mobility/counter-mobility
8. **Global Access Engineering**: Remote sensing, tactical/experimental methods for assessing soils, ice/snow, pavements, bathymetry, port depths, coastal regions, airfields, infrastructure
9. **Infrastructure Maintenance, Repair and Reconstruction**: Advanced physics-based assessment, rapid repair technologies, prototype kits for technology transition
10. **Engineering Analysis Tools and Decision Aid Prototype Software**: Software integrating advanced algorithms for evaluation, design, repair of critical infrastructure

### Engineered Resilient Systems (ERS)
1. **Cybersecurity**: Protection of ICS/SCADA/PLC systems and networks; networked-, host-, and behavior-based defense approaches
2. **High Performance Computing Enabled Advanced Manufacturing**: 3D printing, multi-physics computational approaches, optimization, trade-space analytics, machine learning, HPC-enabled process control, large-scale component fabrication
3. **High Performance Data Analytics**: Techniques for examining large/complex datasets; heterogeneous computing resources; AI/ML algorithms
4. **System Engineering Techniques**: Design trade-space development, Condition Based Maintenance, massive data processing, AI/ML algorithms
5. **HPC Enabled Development of Surrogate Models and Data Analytics**: Computationally efficient models; multi-physics interactions; CFD/FEA applications; anomaly detection; physics-informed machine learning
6. **Leveraging HPC Capabilities for On-the-Edge Computing**: HPC at point of need; electro-optical/thermal/radar/acoustic sensor processing; terrain characterization; sensor fusion; anomaly detection
7. **Computational Material Testing and Validation**: Numerical tools connecting advanced manufacturing techniques to engineering mechanics simulations

## White Paper Requirements
**Format**: Max 3 pages (cover page not counted)
- 12pt Times New Roman, single-spaced, 1-inch margins
- PDF format, <20 MB
- No classified information

**Content**:
- Cover page (auto-generated from submission form): POC details, company info, business status, focus area(s), title, description, DoD purpose, ROM price
- Technical requirements: Background/benefits, technical approach, data rights assertions
- ROM pricing with supporting documentation

## Proposal Requirements (if white paper selected)
- Cover page with white paper ID, title, company info, submission date
- Statement of Work: background, safety/environmental/security requirements, technical objectives, success criteria, reporting/deliverables, timeline, Government-furnished resources
- Milestone Payment Schedule: firm fixed-price events with descriptions and target timeframes
- Security clearance requirements assessment
- Data rights assertions
- Key personnel resumes (Program Manager and others); commitment terms if not currently employed
- Significant participation rationale (if applicable)
- Detailed pricing: labor rates, materials/equipment list, indirect costs with supporting calculations

## Evaluation Criteria

**White Papers**:
- Degree to which solution meets government problem/need/capability gap in identified focus area
- ROM price commensurate with solution
- Government funding availability
- Demonstration of required participation (NDC, nonprofit, small business, or cost share)

**Proposals**:
- Scientific/technical merit: feasibility, clarity, state-of-the-art approach, clear objectives, innovative methodology
- Key personnel qualifications
- Significant participation extent (new technology/product, novel application, material performance increase, significant effort contribution, cost/schedule reduction)
- Budget/price: fair, reasonable, fully justified, commensurate with complexity

## Key Administrative Details
- Registration in System for Award Management (SAM) required prior to award
- Subject to International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) and Export Administration Regulations (EAR)
- NOT subject to Competition in Contracting Act or FAR regulations
- Proposals may be disclosed to subject matter experts for evaluation
- Proposals subject to Freedom of Information Act (FOIA); confidential information should be marked
- Follow-on production available after successful prototype completion using non-competitive procedures
- U.S. Government does not fund proposal preparation; no reimbursement for pre-agreement costs

## Notable Details
- **Continuous submission**: White papers accepted at any time; selected papers can be held in electronic library for up to 3 years pending funding
- **Flexibility**: Other Transaction authority allows departures from standard FAR procurement rules
- **Cost share options**: Cash contribution or in-kind contribution accepted
- **Follow-on production**: Successful prototype completion enables non-competitive follow-on production awards
- **Diverse participation**: Strong emphasis on inclusion of nontraditional defense contractors and small businesses to meet statutory requirements

## Document Metadata
- Type: Request for Information (RFI) Response
- Client/Agency: U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center (ERDC), Environmental Laboratory (EL)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies responds to ERDC's RFI for multiple uncrewed aerial systems by offering a portfolio of specialized electric VTOL and fixed-wing UAS (S0, S2, S3 models) built on the proprietary SwiftCore Flight Management System. BST emphasizes ruggedized design for extreme environmental conditions, modular payloads, autonomous swarming capabilities, and proven federal agency adoption (NOAA, USGS, NASA, USAF, DoD).

## Technical Approach
BST's technical foundation centers on:
- **SwiftCore™ FMS**: Proprietary flight management system including autopilot, ground station, user interface, and support electronics; enables modular customization and multi-UAS/swarming control
- **Quality assurance**: NDAA and ASDA compliant; proprietary avionics (not open-source) providing guaranteed supply and robustness
- **Modular architecture**: Field-swappable payload nose cones; components replaceable/reconfigurable within 30 minutes
- **Open systems approach**: Integration of government-developed platform-agnostic collaborative plugins; third-party sensor integration capability
- **Autonomous capabilities**: Terrain-aware navigation, computer vision for ATR, GPS-denied navigation, autonomous launch/landing in mountainous terrain
- **Integration with military command systems**: Mission data transmitted to Android Team Awareness Kit (ATAK)

## Use Cases & Applications

### 1. **Extreme Environmental Monitoring / Volcano Observation**
- S2 demonstrated 20+ nautical mile operations in 50 kt winds and icing conditions observing volcanoes in Alaska with USGS
- Engineered for high-altitude flights with strong winds and damaging particulates

### 2. **Hurricane Data Collection (NOAA)**
- S0-AD air-deployed from NOAA P3 hurricane hunter
- Provides wind, pressure, temperature, and video data collection
- 20-unit delivery to NOAA for 2024 hurricane season
- Development contract for 2025 season includes multi-UAS swarming and automatic path planning in hurricanes
- Mission flown into Tropical Storm Tammy (late 2023, off Barbados coast)
- Capacity to scale to orders of 100+ units

### 3. **Multi-UAS Swarm Operations for Wildfire Wind Monitoring (NASA SBIR)**
- Coordinated team of S0 UAS for atmospheric forecasting around wildfires
- Two UAS demonstrated in 2023; planned expansion to 6-UAS team
- Autonomous guidance to highest-uncertainty sampling locations
- Data used by National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) for 12-hour weather forecasting
- Data shared via ATAK to firefighting teams and command centers
- Supports safety for both manned aviation and ground-based firefighting

### 4. **RF Emitter Localization and Tracking (NSF/Air Force)**
- Mesh-networked S0 UAS team for autonomous RF source detection
- Autonomous path planning optimizing localization while maintaining mesh communications
- Tested with WiFi (2.4GHz) and 433MHz emitters
- Field experiments achieved ~20m localization accuracy
- UAS automatically reconfigured as relay when emitter outside primary comm range
- Demonstrated system portability across different small fixed-wing UAS types

### 5. **Soil Integrity/Runway Assessment (AFWERX SBIR Phase II with AFRL)**
- S2 equipped with commercial soil moisture sensor for runway integrity assessment
- Supports C-130 aircraft operations on unimproved/dirt runways
- Multi-UAS swarm extension (coordination with NASA) for vastly increased coverage and reduced collection times
- TRL 9 maturity (operational experience with USGS, NOAA, NASA)
- Wildfire application focus; potential Army Corps of Engineers extension for trafficability assessment in remote/disadvantaged locations

### 6. **Advanced Cooperative Control / Swarming (AFWERX/AFRL)**
- S0 UAS intended as low-cost platform enabling hierarchical control and advanced cooperative autonomy
- Supports multi-domain command and control for battlespace operations
- Air-deployable from C-130 or ground-launched
- Enables "unpredictability and mass" through large numbers of inexpensive systems
- Reduced operator overhead through advanced autonomy for complex multi-UAS tasks

### 7. **Perimeter Security and Surveillance (S3 Application)**
- Computer vision-based automatic target recognition
- Real-time threat detection (unauthorized personnel/vehicles)
- Integrated with ATAK for tactical information sharing

## Document Metadata
- Type: Internal strategic notes / submission planning document
- Client/Agency: DARPA
- Program/Solicitation: ERIS 2026 (Evidential Reasoning for Intelligence Systems)
- Date: 2026-02-16
- BST Products/Systems Referenced: S0-AD, S0, S2, SwiftCore, NightFOX
- Key Personnel: Beck Cotter (last editor)

## Executive Summary
Internal strategic analysis for DARPA ERIS 2026 submission emphasizing need to reframe BST capabilities around "disruptive" paradigm shifts rather than incremental improvements. Document argues that current framing of BST's extreme-environment sensing, rapid deployment, and integrated autonomy reads as optimization of existing approaches rather than fundamental breaks with assumptions in how sensing systems are designed and deployed.

## Strategic Problem Identified
Current BST positioning conflates "many impressive capabilities" with disruptive innovation. DARPA ERIS requires demonstration of paradigm shifts, not better sensors/longer endurance/harsher environment tolerance. Core issue: submission reads additive ("we can do A, B, C in hard places") rather than subtractive ("we eliminate the need for X entirely").

## Three Proposed Disruptive Frames

### Frame 1: Platforms → Deployable Sensing Fields (Strongest)
**Broken Assumption:** Valuable sensing assets must survive, return, and be protected.

**Disruptive Claim:** Replace exquisite, survivable platforms with rapidly deployable, loss-tolerant sensing fields. Vehicles become consumable carriers of calibrated measurements; value is in coverage and adaptation, not platform survival.

**BST Assets Supporting:**
- S0-AD (magnetic detection, air-deployed, expendable)
- Tube-launched/air-deployed architectures
- Designed-for-loss platform philosophy
- Cost-per-measurement vs. cost-per-vehicle economics
- Sensor placement optimized for loss tolerance

**Reframed Applications:**
- ASW without capital ships
- ISR without airspace dominance
- Plume tracking without manned assets
- Wildfire detection without perimeter infrastructure

**Why DARPA Values:** Changes cost-risk equation fundamentally, not just performance metrics.

---

### Frame 2: Preplanned Autonomy → Information-Seeking Autonomy (Primary)
**Broken Assumption:** Vehicles navigate first; sensing happens along the way.

**Disruptive Claim:** Sensing objectives drive motion in real time based on uncertainty reduction. Vehicles move to reduce uncertainty; models command motion.

**BST Assets Supporting:**
- Sensor-directed navigation
- Pressure-based wind estimation + online calibration
- Coordinated multi-UAS sampling
- 3D wind field reconstruction

**Reframed Positioning:** Self-tasking measurement system, not UAV fleet.

**High-Value Applications:** Hurricanes, wildfire plumes, volcanic ash, unknown airborne threats where live information gain drives platform repositioning.

**Why DARPA Values:** Step toward adaptive, self-tasking systems beyond scripted autonomy.

---

### Frame 3: Data Delivery → Closed-Loop Model Control (Supporting)
**Broken Assumption:** Sensing systems stop at data delivery.

**Disruptive Claim:** System is incomplete until measurements actively reshape operational models in real time. Sensing + autonomy + modeling = one closed-loop system.

**BST Assets Supporting:**
- Measurement → model assimilation
- WRF-SFIRE integration
- Hurricane model feedback loops
- NWS operational inclusion

**Reframed Positioning:** Operational infrastructure provider, not platform vendor.

---

## Submission Strategy Analysis

### Option A (Flagship Umbrella)
**Risk:** "Extreme-Environment Distributed Sensing" framing reads as "very good multi-mission system" without explicit disruption focus. Only viable if umbrella explicitly positions as "Deployable, loss-tolerant sensing fields."

### Option B (Two Focused Submissions—Recommended)
**Submission 1:** Air-Deployed, Expendable Sensing Fields for Denied ISR
- Explicitly challenges survivability economics
- Anchors S0-AD, magnetic sensing, tube launch
- Native DARPA disruption narrative

**Submission 2:** Self-Directing Atmospheric Sensing for Persistent Environmental Awareness
- Breaks preplanned autonomy assumption
- Anchors hurricanes, wildfire, plume tracking
- Strong dual-use story

**Advantages:** More reviewer surface area, clearer disruptive hypotheses, reduced "too broad" rejection risk.

---

## TRL Framing Guidance
**Risk:** Stating "TRL 8–9" can reduce perceived disruption.

**Correct Framing:**
- "Operationally proven components enabling new system architecture"
- Emphasize architectural novelty over component maturity
- DARPA prefers: "new ways to assemble proven things" over "very mature versions of known systems"

---

## Critical Assessment of Current Draft
**What Falls Short:**
- Problem statement (expensive, fragile, SWaP-constrained) describes optimization pressure, not paradigm break
- "State-of-the-art advance" framing still sounds like "very good platform," not "different way of doing sensing"

**Path to Actual Disruption:**
1. Pick ONE assumption to kill
2. Explicitly state what becomes unnecessary
3. Reinforce assumption break in every section
4. Avoid structure where disruption is buried; embed it in problem/advance/impact sections

---

## Notable Strategic Insights
- Disruption ≠ "cheaper / smaller / tougher" or "more integrated" or "flown more"
- Disruption = "eliminate a class of assets" / "invert who adapts to whom" / "change sensing economics under risk"
- DARPA-familiar problem structure (problem → advance → team → impacts → TRL) won't carry disruption unless disruption lives *inside* each section
- Emphasis on architectural inversion (loss tolerance, information-driven motion, closed-loop model control) over capability breadth# ESCR Full Application Preview

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** ESTCP Pre-Proposal (Environmental Security Technology Certification Program)
- **Client/Agency:** U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) / Environmental Security Technology Certification Program
- **Program/Solicitation:** ESTCP Natural Hazards Adaptation Program; Topic Area: Advancing Wildfire and Prescribed Fire Forecasting and Assessment Tools
- **Proposal Number:** NH26-A1-9078
- **Date:** Submitted 2024–2025 period (document modified through March 2025)
- **BST Products/Systems Referenced:** UAS-mounted dual polarized L-band radiometer (Lobe Differencing Correlation Radiometer / LDCR); multi-UAS coordination capability; onboard real-time data processing
- **Key Personnel:** 
  - Dr. Jack Elston (Black Swift Technologies, Lead PI/CEO)
  - Dr. Michelle Stern (USGS California Water Science Center)
  - Dr. Seungbum Kim (UCLA/Jet Propulsion Lab)
  - Eryan Dai (Weather Stream; instrument lead for L-band radiometer)
  - Ryan Ferrell (Pepperwood Foundation)

---

## Executive Summary

Black Swift Technologies proposes to develop and demonstrate an operationalized UAS-based fuel moisture mapping system that provides near real-time, high-resolution soil and live fuel moisture (LFM) maps to support DoD wildfire risk assessment and prescribed burn planning. By integrating UAS L-band radiometer data with satellite-derived soil moisture from NISAR and USGS Basin Characterization Model forecasting, the system will bridge the gap between coarse-resolution satellite products and labor-intensive ground sampling, enabling DoD installations to transition from reactive fire suppression to proactive risk mitigation over a 1–10 year planning horizon. The two-year demonstration will include four flight campaigns, hardware refinements, forecasting software development, and validation at DoD installations and non-DoD test sites (Pepperwood Preserve, CA).

---

## Technical Approach

### Core Technology
- **Sensor Platform:** UAS-mounted dual-polarized L-band radiometer (LDCR) developed in partnership with NASA
- **Resolution:** Sub-5m soil moisture mapping (vs. 250m–1km satellite products)
- **Data Products:**
  - Real-time soil moisture maps (target accuracy: ±6% RMS)
  - Live fuel moisture maps (target accuracy: ±10% RMS)
  - Wildfire risk forecasts integrated with climate scenarios
  
### Integration Strategy
1. **Satellite Layer:** NISAR soil moisture data at 100–200m resolution, collected regularly throughout the year
2. **UAS Layer:** High-resolution data collection several times per year (especially near prescribed burn dates) to validate and refine satellite products
3. **Modeling Layer:** USGS Basin Characterization Model (BCM)—a gridded water balance model—ingests UAS and satellite data to generate soil moisture–LFM relationships and forecast wildfire risk
4. **Climate Scenarios:** Downscaled CMIP5 Global Climate Model outputs run through BCM to provide ensemble-based fire danger estimates for 1–10 year periods

### Key Technical Objectives (Year 1–2)
- Operationalize forecasting tools for wildfire exposure and prescribed burn window assessment
- Develop forecasting software that ingests UAS data and NISAR satellite inputs
- Enable multi-UAS coordination for enhanced spatial coverage
- Demonstrate utility in real-world DoD wildfire-prone environments
- Fuse UAS-collected data with NISAR-derived soil moisture at multiple spatial and temporal scales

### Performance Metrics & Success Criteria

| Performance Objective | Metric | Data Requirements | Success Criteria |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Quantitative** | | | |
| Remote sensing vs. ground truth | Soil moisture ±6% RMS; LFM ±10% RMS | NISAR data, UAS data, ground data | Accuracies meet defined thresholds |
| Historical forecast accuracy | Modeled soil/fuel moisture within ±6%/±10% RMS | Historical soil and live moisture data; fire susceptibility maps | Historical performance meets thresholds |
| **Qualitative** | | | |
| Realistic spatial/temporal variations | Soil/LFM maps with realistic variability at 1–10 year scales | NISAR, UAS, ground data | Visual variations appear realistic for forecast periods |
| Wildfire risk forecast | Reasonable risk estimates for locations with historical wildfires (1–10 year timeframe) | Model data, sensor data | High-risk locations coincide with historical wildfire occurrence |

---

## Products & Capabilities Described

### 1. L-Band Radiometer (LDCR) on UAS
- **What It Is:** Dual-polarized microwave radiometer mounted on small UAS; developed with NASA in partnership with Orbital Micro Systems
- **Specifications:**
  - L-band frequency (inherently penetrates vegetation/soil to measure root-zone moisture)
  - Lobe differencing correlation radiometer design for spatial resolution enhancement
  - Onboard FPGA-based real-time data processing
  - Proven heritage from SMAP and airborne campaigns
- **Validation Data:** Field experiments at BST test site (April 2023) and Pepperwood Preserve (2021–2023) show good agreement with in-situ soil moisture probes across three seasonal campaigns; over 900 mobile TDR measurements collected for validation
- **Prior Demonstrations:** Over 100 soil moisture missions flown for NASA, NOAA, USGS, and commercial customers

### 2. Multi-UAS Coordination Capability
- **What It Is:** Enhanced capability for coordinating multiple UAS to achieve broader spatial coverage
- **Proposed Use:** Enable simultaneous or sequential flights to map larger installation areas efficiently
- **Status:** Capability referenced but not extensively detailed in proposal

### 3. Basin Characterization Model (BCM) Integration
- **What It Is:** USGS-developed gridded water balance model that converts soil moisture and LFM data into wildfire risk maps and climate-scenario forecasts
- **How Used:** Ingests UAS high-resolution data and NISAR satellite products to create empirical soil moisture–LFM relationships; runs through downscaled climate models (CMIP5) to forecast fire danger over 1–10 year periods
- **Previous Validation:** BCM previously validated on 3,200-acre Sonoma County preserve with historical wildfire data

### 4. Real-Time Data Processing
- **Onboard Computing:** UAS equipped with onboard computing for real-time radiometer data processing, reducing post-flight processing requirements and enabling rapid decision support

---

## Use Cases & Applications

### Primary DoD Applications
1. **Prescribed Burn Planning:** Optimize burn windows by identifying periods when soil and live fuel moisture are within acceptable ranges for controlled burns
2. **Wildfire Risk Mitigation:** Identify high-risk areas on installations (Army, Air Force, Navy/Marine Corps lands) to preposition resources and deactivate power lines during critical fire weather windows
3. **Long-Term Fuel Management Prioritization:** Build regional models over recurrent operational flights to identify chronic low-moisture areas requiring fuels management and forest stewardship treatment
4. **Mission-Critical Land Use Sustainability:** Maintain training area availability and infrastructure protection

### Test Sites & Target Installations
- **Pepperwood Preserve, Sonoma County, CA:** 3,200-acre nature preserve with 40 active climate/soil stations, 170 soil sensors, extensive fuel and vegetation monitoring; used for validation and baseline flights
- **DoD Installations:** Proposed deployment on Army (ITAM sites), Air Force, Navy/Marine Corps lands; specific installations to be identified during execution
- **Secondary Use Case (Related):** Air Force SBIR parallel effort uses same radiometer for runway soil integrity assessment for C-130 operations

---

## Key Technical Risks & Mitigation

| Risk | Description | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| **Risk 1: Forecasting Accuracy** | Cannot retroactively validate against historical wildfires (remote sensing data did not exist) | Validate soil/LFM maps against historical data; simulate historical wildfires using modeled soil moisture conditions; expand validation to multiple regions |
| **Risk 2: Flight Permissions on DoD Bases** | FAA Beyond Visual Line of Sight (BVLOS) regulations restrict long-range UAS operations; requires site-specific waivers | L-band radiometer UAS already approved by AFWERX under separate Phase II SBIR; fallback to Pepperwood test site if base access delayed |
| **Implicit: Cybersecurity/OPSEC** | DoD data must meet encryption and security standards | Develop procedures for encrypted data transfer; ensure compliance with DoD operational security protocols (noted in transition section) |

---

## Technology Maturity

**Technology Readiness Level (TRL):** 7 (validated in relevant environment; requires refinement for operational status)

### Evidence of Maturity
- **Sensor Heritage:** L-band radiometry proven over 10+ years through SMAP satellite and airborne campaigns
- **Field Validation:** Over 100 BST-operated soil moisture missions; dedicated validation campaigns at Pepperwood (2021–2023) with 900+ TDR measurements
- **Published Results:** Peer-reviewed publications demonstrate soil–LFM correlation and high-resolution mapping capability (Stern et al. 2024, Dai et al. 2020)
- **Parallel Government Funding:** Air Force SBIR Phase II approval validates system operability

### Development Work Required
- Integration of all components into single operationalized system for DoD use
- Development of forecasting software to ingest UAS data into BCM
- Refinement of L-band radiometer hardware for improved performance
- Validation across multiple DoD installations and climate regions
- Development of DoD-compliant data handling and transition workflows

---

## Related Efforts & Partnerships

| Project | Funding Source | Relevance |
|---|---|---|
| **Air Force SBIR – Runway Integrity from Soil Moisture** | AFWERX | Uses same L-band radiometer technology; validates system operability on military bases; parallel funding demonstrates government confidence |
| **Pepperwood Deployments (2021–2023)** | USGS | Multi-season UAS flights validating soil–LFM correlation; established strong baseline for wildfire risk assessment |
| **NASA Partnership** | NASA (historical) | Co-developed L-band radiometer; heritage from Earth science missions |
| **SMAP Satellite Program** | NASA | Technology foundation for current L-band radiometry approach |

---

## Expected DoD Benefits

### Cost & Operational Impact
- **Reduced Suppression Costs:** High-resolution fuel moisture maps enable targeted prescribed burns, reducing catastrophic wildfire risk
- **Operational Efficiency:** On-demand UAS flights replace infrequent satellite overpasses and labor-intensive ground sampling; enables rapid decision-making for prescribed burn windows
- **Personnel Safety:** Proactive wildfire mitigation reduces uncontrolled fire risks threatening personnel, training areas, and infrastructure
- **Training Area Availability:** Optimized fuel management sustains mission-critical land use activities

### Financial Projections
- **Projected ROI:** Under 2 years at single installation
- **Scalability:** System easily deployed across multiple wildfire-prone DoD installations for significant aggregate annual savings
- **Asset Protection:** Potential savings equivalent to replacement cost of high-value installation assets (quantified on per-base basis)

### Aggregate DoD Impact
- **Deployment Timeline:** 5–10 pilot installations within 24 months post-demonstration; broader DoD-wide rollout based on mission needs
- **Long-Term Vision:** Transition from reactive fire suppression to proactive risk assessment across DoD wildfire-prone lands

---

## Notable Technical Details

### Live Fuel Moisture Validation
- **Pepperwood Results:** Strong empirical correlations between soil moisture and LFM measured for multiple species (chamise as indicator species)
- **Figure References:** Proposal includes soil moisture maps (Figure 2) showing agreement between modeled UAS products and field TDR measurements; LFM maps (Figure 4) derived from soil moisture anomalies

### Satellite Integration
- **NISAR:** 100–200m resolution soil moisture; regular collection throughout year; chosen over SMAP (which has 25km or 1–3km resolution with 14-day revisit) for superior spatial resolution
- **Climate Scenarios:** Downscaled CMIP5 models run through BCM to# Call When Needed (CWN) Unmanned Aerial Systems – Statement of Work

## Document Metadata

## Executive Summary
The Colorado Division of Fire Prevention and Control solicited vendor-provided and operated long-endurance vertical take-off and landing UAS on a call-when-needed basis for wildfire suppression, search and rescue, and other public safety incidents throughout Colorado and neighboring states. The contractor must provide fully crewed and equipped aircraft with defined performance specifications, payload capabilities, crew certifications, and operational compliance with federal and state regulations.

## Technical Approach
This is a performance-based statement of work outlining requirements for a vendor to provide on-call UAS services. Key operational framework:

- **Service Model**: Call-when-needed contracting with no guaranteed minimum orders; State retains exclusive 24/7 control of aircraft during ordered periods
- **Crew Requirements**: FAA Remote Pilot Certificate (14 CFR 107) minimum; duty limits of 14 consecutive hours with 2 calendar days rest within any 14-day period; minimum 10 consecutive hours rest before any duty period
- **Response Time**: Personnel must be ready for takeoff within 15 minutes of dispatch (or longer if authorized for flight planning)
- **Operational Period**: Standard 14-hour operational periods with optional extended periods up to 24 hours at negotiated rates

## Products & Capabilities Described

### Aircraft Requirements
- **Type**: Fixed or rotor-wing vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) UAS
- **Flight Performance**:
  - Capable of flying 12,000 feet density altitude including takeoff and landing
  - 2 hours continuous flight with fuel/batteries sufficient for 12-hour shift
  - Takeoff/landing capability in 20-knot winds; sustained operation in 25-knot winds
  - Day and night operations
- **Command & Control**:
  - Mode C transponder minimum (higher capability acceptable)
  - Two-way radio communication with incident ground and aviation resources
  - Ground Control Station (GCS) capable of connecting to 50-inch video monitor displaying live payload feed and contextual mapping

### Payload Requirements
- **Video Camera**: 1280x720 resolution, 10x zoom lens, live transmission to GCS
- **Infrared Sensor**: 640x480 resolution, live transmission to GCS
- **Capability**: Both sensors capable of tracking stationary point of interest (POI)
- **In-flight Re-tasking**: Capable of responding to unplanned payload tasking within 30 minutes
- **Data Standards**: 
  - MISB (Motion Imagery Standards Board) compliant video as multicast/unicast stream for EO and IR, compatible with TAK (Team Awareness Kit)
  - Real-time Cursor on Target (CoT) data as multicast and TLS stream to TAK Server
  - Still image capture with geo-tagging (lat/lon, DDD MM.MM format)
  - Fire perimeter mapping capability using target cursor with SPI (Sensor Point of Interest) coordinates (~100 feet horizontal accuracy); export as KML, SHP, or compatible format

## Use Cases & Applications
- **Wildland fire operations**: Real-time situational awareness, fire perimeter mapping, payload video collection
- **Search and rescue (SAR)**: Real-time video reconnaissance, EO/IR capability for personnel location
- **Emergency management**: General incident support
- **Other public safety missions**: As directed by incident command

**Geographic Scope**: Throughout Colorado with potential for missions in neighboring states

## Key Results
Not applicable—this is a solicitation document, not a report with results.

## Notable Details

### Operational Control & Authority
- State maintains exclusive control of aircraft 24/7 during ordered periods
- Incident Commander or designee provides tasking and point of contact
- UAS Manager has full contract administration authority including suspension of operations and pilot suspension upon flight safety concerns
- Data Standards Integration: Contractor must deliver data compliant with DoI/USFS standards (MISB, CoT, TAK Server) for interoperability with federal and state incident management systems

### Safety & Compliance Requirements
- All personnel must hold applicable FAA certifications and maintain compliance with relevant Certificates of Waiver or Authorization (COA)
- Mandatory NTSB and DFPC notification for accidents/incidents
- SAFECOM reporting required within 2 days of any aviation safety concerns
- Preservation of evidence and aircraft following mishaps until DFPC authorization
- Full cooperation with federal agencies in mishap investigations
- Contractor bears all costs for search, rescue, salvage, and reassembly following incidents not caused by DFPC negligence
- Personnel replacement mandated for non-compliance with facility rules, unsafe flying, or unsatisfactory performance (within 24 hours if directed)

### Payment Structure
- **Daily Availability Rate**: Per Exhibit B (prices not included in this document)
- **Flight Time**: Paid per hour for authorized revenue flights; measurement begins when aircraft moves under own power for flight, ends when comes to rest
- **Proficiency Flights**: Authorized by UAS Manager, paid as revenue flights
- **Mobilization/Demobilization**: Actual drive time from home base or agreed point to assigned location and return
- **No Guarantees**: Minimum/maximum flight hours not guaranteed
- **Deductions**: 1/28th of 14-hour rate or 1/48th of 24-hour rate deducted per 30 minutes of unavailability
- **Per Diem**: Not paid; lodging and subsistence included in daily rate
- **Fuel**: Contractor responsible for all fuel costs

### Data Ownership
All payload data acquired is property of the agency managing the incident and must be stored per agency/incident management direction.

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies (BST) was contracted by JPL to conduct an engineering feasibility study for integrating JPL's P-band reflectometry instrument (a snow remote sensing technology) onto BST's S2 unmanned aircraft system. The work encompasses design, integration, bench testing, and preparation of a flight test plan for regulatory approval, but does not include full flight campaign execution.

## Technical Approach
- **Integration onto S2 airframe**: Incorporate P-band receiver antenna (designed and built by Ohio State University) into the nose cone section with minimal design changes
- **Mechanical design**: Construct scaffolding to house antenna, frontend, and logging hardware
- **Power trade study**: Determine optimal power source—either separate battery system or power from aircraft propulsion pack
- **Telemetry & control analysis**: Examine requirements for real-time payload telemetry and ground-based payload control during operations
- **Integration work**: Construct mechanical, electrical, and software interfaces
- **Testing**: Conduct initial bench testing at BST offices in Boulder, Colorado; additional testing at local facilities as needed
- **Flight approval**: Prepare Flight Test Plan for Armstrong review and approval; prepare for and conduct review

## Products & Capabilities Described

### S2 Airframe
- BST's unmanned aircraft platform being adapted for scientific payload integration
- Nose cone section modified to accommodate P-band receiver antenna
- Can supply power to payload via propulsion pack or separate battery
- Supports real-time telemetry and ground-based payload control

## Use Cases & Applications
- **Primary application**: Airborne testing of P-band reflectometry instrument for remote sensing of snow over varied terrains
- **Purpose**: Maturation of reflectometry concept following ground-based receiver testing

## Notable Details
- **Partnership**: Collaboration between JPL (technology developer), Ohio State University (antenna design/build), and BST (airborne integration platform)
- **Deliverable**: Final nose cone design and integrated instrument to be delivered to JPL post-experiments for future campaigns
- **Approval pathway**: Design requires JPL researcher approval; flight operations require Armstrong approval via Flight Test Plan review
- **Scope limitation**: Engineering study only; full flight campaigns explicitly excluded from this scope# Expertise and Resources for ROSES 2024 A.59: On-demand Wildfire Susceptibility from Fuel Moisture and Vegetative Index Maps

## Executive Summary
This is a personnel and resources document supporting a 3-year NASA ROSES proposal to develop on-demand wildfire susceptibility mapping using fuel moisture (via L-band radiometry) and vegetation indices from UAS platforms. The team includes Black Swift Technologies (aircraft and systems), JPL (soil moisture retrieval algorithms), USGS (hydrology and fire science), Pepperwood Reserve (field site and validation), and Orbital Micro Systems (radiometer expertise). The project aims to provide fire managers with high-resolution, spatially-resolved soil and vegetation moisture data to predict fire risk.

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposes the S0 VTOL, a lightweight, rapidly deployable fixed-wing VTOL aircraft for expeditionary ISR, counter-UAS operations, and environmental characterization. The system enables persistent airborne sensing from austere locations without runway infrastructure, combining fixed-wing persistence with VTOL operational flexibility for DoD counter-UAS and air defense missions.

## Technical Approach
**S0 VTOL Design Philosophy:**
- Fixed-wing VTOL hybrid configuration emphasizing rapid deployment from austere sites
- Lightweight design enabling small-team launch and operation
- Modular, open-architecture avionics for mission adaptation and integration with C5ISR ground systems
- Supervisory autonomy with degraded-PNT (positioning, navigation, timing) capability
- High-wind and complex-terrain operational capability

**Operational Advantages Over Alternatives:**
- Outperforms multirotor systems in range and endurance
- Faster response than multirotor platforms
- Greater area coverage per sortie
- Extended custody maintenance with reduced operator burden and fewer sorties

  - High-wind and complex-terrain operation

## Executive Summary

BST proposes the S0 VTOL uncrewed aircraft system as a demonstration-ready ISR and sensing-extension capability for the EXTiC 26-1 experimentation event. The S0 VTOL is a 5.7-lb fixed-wing VTOL platform designed for operations in high-wind, austere, and contested environments, capable of rapid deployment, persistent airborne presence, and low logistical burden. The system provides critical ISR capabilities that support the detection-to-response mission thread while maintaining resilience under environmental and operational stress.

---

## Technical Approach

**Core Design Philosophy:**
- Fixed-wing VTOL architecture combining vertical takeoff/landing flexibility with efficient cruise performance
- Originally developed for scientific/environmental missions (wildfire monitoring, volcanic gas sampling, atmospheric profiling), with design characteristics directly applicable to defense ISR
- Purpose-built for extreme conditions rather than optimized for benign environments

**Key Performance Characteristics:**
- Weight: ~5.7 lbs (highly portable)
- Cruise speed: Exceeding 85 knots
- Endurance: ~1 hour (depending on configuration)
- Launch/recovery: No runway, launch rails, or recovery equipment required; operates from austere/confined sites with small teams
- Flight envelope: Designed for high-wind and turbulent operations, providing greater environmental margin than typical small multirotor systems

**Operational Architecture:**
- Fully autonomous flight from launch through recovery with supervisory control paradigm
- Tablet-based mission planning interface for rapid area-of-interest definition and flight pattern configuration
- Electronic centralized aircraft monitoring (ECAM) with continuous health/navigation/sensor status evaluation
- Fault detection with severity categorization and autonomous mitigation response if operator input unavailable

---

## EXTiC 26-1 Demonstration Concept

**Proposed Mission Role:**
- Downstream ISR asset operating after initial detection
- Scoped to: rapid response, situational awareness establishment, persistent coverage, C2 data handoff
- Explicitly excludes engagement/defeat actions

**Representative Scenario Phases:**

1. **Cueing and Launch:** Receipt of detection cue; VTOL launch from confined/unimproved site
2. **Transit and Repositioning:** High-speed transit to area of interest; demonstration of terrain coverage impractical for multirotors
3. **ISR Establishment and Custody:** Loiter/patrol pattern establishment; maintenance through environmental disturbances
4. **Integration and Handoff:** Data product display locally and integration into broader C2 environment; sensor fusion with other systems
5. **Stress and Degradation:** Introduction of environmental/operational stressors (wind, navigation degradation, communications constraints); observation of system behavior and mission impact
6. **Recovery:** VTOL recovery with minimal ground footprint

**Proposed Evaluation Metrics:**
- Response Time: Detection cue to airborne ISR presence
- Persistence: Continuous coverage duration vs. multirotor systems
- Environmental Tolerance: Stable flight/sensing in high-wind/turbulent environments
- Operator Workload: Interaction levels during nominal/off-nominal conditions
- Integration Effectiveness: Data ingestion into C2; contribution to common operating picture
- Degraded Operations: System behavior and mission impact under degraded navigation/communications

**Experimentation Value:**
- Low-risk, high-value evaluation of lightweight fixed-wing VTOL ISR class
- Assessment of complement to existing detection, EW, defeat systems
- Evaluation of gap reduction between detection and response
- Identification of integration priorities and future development pathways

---

## Integration, Communications, and Connectivity

**Ground Segment:**
- Portable, self-contained ground control station with integrated battery power
- No external power, fixed infrastructure, or specialized facilities required
- Tablet-based interface for mission planning, flight monitoring, system health display, data recording
- All core functions available locally enabling operation in connectivity-limited environments

**Communications Architecture:**
- Organic point-to-point radio data link (part of system)
- Supports command/control, telemetry, sensor data exchange
- Does not require IP-based networking for essential flight/data functions
- Intentionally simple and robust, minimizing external network dependencies
- Well-suited to scenarios with constrained, intermittent, or deliberately stressed network conditions

**Data Products and Interfaces:**
- Environmental measurements, aircraft state, mission metadata displayed at ground station and recorded
- Well-defined APIs for sharing data with external systems when connectivity available
- Interface-based approach enabling integration with C2, data fusion, visualization tools without core flight system modification

**Growth Path:**
- Future integration of digital data link (DDL) for live video dissemination identified as growth area
- Not required for EXTiC 26-1 but represents logical extension informed by experimentation
- Current demonstrated capabilities separated from future enhancements

**Integration Risk Mitigation:**
- Self-contained communications/control architecture minimizes risk to overall experiment
- Simplicity, modularity, transparency in integration strategy
- Meaningful integration touchpoints without undue burden on event infrastructure

---

## Technology Readiness and Operational History

**TRL Assessment:** TRL 7
- Fully functional system-level demonstrations in operationally relevant environments
- Aircraft, avionics, ground control station, communications architecture all fully functional

**Operational Heritage:**
- BST's extensive history designing/deploying uncrewed aircraft in demanding environmental conditions
- Platforms derived from same design philosophy as S0 VTOL used in U.S. Government agency, academic, and commercial missions
- Operations include: strong/variable winds, turbulent boundary layers, complex terrain, austere/limited-infrastructure locations

**S0 VTOL-Specific Development:**

- Wildfire monitoring, volcanic gas sampling, environmental profiling missions
- Missions required reliable autonomous flight, precise navigation/control, robust system behavior in environments where conventional small UAS degrade

**System Maturity:**
- Mature, integrated system with known performance characteristics, documented limitations, established operating procedures
- Not a prototype assembled for this submission
- Enables experimentation focus on mission-thread integration and system-of-systems behavior rather than basic platform viability

## Risks, Limitations, and Experimentation Opportunities

**Known Limitations and Experimentation Value:**

1. **Navigation Dependency:**
   - Reliance on conventional satellite-based (GPS) navigation for nominal operations
   - Includes fault monitoring and defined behaviors for degraded navigation quality
   - Does not claim assured performance under all forms of electronic attack/GPS denial
   - **Experimentation opportunity:** Characterize navigation degradation effects on mission execution, operator workload, ISR continuity; identify system-of-systems mitigation strategies

2. **Communications Bandwidth:**
   - Current point-to-point radio link optimized for robustness/simplicity vs. high-bandwidth dissemination
   - Limits real-time transmission of rich data products (live video)
   - Ensures reliable command/control and telemetry under constrained conditions
   - **Experimentation opportunity:** Inform trade studies on expanded connectivity, data prioritization, external network integration

3. **Environmental Stressors:**
   - High winds, turbulence, dust, thermal activity can affect operations
   - System explicitly designed to operate in such conditions
   - **Experimentation opportunity:** Evaluate availability, persistence, graceful degradation; observe system behavior as conditions deteriorate; inform mission resilience and operator decision-making understanding

**Experimentation Perspective:**
These limitations framed as enablers rather than detractors—exposing known seams and trade spaces allows EXTiC participants to understand S0 VTOL complement to other capabilities, identify high-benefit integration approaches, and design mission threads accommodating real-world system behavior vs. idealized assumptions.

## Executive Summary
NASA's Science Mission Directorate is soliciting proposals for the Science Activation Program (SciAct) under ROSES-2025, seeking collaborative projects that engage the public in active participation with NASA science during 2026-2030. The program aims to inspire people of all ages, build STEM workforce capacity, and enable substantive public contribution to NASA science initiatives.

## Program Overview
- **Program Status**: Second phase of 5-year awards; originally began in 2016
- **Period of Performance**: Calendar years 2026-2030 (not to exceed 5 years)

## Executive Summary
Black Swift Technologies proposes to develop an all-weather UAS system based on the S3 platform for persistent base security and rapid response operations at Air Force bases, particularly in extreme environments like Grand Forks AFB. The system leverages BST's proven heritage in harsh-environment operations (high altitude, Arctic, volcano, hurricane, and severe weather missions) and integrates the modular SwiftCore avionics architecture to reduce operator workload and enable advanced autonomous capabilities.

## Technical Approach
- **Platform**: S3 VTOL fixed-wing UAS as the base system
- **Avionics**: SwiftCore modular architecture with well-defined intelligent node interfaces
- **Key Features**:
  - Modular payload system for mid-flight mission conversion
  - User-friendly autonomous operation with on-board vision monitoring (aircraft and terrain)
  - Open system interfaces for integration of third-party equipment and additional functionality
  - Subsystem tracking, preventative maintenance, safety redundancy, and automated sensor-driven control capabilities
- **Duration**: 18 months (Phase II base performance period)
- **Work Location**: 100% at BST facilities by BST employees
- **Work Distribution**: 100% BST, 0% subcontractors

## Products & Capabilities Described

### S3 (VTOL Fixed-Wing UAS)
- **What it is**: A vertical takeoff and landing fixed-wing unmanned aerial system with proven heritage in extreme environments
- **Proposed Use**: Persistent base security perimeter surveillance and rapid incident response missions
- **Heritage Applications**: High altitude observations, remote volcano monitoring, Arctic surveys, hurricane and fire weather observations, flights into tornadic thunderstorms
- **Key Capability**: All-weather operation suitable for locations with significant temperature and wind extremes

### SwiftCore Avionics System
- **What it is**: A truly modular avionics architecture with well-defined interfaces between intelligent nodes
- **Proposed Use**: Core enabler for the S3 base security system
- **Key Features**:
  - Simplified third-party component integration through open interfaces
  - Advanced capabilities: subsystem tracking, preventative maintenance, safety redundancy, automated sensor-driven control
  - Designed and programmed exclusively by UAS technology experts
  - Proven field performance across diverse difficult applications and multiple aircraft platforms
  - Applicable to replacement of proprietary interfaces on other airborne assets

## Use Cases & Applications
- **Primary**: Persistent perimeter security and rapid response at Air Force bases
- **Specific Application**: Grand Forks Air Force Base operations in extreme temperature and wind conditions
- **Mission Flexibility**: Modular payload system allows conversion on flight line for different data-gathering missions
- **Operational Benefits**: Reduced operator workload, reduced training requirements, reduced programmatic risk, enabled preventative maintenance capabilities
