- **Key Differentiators:** Combines VTOL deployment, GPS-denied autonomy, and solar-based endurance at fraction of logistical burden/cost compared to Group 4/5 ISR assets
- **Endurance:** Days to months of autonomous operation without returning to base through solar recharge and hopping between landing sites
- **Performance Specs:**
  - Gust tolerance: exceeds 50 knots
  - All-weather operation: precipitation, icing, high winds

- Advanced autopilot system anchoring all avionics work at BST

## Executive Summary
NightFOX proposes to design, integrate, and validate two lightweight instrument packages (one for in situ fire plume sampling, one for remote fire observations) on a Black Swift Technologies SuperSwift UAS to enable nighttime wildfire emissions and perimeter measurements—a critical data gap left unfilled by manned aircraft due to safety constraints. The system will be field-deployed during NOAA's planned FIREX field mission (July-September 2019) to improve fire weather forecasting and support air quality and climate research on wildfire impacts.

## Technical Approach

### Overall Strategy
- **Platform:** SuperSwift UAS (5 lb payload capacity) operated by University of Colorado Research and Engineering Center for Unmanned Vehicles (CU RECUV)
- **Two integrated instrument packages:**
  1. **In situ package:** CO₂, CO, aerosol (fine and coarse modes), relative humidity (RH), temperature (T), pressure (p); winds derived from UAS avionics
  2. **Remote-sensing package:** Visible and infrared imagers, thermal imager, single-element mid-infrared (MIR, ~4 µm) fire radiative power (FRP) sensor(s), ambient RH/T/p sensors

### In Situ Payload Development
- Target 1-second response time (critical for spatial resolution; at 20 m/s cruise speed, 25-s response time = 0.5 km spatial resolution)
- Candidate CO₂/CO sensors to be identified and tested; modifications planned to improve response time
- Fine-mode aerosol sensor already developed by team; iMet sensors for RH/T/p
- If commercial sensors prove inadequate, custom solutions will be developed

### Remote-Sensing Payload Development
- **Challenge identified:** Long-wavelength IR (LWIR, 7-14 µm) thermal imagers saturate at fire temperatures; mid-infrared (MIR, 4 µm) imagers ideal for FRP but costly and bulky
- **Solution:** Single-element 4 µm MIR sensors (small, low-cost) for FRP determination with cross-track scanning; lightweight visible camera and thermal imager for spatial context
- Target package cost: $15-20K
- Laboratory calibration of remote-sensing sensors; validation through satellite data comparison

### Integration & Testing
- Data recorded onboard; small subset transmitted real-time for monitoring and decision-making
- Multiple test flights planned in Year 2; field deployment to prescribed burn opportunities
- FIREX mission deployment: UAS based next to Aerodyne mobile lab; 2-4 sorties per night; target 30-60 flight hours over ~15 nights; minimum 20 hours needed to meet objectives

### Flight Operations
- Hand-launched, lands on paved road
- Two pilots per deployment
- Extended FAA Certificates of Authorization (COA) sought for nighttime BLOS (beyond line-of-sight) operations
- Coordination with FAA, Department of Interior, USFS for airspace access

## Products & Capabilities Described

### SuperSwift UAS
- **Specifications:**
  - 5 lb payload capacity
  - ~20 m/s cruise speed
  - Operational radius: 30-60 km (depending on flight strategy)
  - Capable of >2 hour endurance
  - Hand-launched; lands on paved road
  
- **Key advantages for this application:**
  - Spacious, forward-located, modular nose-cone payload bay enabling atmospheric sampling and rapid payload exchange
  - Inexpensive nose cones allow easy instrument integration
  - Electric motor (not air-breathing), eliminates concerns about engine damage from dense fire plumes
  - Inherently suited to nighttime/BLOS operations (beyond line-of-sight)
  
- **Selection rationale:** Compared to alternatives (Tempest/UASUSA, Penguin BE/UAV Factory, Puma AE/AeroVironment), SuperSwift offers:
  - Lower cost
  - Modular payload bay (competitors lack this)
  - Rear-mounted propeller (cleaner for ambient sampling than nose-propeller designs)
  - Minimal launch/recovery overhead
  
- **Current readiness level:** RL 4 (test flown); target RL 8 (operational) by project end

### In Situ Instrument Package
- **Measurements:** CO₂, CO, aerosol (fine & coarse), RH, T, p, winds (from avionics)
- **Readiness level:** RL 3 (feasible; ~30% of sensors identified) → RL 8
- **Technical innovations:** 
  - 1-second response time (vs. standard 10-60 s for commercial sensors)
  - Modification of commercial solid-state sensors as alternative to custom builds
- **Status:** Candidate CO₂/CO/coarse aerosol sensors already identified; fine-mode aerosol sensor developed; iMet sensors for RH/T/p identified

### Remote-Sensing Instrument Package
- **Measurements:** Fire radiative power (FRP), fire perimeter, ambient RH/T/p
- **Readiness level:** RL 3 (feasible) → RL 8
- **Technical approach:**
  - Single-element 4 µm MIR sensors for FRP (small, low-cost, avoids saturation issues of LWIR thermal imagers)
  - Cross-track scanning to improve spatial resolution
  - Visible and thermal imagers for contextual mapping
- **Target cost:** $15-20K per package
- **Status:** Candidate visible, IR, thermal imagers and MIR FRP sensors identified

### UAS Observation System (UASOS)
- Integration of SuperSwift + dual instrument packages + flight planning + data assimilation into fire weather models
- **Readiness level:** RL 2 (concept formed) → RL 8
- **Deliverables:** 
  - Proven nighttime observation system with ambient wind data capability
  - Sampling strategies for in situ and remote-sensing flights (Figure 1 shows basic flight patterns)
  - Data ingestion protocols for WRF-Sfire fire weather model

### Observation Strategies
- **Readiness level:** RL 3 (feasible) → RL 8
- Two distinct flight patterns: in situ (plunge through/sampling) vs. remote-sensing (hovering/scanning over fire)
- Development led by Karen Rosenlof and Brian Argrow, beginning Year 1
- Coordination with FAA, DoI, USFS on flight permission requirements

## Use Cases & Applications

### Primary Mission: FIREX Field Campaign (2019)
- **Context:** NOAA's Fire Influence on Regional and Global Environments (FIREX) mission planned July-September 2019; coordinates with NASA FIREChem and USDA/DoI FASMEE
- **Critical gap filled by NightFOX:** Nighttime fire measurements impossible with manned aircraft due to safety concerns; fire plumes more concentrated at night (lower boundary layer), worse air quality, but no current observing capability
- **Scientific objectives:**
  - Study wildfire emissions and chemical transformations
  - Measure fire plume distributions and perimeter
  - Characterize nighttime fire emissions and plume characteristics
  - Provide data for air quality and fire weather forecasting
  - Support land management decisions

### Secondary Applications (Mentioned)
- **Oil and gas field flares:** SuperSwift proposed for calibration/validation of satellite measurements of flare FRP
- **Future capability:** Swarming (coordinated multi-UAS network) for continuous high-resolution spatial information

### Fire Weather Modeling Integration
- Data assimilation into WRF-Sfire model
- Incorporation of high-resolution nighttime fire perimeter, spatially resolved FRP, and ambient RH/p/T/wind measurements
- Expected outcome: Improved fire weather forecasts and air quality predictions

## Executive Summary
NightFOX proposes to design, build, and deploy an integrated UAS Observation System (UASOS) based on the SuperSwift platform to conduct nighttime measurements of wildfire emissions and properties. The system addresses a critical data gap in fire research by combining in situ (CO2, CO, aerosol, meteorology) and remote sensing (fire radiative power, fire perimeter) instrument packages to support NOAA's FIREX field mission (July-September 2019) and improve fire weather forecasting models. Nighttime measurements are impossible with manned aircraft due to safety concerns but essential for understanding the full diurnal fire emission cycle and localized air quality impacts.

## Technical Approach

### UAS Platform Selection
- **SuperSwift UAS** (Black Swift Technologies, Boulder, CO)
  - Selected over alternatives (Tempest, Penguin BE, Puma AE) for three key attributes:
    1. Sufficient 5 lb payload capacity for planned instruments
    2. Operational radius 30-60 km adequate for fire observations
    3. Forward-located, spacious, interchangeable nose-cone payload bay ideal for atmospheric sampling and instrument swapping
  - Specifications: MTOW 16 lbs, 10 ft wingspan, 2+ hr endurance, 18 m/s cruise speed, 20 kft ceiling, hand launch, belly-skid landing
  - Key advantage for fire work: electric propulsion avoids air-breathing engine vulnerability to dense fire plume encounters

### In Situ Payload Development
- **Sensors planned**: CO2, CO, aerosol (fine and coarse modes), ambient RH, temperature, pressure, wind
- **Design goals**:
  - Research-grade sensitivity for fire plume measurements
  - 1-second response time (critical for spatial resolution at 20 m/s aircraft speed; 25-s response = 0.5 km blur)
  - Cost target: $10-15K per package (~10× cheaper than manned aircraft equivalents)
  - Total weight: <5 lbs
  
- **Specific instruments**:
  - **CO2/CO**: Commercial sensors with modifications for improved response time; custom sensors if needed
  - **Fine-mode aerosol (140-3000 nm)**: Custom sensor previously developed (Gao et al., 2016)
  - **Coarse-mode aerosol (1-10 µm)**: Commercial sensors to be identified and tested
  - **RH/T/p**: InterMet iMet-XQ sensors
  - **Wind**: 5-hole probe developed by BST

### Remote Sensing Payload Development
- **Measurement objectives**: Fire radiative power (FRP), fire perimeter, ambient RH/T/p
- **Technical challenge**: FRP measurement requires spectral detectors without saturation in fire radiances
  - Mid-infrared (MIR, ~4 µm) single-element sensors selected for small size and low cost
  - LWIR (7-14 µm) thermal imager for context (becomes saturated but provides spatial coverage)
  - Visible wavelength camera for higher-resolution context
  - Cross-track MIR scanning to improve spatial resolution
- **Design goal**: $15-20K per remote-sensing package
- **Data handling**: Onboard computer stores complete dataset; real-time monitoring subset sent to ground

### System Integration & Testing
- Year 1: Sensor selection and acquisition; establish FAA/DoI/USFS relationships; planning observation strategies
- Year 2: Prototype payload development; integration onto SuperSwift; test flights (nighttime and Beyond Line of Sight); opportunistic prescribed burn sampling
- Year 3: Payload finalization; build two spare packages; participate in FIREX mission (August 2019); two pilots on duty; 2-4 sorties per night planned; 60-120 flight hours target (15 flying nights minimum 30 hours)

## Products & Capabilities Described

### SuperSwift UAS
- **Role**: Primary airborne platform; must be procured independently by University of Colorado during FY2017
- **Capability for NightFOX**: Enables nighttime fire observations safely without pilot risk; electric propulsion avoids fire plume engine damage; rapid payload exchange for multi-mission flexibility
- **Payload bay specifications**: >6" × 6" × 20" volume; 5 lb capacity
- **Operational context**: Hand-launched, lands on any paved road; fits mobile deployment model for unpredictable wildfire locations
- **Readiness level**: Currently RL4 (test flown); expected to reach RL8 (sufficient performance for fire observations) by project end

### In Situ Instrument Package
- **Current readiness**: RL3 (feasible, ~30% of sensors identified)
- **Expected final capability**: RL8 (production of research-grade data)
- **Key performance metrics**:
  - CO2 & CO detection in fire plumes
  - Aerosol size distributions and concentrations
  - Modified Combustion Efficiency (MCE = ΔCO2/(ΔCO2 + ΔCO)) derivation for fire characterization
  - Simultaneous meteorological context
- **Cost efficiency**: Target $10-15K/package vs. $100K+ for manned aircraft equivalent

### Remote Sensing Instrument Package
- **Current readiness**: RL3 (feasible)
- **Expected final capability**: RL8
- **Key performance metrics**:
  - Spatially-resolved fire radiative power (FRP) determination
  - Fire perimeter/extent mapping
  - Ambient meteorology (RH/T/p)
- **Cost**: $15-20K/package
- **Calibration approach**: Laboratory for remote sensing package; field intercomparison with ground measurements and established instruments

### UAS Observation System (UASOS)
- **Current readiness**: RL2 (concept formed)
- **Expected final readiness**: RL8 (data coverage sufficient to characterize medium-sized wildfire)
- **Deliverable**: Proven small UAS capable of nighttime and Beyond Line of Sight (BLOS) operation
- **Observation strategy** (RL3→RL8):
  - **In situ flights**: Vertical and horizontal sampling patterns through fire plumes
  - **Remote sensing flights**: Cross-track scanning patterns over fire perimeter
  - Both support nighttime fire plume characterization and fire weather model validation

## Use Cases & Applications

### Primary Mission: NOAA FIREX (FY2019)
- **Context**: Comprehensive NOAA research effort to understand wildfire impacts on atmosphere, climate, and air quality; July-September 2019 field campaign in western U.S.
- **NightFOX role**: Fill critical nighttime measurement gap; manned aircraft cannot operate safely at night
- **Specific scientific goals**:
  - Quantify nighttime fire emissions (CO2, CO, aerosol) overlooked by day-only manned missions
  - Characterize fire plume vertical and horizontal distributions at night
  - Determine modified combustion efficiency (MCE) and fire regime (flaming vs. smoldering) under nighttime conditions
  - Support WRF-Sfire fire weather model improvement

### Secondary Applications
- **Prescribed burn evaluation** (FY2018): Test deployments during controlled summer burns, potentially with Aerodyne mobile laboratory co-location
- **Oil and gas flare detection/validation**: Remote sensing package calibration and validation of satellite measurements for gas flaring
- **Satellite algorithm validation**: NESDIS collaboration for fire parameter retrieval algorithm refinement

### Operational Deployment Model
- CU mobile command center with UASOS drives to wildfire location (1-2 day mobilization)
- Operations next to Aerodyne mobile lab during FIREX for coordinated measurements
- Real-time coordination with incident management teams (IMTs) and FAA/DoI/USFS airspace control
- Hand-launched from any paved road; no runways required
- Nighttime operations over active fire areas (primary unique capability)

## Key Technical Decisions & Justifications

### Sensor Response Time Emphasis
- Recognized that standard industrial solid-state sensors (10-60 s response time) inadequate for UAS spatial resolution
- At 20 m/s cruise speed, 25-s delay = 0.5 km spatial blur
- Commitment to achieve <1 s response time through commercial modifications or custom instruments
- Addresses fundamental SWaP (size, weight, power) constraint while maintaining research quality

### Cost-Effectiveness Strategy
- Target $10-15K per in situ package vs. $100K+ for manned aircraft equivalents (10× reduction)
- Target $15-20K per remote package vs. equivalent standalone thermal/IR systems
- Achieved through miniaturization and commercial sensor integration with custom modifications
- Enables future operational deployments and network flying concepts

### Redundancy & Risk Mitigation
- Plan to build two complete instrument packages (in situ and remote) to survive UAS loss scenario
- Identified fallback UAS platforms (CU Tempest and Mistral) if SuperSwift purchase delayed or aircraft damaged
- Primary and secondary sensor candidates identified from project start; switching strategy if primary inadequate
- CSD internal funding identified for cost overrun contingency (typical overage risk flagged as moderate-high)

## Notable Details

### Institutional & Personnel Strengths
- **Team expertise**: Dr. Gao (proven instrument developer, three NOAA/NASA mission leads); Thornberry (instrument PI experience, NASA missions); Argrow (UAS expert, FAA regulatory relationships); Schranz (fire weather modeling)
- **Support infrastructure**: NOAA ESRL/CSD engineering staff (mechanical, electrical, software); University of Colorado IRISS Program for UAS operations
- **Coordination**: All key personnel located in Boulder, CO; monthly meetings + ad-hoc coordination

### FIREX Steering Committee Endorsement
- Strong written support from FIREX project members (Schwarz, Roberts, Warneke)
- Identified NightFOX as addressing "high-value goal" of FIREX; fills "critical need"
- Highlighted unique value: (1) geographic extent of nighttime emissions, (2) vertical dimension unavailable to mobile labs, (3) fire regime determination via MCE from CO2/CO, (4) near-source emission rates with high spatial resolution

### Regulatory & Airspace Strategy
- **FAA coordination**: Brian Argrow experienced in COA (Certificate of Waiver or Authorization) applications; early engagement planned
- **Multi-agency coordination**: DoI (Department of Interior), USFS (Forest Service), NOAA AOC (Aircraft Operations Center), incident management teams
- **BLOS operations**: UAS must secure Beyond Line of Sight waiver; CU currently has COAs for Pawnee Grasslands and Table Mountain (nighttime BLOS expansion in Year 2)
- **NEPA clearance**: Categorical Exclusion (CE) determination completed; no significant environmental impact identified

### Readiness Level Trajectory
| Component | Current | Target |
|-----------|---------|--------|
| UAS Platform | RL4 | RL8 |
| UAS Payload | RL3 | RL8 |
| UAS Observing System | RL2 | RL8 |
| UAS Observing Strategy | RL3 | RL8 |

Success criteria emphasize demonstration (favorable intercomparison with established instruments), operational performance (>2 hr flights, data recovery), and scientific utility (fire weather model improvement).

### Budget & Resource Plan
- **Total requested**: $488.9K (3 years)
- **In-kind contributions**: $559.8K (>100% match)

This is the official FY2016 NOAA SBIR Program solicitation document outlining the Phase I, Phase II, and Phase III structure for federally-funded R&D projects. It establishes eligibility requirements, proposal submission guidelines, evaluation criteria, and funding parameters for small business concerns seeking innovation research contracts with NOAA.

## Technical Approach
This document describes a three-phase federal funding model rather than proposing a specific technical approach:

**Phase I – Feasibility Research**
- Purpose: Determine scientific, technical, and commercial merit and feasibility
- Funding: Up to $120,000
- Duration: Up to 6 months
- Requirement: 2/3 of research/analytical effort must be performed by awardee
- Focus: Proving feasibility as prerequisite for Phase II

**Phase II – Research and Development**
- Purpose: Prototype development and comprehensive R&D
- Funding: Up to $400,000
- Duration: Up to 24 months
- Requirement: 1/2 of research/analytical effort must be performed by awardee
- Requirements: Detailed commercialization plan, possible presentation to NOAA SBIR Selection Committee

**Phase III – Commercialization**
- Purpose: Move prototype to viable product/service
- Funding: Non-SBIR sources (private sector, other government sources)
- Scope: Product development, production, services, or combination thereof

## Executive Summary
This is the official NOAA SBIR Phase II solicitation document for FY2019, announcing research topics and submission requirements for Phase II proposals. The solicitation invites Phase I awardees from NOAA2018-1 to submit comprehensive Phase II R&D proposals with awards up to $400,000 and 24-month performance periods. It covers program rules, eligibility requirements, evaluation criteria, and 27 specific research subtopics across four main technical areas.

## Document Structure & Content

This is a regulatory/administrative solicitation document rather than a proposal or technical report. It does not contain BST-specific information. Key sections include:

### Program Framework
- **Phase I**: Up to $120,000, 6-month feasibility research (already completed for Phase II applicants)
- **Phase II**: Up to $400,000, up to 24 months R&D/prototype development + 1-year commercialization activity period
- **Phase III**: Commercialization using non-SBIR funding sources
- Target award date: June 2019

### Eligibility Requirements
- Small business concern (SBC) status required (max 500 employees)

- Minimum 50% of research performed by awardee

- No venture capital operating companies, hedge funds, or private equity firm participation
- Only Phase I awardees from NOAA2018-1 may submit Phase II proposals

### Evaluation Criteria

- Commercial potential
- Available funds

- Importance to NOAA mission needs

The solicitation lists 27 specific research subtopics organized under 4 main topics:

## Document Metadata

## Executive Summary
This document is a USDA NIFA SBIR Phase I solicitation for FY2019 announcing research funding opportunities for small businesses to develop innovative agricultural and food-related technologies. The RFA provides 13 topic areas with specific research priorities, offering Phase I grants up to $100,000 for 8 months to demonstrate technical feasibility of proposed innovations with commercial potential.

## Document Purpose & Context
**This is NOT a Black Swift Technologies document.** It is a government Request for Applications (RFA) from the USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture (NIFA) announcing the FY2019 Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I program. The document outlines eligibility, funding, application procedures, and 13 research topic areas that small businesses can apply to.

## SBIR Phase I Program Structure

### Funding & Award Details
- **Phase I Award Amount:** Up to $100,000
- **Phase I Duration:** Normally not to exceed 8 months
- **Purpose:** Demonstrate technical feasibility of proposed innovation
- **Phase I Focus:** Research that proves scientific/technical feasibility as prerequisite to Phase II
- **Phase II:** Continuation of R&D toward commercialization (only open to Phase I recipients)
- **Phase III:** Commercialization phase funded by sources other than SBIR

### Eligibility & Requirements
- Small business applicants must be registered with SBA
- Projects must demonstrate:
  - High degree of technical risk (novel, unproven approach)
  - Potential for significant commercial impact and/or societal benefit
  - Good product-market fit (validated by customers)
  - Path to disrupt market or remove barriers to entry
- Applicants encouraged to contact National Program Leaders (NPLs) for each topic area before applying

## SBIR Phase I Topic Areas (13 Total)

### Topic Area 8.1: Forests and Related Resources
**NPL:** Dr. Charles Cleland (ccleland@nifa.usda.gov)

**Research Priorities:**
1. Growth and Yield - tree regeneration, pest/pathogen monitoring and control
2. Increasing Utility of Forest-Grown Material - lumber, pulp yield improvement
3. Reducing Ecological Damage by Forest Operations - erosion/water quality mitigation
4. Urban Forestry - greenways, parks, urban tree programs
5. Climate Change - ecosystem adaptation, carbon sequestration, decision support tools
6. Wildfire Management Technology - detection, fuel reduction, firefighter tools, communications
7. Sustainable Bioenergy and Value-Added Products - cellulosic biofuels (ethanol, biobutanol, jet fuel), wood composites, local energy conversion

**Key Guidance:** Biofuels from non-woody crops should go to Topic 8.8; genetic improvement of woody biomass feedstock goes here; applications strongly encouraged to contact NPL.

---

### Topic Area 8.2: Plant Production and Protection (Biology)
**NPL:** Dr. Robert Nowierski (rnowierski@nifa.usda.gov)

**Research Priorities:**
1. Plant Improvement - molecular biology, mutagenesis, genomics, tissue culture, embryogenesis to develop crops with improved quality, yield, agronomic traits
   - Sub-focus: Commercial floriculture production improvement
   - Sub-focus: Development of new crops
2. Pollinators and Crop Production - health and success of domesticated and natural pollinators
3. Plant Protection Against Abiotic/Biotic Stress
   - Sub-focus: Improved plant disease diagnostics (rapid, cost-effective identification)
   - Sub-focus: Bio-based approaches for pest/disease protection (organic and conventional crops)

**Key Guidance:** Transgenic crops should include regulatory/commercialization pathway; non-biological engineering technologies go to Topic 8.13; algae genetic improvement goes to Topic 8.7; woody biomass genetic improvement goes to Topic 8.1.

---

### Topic Area 8.3: Animal Production and Protection
**NPL:** Dr. Robert M. Smith (rsmith@nifa.usda.gov)

**Research Priorities:**
1. Improve Production Efficiency - fertility, feed efficiency, genomic applications
2. Improve Safety/Quality of End Products - pre-harvest technologies
3. Improve Animal Health and Well-being - rapid diagnostics, therapeutics, vaccines, biosecurity, traceability, alternatives to antibiotics
4. Improve Productivity in Modified/Alternative Production Systems - non-confinement, pasture-based, organic systems
5. Mitigate Impacts on Natural Environment - reduce greenhouse gas emissions, reduce phosphorus/nitrogen excretion (excluding manure management)

**Key Guidance:** Post-harvest technologies go to Topic 8.5; aquaculture species go to Topic 8.7.

---

### Topic Area 8.4: Conservation of Natural Resources
**NPL:** Dr. Karelyn Cruz (karelyn.cruz@nifa.usda.gov)

**Research Priorities:**
1. Water Quality and Quantity - farm/watershed-scale management, groundwater/surface water monitoring, nontraditional water sources (wastewater, agricultural return flows, produced water), improved irrigation technologies
2. Soil Health - physical/chemical/biological property measurement, microbial functional activity, soil remediation, erosion monitoring/prevention
3. Air Resources - monitor air quality, reduce agricultural air pollution (manure/livestock emissions)
4. Nutrient Management - macro/micronutrient practices to maximize productivity while minimizing environmental impact

**Key Guidance:** Animal manure/carcass waste for biofuels goes to Topic 8.8; food-borne hazard detection goes to Topic 8.5; should demonstrate innovation/non-redundancy with existing technologies; software/data-intensive applications encouraged.

---

### Topic Area 8.5: Food Science and Nutrition
**NPL:** Dr. Jodi Williams (jwilliams@nifa.usda.gov)

**Research Priorities:**
1. Food Safety - detection/mitigation of foodborne hazards (microorganisms, chemicals, toxins) during pre/post-harvest processing/distribution
2. Food Quality-Engineering - processing/packaging technologies/materials to reduce losses, maintain safety/quality, extend shelf life
3. Food Quality-Science - understand physical/biological/chemical interactions to develop food ingredients/formulations
4. Nutrition-Education - effective programs for educators/parents to foster healthy choices, combat childhood obesity
5. Nutrition-Science - improve functionality of foods, nutrients, bioactive components
6. Nutrition, Food Safety and Quality Data Tools - software tools to collect/analyze data for producers, consumers, retailers

**Key Guidance:** New detection tests should detect ≥1 cfu/25g without enrichment, allow large volume sampling; novelty screening methods need Federal agency letters of support; focus on functional foods/value-added products encouraged; avoid nutritional supplements (not food ingredients); include appropriate field expert collaborations.

---

### Topic Area 8.6: Rural and Community Development
**NPL:** Dr. Toija Riggins (toija.riggins@nifa.usda.gov)

**Research Priorities:**
1. Services, Information, and Managerial Systems - educational programs (virtual/apps/gaming), big data in planning, housing design, improved healthcare delivery (mobile/virtual), transportation/communication innovations, rural marketing
2. Technologies for Environmental Protection + Economic Development - renewable energy, big data for rural knowledge, food loss/waste reduction, energy conservation, wind/solar (not biofuels)
3. Reducing Rural Community Vulnerabilities - hazard mitigation (food-borne illness, contamination, drought, wildfire, hurricane, climate variability), preparation/forecast/warning/response/rebuilding
4. Technologies for Vulnerable Rural Populations - youth, elderly, disabled, veterans, low-income; human capital development, workforce development, food security/access
5. Employment and Income Generation - creative place-making, recreational economies, rural tourism, agri-tourism, e-commerce, off-farm value-added agriculture
6. Expanding Broadband Access - white space spectrum, increased bandwidth/speed/reach, adoption/diffusion initiatives, infrastructure investment

**Key Guidance:** Community letters of support highly encouraged; must assess environmental/socio-economic impacts; must provide evidence of rural market; identify commercialization barriers; on-farm production research goes to Topic 8.12; biofuel development goes to Topic 8.8.

---

### Topic Area 8.7: Aquaculture
**NPL:** Dr. Gene W. Kim (Gene.W.Kim@nifa.usda.gov)

**Research Priorities:**
1. Reproductive Efficiency - control of maturation/ovulation/fertilization, gamete/embryo storage, larval rearing, broodstock performance, cryopreservation, sex determination
2. Genetic Improvement - sex determination mechanisms, inheritance of commercial traits (growth, temperature tolerance, disease susceptibility), molecular biology/genomics integration, crossbreeding/hybridization
3. Integrated Aquatic Animal Health Management - stress management, genetic/environmental/nutritional components, predation control, vaccines/immunization, disease diagnostics, treatment methods
4. Improved Production Systems and Management Strategies - system design/models, water quality enhancement, effluent characterization/treatment, harvesting methods, recirculation efficiency
5. Algal Production Systems - species identification/improvement, bioreactor technology, biomass harvesting

**Key Guidance:** Aquaponics with current technology goes to Topic 8.12; new food products from aquaculture go to Topic 8.5; algae biomass conversion/products go to Topic 8.8.

---

### Topic Area 8.8: Biofuels and Biobased Products
**NPL:** Dr. Charles Cleland (ccleland@nifa.usda.gov)

**Research Priorities:**
1. New Non-food Biobased Products from New Industrial Crops - economically competitive, environmentally sustainable alternatives to petroleum products
2. New Processes for Industrial Products, Chemicals, or Biofuels - sustainable conversion of crops/agricultural residues into conventional/cellulosic/advanced biofuels or coproducts; minimize environmental impacts (energy, water, harmful byproducts, life cycle carbon)

**Key Guidance:** Forest biomass biofuels go to Topic 8.1; small farm bioenergy goes to Topic 8.12; genetic improvement of non-woody biomass feedstocks goes to Topic 8.2; woody biomass genetic improvement goes to Topic 8.1; engineering aspects of biomass handling go to Topic 8.13; algae genetic improvement goes to Topic 8.7; animal manure/carcass waste acceptable; microbial approaches must show credible path to industrially-relevant conversion rates/yields/titers.

---

### Topic Area 8.12: Small and Mid-Size Farms
**NPL:** Dr. Denis Ebodaghe (debodaghe@nifa.usda.gov)

**Research Priorities:**
1. New Agricultural Enterprises - small-scale specialty farm products (plant/animal), direct marketing (farmers markets, cooperatives), organic/natural foods, specialty products (free-range poultry, natural beef, medicinal herbs), value-added products
2. Development of New Marketing Strategies - assessment of consumer demand, product characteristics, packaging/processing innovations, efficient assembling/packing/advertising/shipping for local/regional/national/international markets
3. Farm Management - tools/skills for efficiency/profitability, farm safety, risk management tools, life-cycle assessment tools for resource efficiency and ecosystem services quantification, agro-tourism
4. On-Farm Natural Resources and Renewable Energy - energy efficiency, scaled technologies for wind/solar/geothermal energy
5. Urban Farming - rooftop/abandoned building/vacant lot farming; energy efficiency, environmental sustainability, profitability, appropriate crop selection

**Definition:** Small farms = <$250,000 annual sales; Mid-size farms = <$500,000 annual sales

**Key Guidance:** Conservation/renewable energy technologies go to Topic 8.4; aquaponics with technological improvements go to Topic 8.7; emphasize rural community benefits and dissemination to small farm community.

---

### Topic Area 8.13: Plant Production and Protection (Engineering)
**NPL:** Dr. Rachel Melnick (rmelnick@nifa.usda.gov)

## Executive Summary
This document is a compilation of abstracts from 31 Phase I SBIR awards granted by NOAA in FY 2024. The awards, each up to $175,000 for a six-month effort, were selected from 217 proposals to demonstrate the feasibility of innovative approaches to marine science, oceanography, weather, climate, and coastal resilience challenges. The awardees represent diverse small businesses developing solutions in oceanographic monitoring, weather prediction, aquaculture, water quality, greenhouse gas detection, and climate adaptation.

## Important Note
**Black Swift Technologies (BST) is NOT featured in this document.** This is a collection of abstracts from 31 competing small businesses that won NOAA Phase I awards. The document is included in BST's files likely for reference or market/competitive analysis purposes.

---

## Award Winners Summary (31 Total)

### Topic 9.1: Weather & Atmospheric Monitoring (6 awardees)
1. **American Veritas Engineering, LLC** - Low-cost dual-polarization Doppler phased array weather radar for NEXRAD network gap filling ($175,000)
2. **Aperi Computational Mechanics Consulting LLC** - Machine learning-enhanced meshfree methods for extreme event simulations, focusing on landslides ($174,835)
3. **Brandon Wong/Hyfi, LLC** - AI and wireless sensing for flood resilience in manufacturing hubs ($174,933)
4. **Care Weather Technologies, Inc.** - Veery nanosatellite-based scatterometer for ocean surface wind monitoring ($175,000)
5. **Gulf Wind Technology, LLC** - Hurricane wind turbine risk analysis method for insurance markets ($174,890)
6. **Trident Sensing LLC** - (Topic 9.1, award amount listed but no abstract provided in document)

### Topic 9.2: Coastal Resilience & Water Quality (6 awardees)
1. **AquaRealTime Inc** - OceanAlgaeTracker (OAT): Low-cost multispectral buoy for harmful algal bloom detection ($174,974)
2. **Quantitative BioSciences, Inc** - Nanobody-based biosensor for real-time cyanotoxin (microcystin) detection ($175,000)
3. **Rapid Radicals Technology** - Decentralized wastewater treatment integrated into municipal infrastructure ($174,536)
4. **RESILIFT, Inc.** - Residential Lifting Safety Sensor System (RLS3) for flood mitigation via house elevation ($175,000)
5. **Sediment** - Instagrain: Hand-held camera system with on-device machine learning for coastal sediment grain size measurement ($174,693)
6. **Tridentis Advanced Marine Vehicles LLC** - (Topic 9.2, award listed but abstract not provided)

### Topic 9.3: Ocean Observation & Marine Robotics (8 awardees)
1. **ARMADA Marine Robotics, Inc.** - Scalable uncrewed underwater sensing platforms with mobility and persistence ($174,798)

3. **IONICSCALE LLC** - Chip-scale mass analyzers for low-cost underwater mass spectrometers ($175,000)
4. **Live Advantage Bait LLC** - Hormone implant manufacturing optimization for fish spawning in aquaculture ($175,000)
5. **Loggerhead Instruments Inc.** - Pogo: Low-cost passive acoustic autonomous vehicle with AI for shallow-water deployment ($175,000)

## Key Technical Themes Across Awards

### Machine Learning & AI Integration
Multiple awardees emphasized ML/AI capabilities:
- ECCO Scientific: GPU-accelerated causal inference (100x speedup anticipated)
- MarineSitu: AI object detection and 3D reconstruction for coral surveys
- Carbon Solutions: ML for object detection, flux estimation, industry classification
- Sediment: On-device ML for sediment grain size measurement
- Hyfi: Transfer learning and dynamic thresholding for flood prediction

### Sensor Innovation & Miniaturization
- Care Weather: Miniaturized scatterometer in nanosatellite form factor
- IONICSCALE: Chip-scale mass spectrometers for underwater deployment
- AquaRealTime: Low-cost multispectral fluorescence buoy (~$3,000)
- Butterfly Photonics: Solar-powered, cloud-connected spectrometer network

### Autonomous/Uncrewed Systems
- ARMADA: Underwater platforms with dynamic persistence via current-riding
- Loggerhead: Pogo shallow-water acoustic vehicle with AI signal detection
- MarineSitu: Low-cost stereo-camera ROV with automated 3D reconstruction
- L.Garde: Solar sailcraft for cislunar space weather observation

### Climate Resilience & Adaptation
- Hyfi: Flood prediction for manufacturing hubs
- RESILIFT: House elevation technology for flood mitigation
- Rapid Radicals: Fast wastewater treatment during intense storms
- Multiple projects addressing coastal resilience and extreme weather

### Oceanographic & Environmental Monitoring
- AquaRealTime: Early HAB detection via algal classification
- Quantitative BioSciences: Real-time cyanotoxin detection
- BeamSea: Coral reef 3D imaging with fluorescence enhancement
- SUBTIDAL: Volumetric carbon flux measurement for CDR verification

## Document Metadata
- **Type:** Request for Applications (RFA) / Program Solicitation
- **Client/Agency:** USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture (NIFA)
- **Program/Solicitation:** SBIR/STTR Phase I Programs, Funding Opportunity Number USDA-NIFA-SBIR-009962
- **Date:** July 25, 2023 (modification date; original version predates this)
- **Fiscal Years Covered:** FY 2024 and FY 2025
- **BST Products/Systems Referenced:** None (this is a general solicitation document, not BST-specific)
- **Key Personnel:** Not applicable (this is a government RFA, not a BST proposal)

## Executive Summary
This is a USDA NIFA Request for Applications soliciting Phase I proposals for the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) and Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) programs. The RFA announces $13 million in SBIR and $2.5 million in STTR funding available for FY 2024, with similar funding anticipated for FY 2025. Phase I awards range from $125,000 to $181,500 and support proof-of-concept research with commercial potential across ten topic areas focused on agriculture, natural resources, and rural development.

## Program Overview & Key Details

### Funding Information
- **FY 2024 Application Deadline:** September 19, 2023, 5:00 P.M. Eastern Time
- **FY 2025 Application Deadline:** September 17, 2024, 5:00 P.M. Eastern Time (Anticipated)
- **FY 2024 Total Funding:** $13,000,000 (SBIR) + $2,500,000 (STTR) = $15,500,000
- **FY 2025 Total Funding:** $13,000,000 (SBIR) + $2,500,000 (STTR) = $15,500,000
- **Average Award Range:** $125,000 - $181,500
- **Grant Duration:** 8 months (SBIR) or 12 months (STTR) for Phase I

### Program Requirements & Structure
- **Three-Phase Structure:** Only Phase I RFA shown; Phase II and III follow after successful Phase I completion
- **Letter of Intent:** Not required
- **Cost Sharing:** No cost sharing or matching requirement specified in this document
- **TABA Option:** Technical and Business Assistance (TABA) available, increases maximum awards to $181,500 for most topics

### National Security Requirements (New)
The SBIR and STTR Extension Act of 2022 requires all FY 2024 Phase I awardees to complete foreign country of concern certifications prior to award, disclosing:
1. Ownership ties and involvement in foreign talent recruitment programs of countries of concern (China, North Korea, Russia, Iran, or others designated by State Department)
2. Joint ventures or subsidiaries in foreign countries of concern
3. Contractual/financial obligations with foreign state-owned enterprises
4. Foreign ownership status
5. Venture capital/institutional investment from entities with foreign affiliations
6. Technology licensing or IP sales to countries of concern (5-year lookback)
7. Foreign business entities or offshore entities related to the small business

## Ten Topic Areas for Phase I Applications

### Topic 8.1: Forests and Related Resources
- **Maximum Award:** $175,000 SBIR / $181,500 with TABA
- **Anticipated Awards:** 6
- **Grant Duration:** 8 months SBIR / 12 months STTR
- **Contact:** Dr. Diomides Zamora, Diomides.Zamora@usda.gov, (202) 590-6049
- **Research Priorities:**
  - Growth and yield improvements in forest trees, tissue culture, genetic manipulation
  - Increasing utility of forest-grown materials (lumber, pulp, specialty chemicals)
  - Reducing ecological damage from forest operations
  - Urban forestry (greenways, parks, invasive species management)
  - Climate change adaptation, carbon sequestration, decision support tools for forest managers
  - Wildfire detection and management technologies, fuel load reduction
  - Sustainable bioenergy and value-added products from forest resources (cellulosic biofuels, wood composites, local scale energy conversion)

### Topic 8.2: Plant Production and Protection (Biology)
- **Maximum Award:** $175,000 SBIR / $181,500 with TABA
- **Anticipated Awards:** 7
- **Grant Duration:** 8 months SBIR / 12 months STTR
- **Contact:** Dr. Christopher Philips, Christopher.Philips@usda.gov, (216) 390-4211
- **Research Priorities:**
  - Plant improvement through breeding, biotechnology, molecular biology, genomics, tissue culture
  - Pollinator health and crop production (varroa mites, bee diseases, integrated pest management)
  - Plant protection against abiotic/biotic stresses (drought, pathogens, arthropods, nematodes)
  - Disease diagnostics for rapid, cost-effective identification
  - Bio-based crop protection approaches
  - Decision aid systems for pest/disease management

### Topic 8.3: Animal Production and Protection
- **Maximum Award:** $175,000 SBIR / $181,500 with TABA
- **Anticipated Awards:** 7
- **Grant Duration:** 8 months SBIR / 12 months STTR
- **Contact:** Dr. Robert Smith, Robert.M.Smith@usda.gov, (202) 445-3468; Dr. Kathe Bjork, Kathe.E.Bjork@usda.gov, (816) 591-7415
- **Research Priorities:**
  - Improved production efficiency (fertility, feed efficiency, genomic application)
  - Safety and quality of animal products (pre-harvest technologies)
  - Animal health and well-being (rapid diagnostics, point-of-care testing, therapeutics, vaccines, biosecurity, traceability, alternatives to antibiotics)
  - Productivity in modified/alternative production systems (non-confinement, pasture-based, organic)
  - Climate change mitigation (greenhouse gas reduction, carbon sequestration, nutrient excretion reduction)

### Topic 8.4: Conservation of Natural Resources
- **Maximum Award:** $175,000 SBIR / $181,500 with TABA
- **Anticipated Awards:** 9
- **Grant Duration:** 8 months SBIR / 12 months STTR
- **Contact:** Dr. Sandeep Kumar, Sandeep.Kumar@usda.gov, (816) 832-7235
- **Research Priorities:**
  - Water quality and quantity (irrigation technologies, water source alternatives, groundwater monitoring)
  - Soil health (nutrient content, microbial activity, remediation, carbon storage, erosion prevention)
  - Air resources (air quality monitoring, pollution reduction from livestock, methane capture)
  - Nutrient management (extraction, utilization, macro/micronutrient optimization)
  - Circular agriculture principles using waste/byproducts
  - Software development and data-intensive technologies encouraged

### Topic 8.5: Food Science and Nutrition
- **Maximum Award:** $175,000 SBIR / $181,500 with TABA
- **Anticipated Awards:** 11 (highest number of awards)
- **Grant Duration:** 8 months SBIR / 12 months STTR
- **Contact:** Dr. Jodi Williams, Jodi.Williams@usda.gov, (202) 424-9722
- **Research Priorities:**
  - Food safety (detection/mitigation of foodborne hazards during pre/post-harvest)
  - Pathogen detection technologies (must detect ≥1 cfu/25g without enrichment where possible)
  - Food quality engineering (processing, packaging, sanitation technologies reducing waste while maintaining safety/quality/nutrition)
  - Food quality science (understanding food chemistry/biology to develop ingredients/formulations)
  - Nutrition education (programs promoting healthy choices, combating diet-related chronic disease)
  - Nutrition science (nutrient efficacy, personalized recommendations)
  - Nutrition security and food safety data tools (portable technologies for data collection/analysis)
